#10433. One UI 9.5 might bring Pixel 11’s ‘Rambler’ feature to Samsung Keyboard before Google’s

The Pixel 11 launched with one AI tool most people got on board with, called “Rambler.” It’s a transcription tool that overhauls and cleans up voice-to-text messages. Too bad this Rambler clone will only be available on Samsung Keyboard.

The Rambler-like keyboard feature was found in an internal test build of Samsung’s One UI 9.5, thanks to SamMobile. The settings include a feature named “Refine Voice Input,” and the description removes any doubt that it might be something other than a Rambler clone.

Clean up filler words, hesitations, and more. Text appears after you finish speaking.

Much like the Pixel 11’s Rambler tool, the final product is only available after you’re done dictating. The audio is then processed and turned into something coherent, devoid of the onomatopoeic words we often say when gathering our thoughts in a voice-to-text message. Unlike Rambler, though, it sounds like Samsung’s tool will automatically process your message instead of requiring an end action, like tapping the checkmark.

The biggest downside to this Rambler variant is that it falls under Samsung Keyboard’s feature set, not Google Keyboard. Even though One UI 9.5 is largely based on Android 17, Samsung still offers its own keyboard as the default experience.

This isn’t the first Google Keyboard feature Samsung Keyboard has emulated. Magic Cue was a massive addition to Samsung Galaxy devices, in the form of Now Nudge. It works wonderfully if you happen to like using Samsung Keyboard.

Google still hasn’t made Rambler available for any other Pixel devices besides the Pixel 11, and it’s the same story for Google Keyboard builds on Galaxy devices. Workarounds exist, but they aren’t official and shouldn’t be treated as such.

#10432. Technical Aspects of AI-Generated Video Assets for Web Design

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI-generated videos are becoming an important part of modern web design. Designers can now create animated backgrounds, product demonstrations, hero section videos, and visual storytelling elements without relying entirely on traditional video production. However, generating a visually appealing video is only one part of the process. To use AI-generated videos effectively on a website, developers and designers must also understand video formats, visual quality, file optimization, and website performance.

These technical factors directly influence how videos appear across devices, how quickly pages load, and how smoothly visitors interact with a website.

Video format selection is one of the first technical decisions when preparing AI-generated assets for the web. Different formats offer different levels of compression, compatibility, and visual quality.

For most websites, MP4 with H.264 remains a dependable default. WebM or AV1 can be offered as additional formats where appropriate.

Developers should also consider browser compatibility before selecting a format. Providing multiple sources allows browsers to choose a supported option.

AI-generated videos can sometimes contain visual inconsistencies, unnatural movements, distorted objects, or changes in lighting between frames. These issues become more noticeable when videos are displayed in large website sections.

Resolution is an important factor in maintaining visual quality. Common resolutions include:

However, higher resolution does not automatically mean better website performance or user experience. A 4K video may look impressive, but loading it unnecessarily can increase bandwidth consumption.

Frame rate also affects the viewing experience. Many website videos work well at 24 or 30 frames per second. Higher frame rates may be useful for fast-moving scenes, but they also increase the amount of visual data that needs to be processed.

Designers should review AI-generated footage before publishing it. Checking transitions, motion consistency, sharpness, and color accuracy helps prevent distracting visual problems.

Large video files can significantly increase website loading times. This is especially important for websites with video backgrounds, animated landing pages, and multiple visual sections.

Video optimization involves reducing file size without making the footage noticeably worse.

Some practical optimization techniques include:

Compression: Video compression reduces unnecessary data while preserving important visual details. Developers can use encoding tools such as FFmpeg to adjust bitrate, resolution, and codec settings.

Bitrate control: Bitrate determines how much data is used to represent each second of video. A higher bitrate generally preserves more detail but increases file size. Selecting an appropriate bitrate depends on the video's resolution, movement, and intended display size.

Trimming unnecessary footage: Website videos rarely need to be several minutes long. Removing unused sections helps reduce file size and keeps visual content focused.

Removing unnecessary audio: Background videos that do not require sound should be exported without an audio track. This reduces unnecessary data and supports a cleaner user experience.

Responsive video delivery: Websites should serve appropriately sized assets for different screen sizes. A smaller video may be sufficient for mobile users, while desktop visitors can receive a higher-resolution version.

These techniques help developers balance visual quality with efficient content delivery.

Even a well-optimized video can affect website performance if it is implemented incorrectly. Developers should consider how videos are loaded, displayed, and processed by browsers.

For example, automatically loading several large videos when a page opens can consume significant bandwidth. Instead, developers can use lazy loading strategies for videos that appear further down the page.

For background videos, the HTML video element offers several useful attributes:

Developers should also avoid autoplaying large videos unnecessarily. A static image can often provide a better experience on mobile devices or slower connections.

Performance testing tools such as Google Lighthouse and Chrome DevTools can help identify whether video assets are affecting loading speed, bandwidth usage, or rendering performance.

Technical optimization should not come at the expense of accessibility. Background videos should not distract users or make website content difficult to understand.

Developers should respect the prefers-reduced-motion media query, which allows users who prefer reduced animation to receive a less motion-intensive experience.

A suitable static background image can be displayed as an alternative.

Mobile compatibility is equally important. Smaller screens, limited data plans, and varying network conditions can make heavy video assets less practical. Testing videos on different devices and connection speeds helps identify potential problems before publication.

AI-generated video assets offer exciting possibilities for modern web design, but their successful implementation requires more than creative output. Choosing suitable video formats, maintaining consistent visual quality, compressing files, and considering website performance are all essential parts of the development process.

By combining thoughtful video production with responsive delivery, accessibility considerations, and performance testing, designers and developers can create engaging websites without compromising loading speed or usability. As AI video technology continues to evolve, understanding these technical fundamentals will remain valuable for building efficient and visually appealing web experiences.

#10431. SOTA OCR with Core ML and dots.ocr

Every year our hardware is a little more powerful, our models a little smarter for each parameter. In 2025, it is more feasible than ever to run truly competitive models on-device. dots.ocr, a 3B parameter OCR model from RedNote, surpasses Gemini 2.5 Pro in OmniDocBench, making OCR a truly no compromises on-device use case. Running models on-device is certainly appealing to developers: no smuggling API keys, zero cost, and no network required. However, if we want these models to run on-device, we need to be mindful of the limited compute and power budgets.

Enter the Neural Engine, Apple's custom AI accelerator that has shipped with every Apple device since 2017. This accelerator is designed for high performance whilst sipping battery power. Some of our testing has found the Neural Engine to be 12x more power efficient than CPU, and 4x more power efficient than GPU.

Whilst this all sounds very appealing, unfortunately the Neural Engine is only accessible through Core ML, Apple's closed source ML framework. Furthermore, even just converting a model from PyTorch to Core ML can present some challenges, and without a preconverted model or some knowledge of the sharp edges it can be arduous for developers. Luckily, Apple also offers MLX, a more modern and flexible ML framework that targets the GPU (not the Neural Engine), and can be used in conjunction with Core ML.

In this three part series, we will provide a reasoning trace of how we converted dots.ocr to run on-device, using a combination of CoreML and MLX. This process should be applicable to many other models, and we hope that this will help highlight the ideas and tools needed for developers looking to run their own models on-device.

To follow along, clone the repo. You'll need uv and hf installed to run the setup command:

If you just want to skip ahead and use the converted model, you can download it here.

Converting from PyTorch to CoreML is a two step process:

Whilst we do have a few knobs we can tweak for step 2, most of our control is in step 1, the graph we feed to coremltools.

Following the programmers litany of make it work, make it right, make it fast, we will first focus on getting the conversion working on GPU, in FLOAT32, and with static shapes. Once we have this working, we can dial down the precision and try and move to the Neural Engine.

Dots.OCR consists of two key components: A 1.2B parameter vision encoder trained from scratch, based on the NaViT architecture, and a Qwen2.5-1.5B backbone. We will be using CoreML to run the vision encoder, and MLX to run the LM backbone.

In order to convert a model, it's best to understand the structure and function before getting started. Looking at the original vision modelling file here, we can see that the vision encoder is similar to the QwenVL family. Like many vision encoders, the vision encoder for dots works on a patch basis, in this case 14x14 patches. The dots vision encoder is capable of processing videos and batches of images. This gives us an opportunity to simplify by only processing a single image at a time. This approach is frequent in on-device apps, where we convert a model that provides the essential functions and iterate if we want to process multiple images.

When kicking off the conversion process, it's best to start with a minimal viable model. This means removing any bells and whistles that are not strictly necessary for the model to function. In our case, dots has many different attention implementations available for both the vision encoder and the LM backbone. CoreML has lots of infrastructure oriented around the scaled_dot_product_attention operator, which they introduced in iOS 18. We can simplify the model by removing all of the other attention implementations and just focusing on simple sdpa (not the memory efficient variant) for now, commit here.

Once we've done this, we see a scary warning message when we load the model:

The model doesn't require Sliding Window Attention to function, so we can happily move on.

Using torch.jit.trace is still the most mature method for converting models to CoreML. We usually encapsulate this in a simple harness that allows you to modify the compute units used and the precision selected.

You can check out the initial harness here. If we run the following on the original code implementation:

We should bump into the first (of many) issues.

It is rare that a model will convert first time. Often, you will need to progressively make changes further and further down the execution graph until you reach the final node.

Luckily this error gives us quite a bit of information. We can look at the VisionRotaryEmbedding layer and see the following code:

Although torch.arange has a dtype argument, coremltools ignores this for arange and always outputs int32. We can simply add a cast after the arange to fix this issue, commit here.

After fixing this, running the conversion again leads us to our next issue at repeat_interleave:

Whilst this error is less informative, we only have a single call to repeat_interleave in our vision encoder:

cu_seqlens is used for masking variable length sequences in flash_attention_2. It's derived from the grid_thw tensor, which represents time, height and width. Since we are only processing a single image, we can simply remove this call, commit here.

Onto the next! This time, we get a more cryptic error:

This is again due to the masking logic to handle variable length sequences. Since we are only processing a single image (not a video or batch of images), we don't really need attention masking at all! Therefore, we can just use a mask of all True. To prepare ourselves for the Neural Engine conversion, we also switch from using a boolean mask to a float mask of all zeros, as the Neural Engine does not support bool tensors commit here

With all of this done, the model should now successfully convert to CoreML! However, when we run the model, we get the following error:

This reshape could be in multiple places! Luckily, we can use a previous warning message to help us track down the issue:

Most ML compilers do not like dynamic control flow. Luckily for us, as we are only processing a single image, we can simply remove the loop and process the single h, w pair, commit here.

And there we have it! If we run the conversion again, we should see that the model successfully converts and matches the original PyTorch precision:

Now that we've got the model working, let's evaluate the size and performance. The good news is the model is working, the bad news is that it's over 5GB! This is completely untenable for on device deployment! To benchmark the computation time, we can use the built in XCode tooling by calling:

which will launch the XCode inspector for the model. After clicking + Performance Report and launching a report on all compute devices, you should see something like the following:

Over a second for a single forward pass of the vision encoder! We have lots of more work.

In the second part of this series, we will work on the integration between CoreML and MLX, to run the full model on-device. In the third part, we will dive deep into the optimizations required to get this model running on the Neural Engine, including quantization and dynamic shapes.

#10429. Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.

By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.

The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers

The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better

One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers

One of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.

Scott Bessent, U.S. Treasury Secretary, admitted that the U.S. export controls cannot prevent all the restricted hardware from reaching China or other adversaries, which is why the country allegedly obtained millions of restricted AI GPUs from Nvidia. At the same time, he questioned the efficiency of Nvidia's internal controls. called for accountability at Nvidia, criticized the company's general counsel, but stressed that it was unclear whether Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang knew about the potentially illicit practices.

"I think that there is a lot of leakage in the system, and we are constantly working to close that down," in an interview with CNBC (via @siliconmemes). "One thing here is that the story has been thus far on Jensen Huang's personal foibles. The real story here should be, did Nvidia know their client? And was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies? And I think it is important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."

Bessent admitted that despite strict U.S. export controls that prohibit sales of advanced AI GPUs to China, considerable quantities of restricted hardware may still make their way to the country. However, the Treasury Secretary does not believe that the U.S. needs to introduce more stringent export restrictions or grant government agencies additional powers to prevent GPU smuggling. Instead, the authorities should properly enforce existing regulations, according to Bessent.

Bessent also criticized Nvidia's general counsel Timothy Teter, who reportedly contacted the U.S. Department of Commerce to inquire whether U.S. authorities were behind the detention of Megaspeed's Alice Wong in Singapore. However, the Treasury Secretary declined to speculate about potential consequences for Nvidia if it turned out that some of its executives knew that their customers acted as intermediaries for Chinese entities. Meanwhile, Bessent expressed confidence that Nvidia's board of directors would conduct a thorough investigation into the matter.

"But let us just say, if this was happening, then there were not robust controls at the company," Bessent said. "We do not know for a fact that Jensen Huang knew this. The [general council] seems to have been very involved here, probably should have done more oversight rather than the haranguing [government officials at the U.S. DoC]."

Bessent also revealed that the Departments of the Treasury, War, and State, as well as the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR), had supported the addition of Megaspeed to the Entity List for months. However, the authority to impose such export restrictions belongs to the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which reportedly stalled efforts to blacklist Megaspeed for months as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick feared that the move could worsen trade tensions with China.

#10427. Nintendo Switch 2 emulation on Android already has The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake up and running

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake now runs surprisingly well on phones after just a week of additional emulator development.

Legend of Zelda fans all over the world have been marveling at the Ocarina of Time remake’s visuals and enhanced gameplay systems on the Nintendo Switch 2, but the Android emulator scene has been busy marveling over something just a little bit different. One Redditor got the latest Zelda game running on Banana Native, a free emulator that’s available right now on GitHub.

Ocarina of Time remake performance has now reached a major milestone into the 30 FPS territory with frame gen, which means the game is actually running at around 15 FPS, but then scaled and interpolated using AI frame generation to appear like 30 FPS. Banana Native isn’t a traditional emulator, as it doesn’t emulate hardware. Rather, it uses the game’s own ARM64 code to run on the phone’s CPU. The Switch 2 is powered by a mobile Nvidia chip, after all.

The user is running the Ocarina of Time remake on a Poco F7 Ultra, which sports a two-generation-old Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite (Gen 4) processor. The latest phones that are coming out, like the Redmagic 12 Pro, run a 6th-gen Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme chip, so performance could be a lot better on a newer phone. Apps like Banana Native require specific driver support for each phone to run, and as I pointed out in my Redmagic 12 Pro review, platforms like Droid Deck and Game Native don’t yet have proper drivers for the newest chips.

9to5Google’s Damien Wilde recently reviewed Droid Deck, another native-type emulator that lets you legally play Steam games you own on your phone by just signing into your Steam account. It works extremely well on lots of Android phones and helps showcase just how far Android emulation has come this year.

#10426. BigCodeArena: Judging code generations end to end with code executions

Evaluating the quality of AI-generated code is notoriously difficult. While humans can easily spot whether a piece of code "looks right," determining if it actually works correctly, handles edge cases properly, and produces the intended result requires running and testing it. This is why today, we're thrilled to announce BigCodeArena -- the first human-in-the-loop platform for evaluating code generation models through execution.

Inspired by LMArena for LLMs, we've built a platform that allows anyone to compare code generation models side-by-side, but with a crucial difference: you can actually run the code and see what it produces. Just submit a coding task, watch two different models generate solutions, execute both programs, and vote on which model produced better results. The outcomes are organized into a leaderboard that displays the community's highest-rated models.

The field of code generation has long struggled with reliable evaluation methods. Traditional benchmarks like HumanEval test code against predefined test cases, but these represent only a tiny fraction of real-world programming tasks. Human evaluation platforms exist for general chatbots, but they fall short for code: reading raw source code and mentally simulating its execution is cognitively demanding and error-prone, especially for longer programs or complex UI applications.

You ask two AI models to build a responsive photo gallery website. Both generate code that looks syntactically correct. But which one is actually better? Without running the code, it's nearly impossible to tell. One might produce a beautiful, functional grid layout, while the other might have subtle bugs or poor styling that only become apparent when rendered in a browser.

This observation led us to a key insight: execution feedback is essential for humans to judge code quality reliably. That's exactly what BigCodeArena provides.

BigCodeArena extends the Chatbot Arena framework with powerful features specifically designed for code evaluation:

Every code snippet generated by models is automatically executed in isolated sandbox environments. Whether it's a Python script, a React web app, a PyGame game, or a C++ algorithm, you can see the actual output, not just the source code.

We currently support 10 languages (Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, HTML, C, C++, Java, Go, Rust, and Markdown) and 8 execution environments:

Unlike static code comparison, you can actually interact with the generated applications:

Real programming isn't one-and-done. BigCodeArena supports multi-turn interactions, allowing you to refine requirements, ask for features to be added, or request bug fixes -- just like working with a real coding assistant.

Since launching in February 2025, BigCodeArena has collected over 14,000 conversations from more than 500 unique users, with 4,700+ high-quality preference votes comparing 10 frontier LLMs.

Our users have explored remarkably diverse coding scenarios:

Python dominates with over 4,000 conversations, followed by JavaScript/TypeScript (3,359), HTML (1,601), and C++ (642). Among frameworks, direct Python interpreters lead usage (6,000 sessions), with React (2,729), Core Web (1,574), Streamlit (1,254), and PyGame (1,087) also seeing heavy use.

Most interactions are focused and efficient: 76% of conversations consist of just 2 turns (one request, one response), with a mean conversation length of 4.12 messages. However, the platform supports extended multi-turn debugging sessions when needed, with some conversations exceeding 10 turns as users refine complex applications.

From our 14K conversations, we filtered for high-quality pairwise comparisons: conversations with at least two turns and actual code execution. This yielded 4,731 voting samples, with each evaluated model receiving at least 700 votes. We aggregate these votes into Elo ratings using the Bradley-Terry model, which estimates the probability that one model beats another based on head-to-head comparisons.

To ensure robust rankings, we use 100 bootstrap resamples to construct 95% confidence intervals, so we can identify statistically significant performance differences between models.

We evaluate models under three settings to control for different factors:

Rankings remain remarkably consistent across all three settings, revealing clear performance tiers:

Top Tier: o3-mini and o1-mini consistently lead with the highest Elo ratings and tight confidence intervals. These models maintain top performance regardless of environment or language constraints, showing strong robustness across coding scenarios. Claude-3.5-Sonnet follows closely, particularly excelling when language is controlled.

Mid Tier: GPT-4o, o1, and Gemini-2.0-Pro/Flash form a competitive middle tier. GPT-4o shows some sensitivity to language matching, suggesting room for improvement in multilingual consistency.

Open Source Models: Qwen2.5 variants and Llama-3.3-70B lag behind frontier proprietary models, highlighting the performance gap that remains between leading closed and open models.

Figure: Overall win rate heatmaps (percentage of all pairwise comparisons won) of each model in the sessions across languages (left) and execution environments (right). For each category, we only keep models that appear in at least 3 conversation sessions.

Breaking down performance by programming language reveals interesting patterns:

Analyzing win rates by execution environment reveals how models handle different runtime contexts:

Robust Performers: o3-mini maintains consistently strong performance across React, Streamlit, Gradio, Core Web, and PyGame, demonstrating excellent environmental adaptability.

Stable but Selective: Claude-3.5-Sonnet and Gemini-2.0-Flash show generally stable performance but with reduced win rates in complex UI-heavy environments like Vue and Mermaid.

Framework-Specific Weaknesses: Qwen2.5 models, while competitive in some web frameworks (Core Web, React), struggle significantly with interactive and visualization-oriented environments like PyGame, Vue, and Mermaid. These environments often require precise handling of control flow, graphics rendering, and package dependencies.

These results highlight an important insight: aggregate Elo scores don't tell the whole story. Some models remain brittle under specific runtime constraints, and execution environment matters significantly for real-world deployment.

To advance research beyond crowdsourced evaluation, we're releasing two complementary benchmarks:

Building on our 4,700+ preference votes, BigCodeReward tests how well LLMs can judge code quality when acting as reward models. The key finding? Execution results dramatically improve judgment accuracy.

When models can see execution outputs (screenshots of web apps, game visuals, program logs), their alignment with human preferences increases substantially:

This reinforces our core thesis: you can't reliably judge code without running it -- and this applies to both humans and AI judges.

Inspired by Arena-Hard-Auto, AutoCodeArena provides a scalable way to evaluate new models without waiting for thousands of human votes. We carefully selected 600 representative prompts from our crowdsourced data, spanning all programming topics and frameworks.

Using automated LLM judges (Claude-3.7-Sonnet) to evaluate code execution results against a GPT-4.1 baseline, we can rapidly benchmark new models. This approach enables weekly leaderboard updates as new models are released.

Our automated benchmark evaluated 20+ cutting-edge models, including recently released systems:

Figure: Win rates of recent LLMs on AutoCodeArena against a GPT-4.1 baseline, judged by Claude-3.7-Sonnet. The 50% mark represents parity with GPT-4.1. Models above this line outperform the baseline, while those below underperform. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals. Note: Claude-3.7-Sonnet is excluded from rankings to avoid self-judgment bias, and GPT-4.1 appears only as the reference baseline.

The results show that while proprietary models maintain an edge, open-source models are rapidly closing the gap, with some approaching GPT-4.1-level performance.

BigCodeArena is open to everyone -- no account required! Visit https://huggingface.co/spaces/bigcode/arena to:

Whether you're building a React dashboard, creating a PyGame game, solving algorithmic challenges, or generating creative visualizations, BigCodeArena lets you see which models truly deliver.

Following the BigCode Project's commitment to transparency, we're releasing:

We envision BigCodeArena as a long-term project that evolves with the community:

Evaluating code isn't like evaluating text -- you need to run it, test it, and interact with it. BigCodeArena makes this possible at scale, combining human judgment with real execution feedback to create the most reliable evaluation platform for code generation models.

Join us in building the future of code generation evaluation. Write a prompt, compare the models, and vote for your favorite. Your feedback helps the entire community understand which models truly deliver on the promise of AI-assisted programming.

We'd love to hear your feedback! Connect with us on GitHub, join discussions in the Hugging Face Space community tab, or reach out to the BigCode Project at contact@bigcode-project.org.

We thank Leandro von Werra for his valuable suggestions and feedback on the blog.

#10425. Best AI Humanizer Tools Tested and Compared: 7 Options for Web Content

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The best AI humanizer for web content is the one that changes how a draft reads without changing what it says. If you need a specific tone, Humanize Max gives you four styles and three lengths in one run. If you already work in QuillBot or Grammarly, their humanizers fit the account you have. GPTinf, Humanize AI and Undetectable AI put an AI check next to the rewrite, and Ahrefs gives you quick variants of a short passage.

To compare them on equal terms, we ran the same 103-word AI-written release note through each tool in November 2026. It contains a product name, two image formats, a settings path and the word "must", so it shows whether a tool keeps the details a reader acts on. We also checked every feature, limit and price on the vendor's own pages on the same day.

A humanizer earns its place only if its output needs fewer fixes than the draft you started with, and these six checks show whether a tool will do that for your content.

Humanize Max is a single-purpose humanizer: you paste an AI draft, upload a file or load the built-in sample, choose a style and a length, and get a rewritten version in a few seconds. The four styles are Academic, Casual, Creative and Formal, and the three lengths are Shorten, Standard and Expand, so you can turn a stiff feature description into casual blog copy and trim it in the same run.

The result highlights every phrase it changed, which makes it quick to check whether a product name or a settings path came through. If the rewrite doesn't land, Run it again produces a different version of the whole text. At the time of writing, it takes up to 2,000 words per run and works without an account.

Pricing: Plans and limits are still being finalized, so check the site for current terms.

Best for: Rewriting AI drafts of blog posts, product pages and emails into a specific tone.

QuillBot's AI Humanizer sits next to its paraphraser, grammar checker and AI detector, which makes it a natural pick if you already use QuillBot for rewording. Basic mode is free for up to 125 words per run, while Advanced mode, which rewrites more deeply, comes with Premium (the pricing page also lists three Advanced uses on the free plan). In our test, it asked us to create a free account before it showed the first result.

Premium removes the word limit and adds Freeze words, which keeps the terms you choose unchanged, along with tone insights, a history of past runs and a Chrome extension that humanizes text inside ChatGPT and Gemini.

Pricing: Basic mode is free. Premium is listed at $8.33 a month, billed annually.

Best for: Quick fixes to a paragraph or two for writers who already use QuillBot.

GPTinf is a writing toolkit built around its humanizer, with an AI detector, plagiarism checker, grammar checker, paraphraser and readability checker on the same site. The humanizer has two modes, Standard and Academic, and takes pasted text or a PDF, Word or plain-text file. File-to-File mode returns the humanized document in its original format, so a long brief keeps its layout.

Custom Style lets you paste 150 to 1,200 words of your own writing, and later runs are shaped to match it, with no account needed. After each run, an AI-likelihood estimate appears under the output, so you can see whether a draft needs another pass. Treat that number as a probability, not proof of who wrote the text.

Pricing: A free plan is available. Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $24.99 and Unlimited at $59.99.

Best for: Freelancers and content teams that want to rewrite and check drafts without switching tools.

Grammarly's AI Humanizer comes in two layers. The tool on its web page is free, works without an account and offers basic humanization of pasted text or an uploaded document. A free Grammarly account adds the Humanizer agent, with four preset styles, a custom voice built from a writing sample, and support for English, Spanish, French, German, Portuguese and Italian.

Grammarly says the humanizer focuses on clarity and readability rather than on AI detectors, which matches how most web teams use these tools. If you need to show how a piece was written, Grammarly Authorship shows which parts came from AI, which came from online sources and which you wrote yourself. The basic tool's word counter allows up to 1,500 words per run.

Pricing: The basic humanizer is free. Grammarly Pro is listed at $12 on the plans page, which doesn't state the billing period.

Best for: Teams that already write in Grammarly and want one voice across documents.

Humanize AI is built for people who want to tune the output. Without an account you get the Free tone, a Rewrite level slider with three stops (Quality, Balanced and Max) and Custom style, which learns your voice from 150 to 1,200 words of samples. A free account opens eight more modes, including Formal, Informal, Academic, Expand and Shorten, and on desktop a Writing level menu sets how plain or dense the result reads.

View changes highlights every edit, and File-to-File accepts PDF, DOCX, TXT and MD documents and returns them in the same format. Paid plans also include a public API that supports the same styles and rewrite levels as the web app, so a developer can add a humanizing step to a CMS or publishing pipeline.

Pricing: Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (10,000 words), with Standard at $19.99 and Unlimited at $59.99. Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Teams that need precise tone control or want to humanize text through an API.

Undetectable AI keeps its humanizer simple: one text box, one button and no style or length settings. Its free allowance works differently from the others, with 1,000 words in total before you need an account and another 1,000 once you create a free one.

Under the output, a Check for AI button runs a detection check on the result, and the same site has a separate AI detector and plagiarism checker. Its FAQ says pasted text isn't published or shared but doesn't say whether it's stored, so keep confidential details out of the drafts you run through it.

Pricing: Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $25 (25,000 words) and Unlimited at $59 (1,000,000 words). Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Trying a humanizer on a full-length draft before you commit to an account.

Ahrefs, best known for its SEO platform, offers a free AI Text Humanizer among its writing tools. You paste up to 2,048 characters, choose one, three or five variants, and pick the version that reads best. It ran without an account in our test.

Variants are the useful part. For a hero headline, a meta description or a product blurb, comparing three rewrites side by side is faster than prompting a chatbot three times, and you can export all results as a text file. The character limit, which fits a few short paragraphs, rules it out for full articles.

Best for: Short marketing copy where you want several options to choose from.

The best AI humanizer tool for a documentation team isn't the one a growth marketer needs, so match the tool to the content in front of you.

There isn't one winner, because these tools solve different problems. The quickest way to decide is to run a paragraph from your own work, ideally one with a product name, a number and an instruction, through two or three of the tools above, and keep the one whose output you'd publish with the fewest fixes.

Google's guidance on using generative AI content is about value rather than the tool: mass-producing pages that add nothing for readers can count as scaled content abuse. A humanizer changes phrasing, not usefulness, so the same rules apply. Google also recommends fact-checking AI-generated titles, meta descriptions and image alt text before you publish.

The best humanizer for your team is the one whose controls match your content: tone presets for blog posts, variants for short copy, change highlighting for docs and a custom voice for marketing. Run one of your own paragraphs through two or three tools from this list, then read every highlighted change, especially names, numbers and words like "must", before anything goes live.

#10423. Google Pixel Tag Initial Review: The gold standard for Find Hub trackers, whatever that’s worth

Google’s Find Hub had a tumultuous launch for its performance, but also for a lack of clear direction in hardware. Over two years later, that’s finally arriving in the Google Pixel Tag which, even just a few days in, is the obvious gold standard in the race to build an AirTag for Android devices.

Google Pixel Tag is now available for purchase at the Google Store and Amazon.

There are plenty of really good Android Find Hub trackers on the market. Pebblebee and Chipolo have been long-standing examples of how to build good dual-network trackers that work on both Android and iOS, while Motorola’s Moto Tag series has delivered two Android-only trackers that deliver better performance and more focused features. But even with the Moto Tag, there’s a clear compromise. Features like the ability to ring your phone are tied to a separate app and, in turn, have some inherent clunkiness.

Pixel Tag is the device that finally brings it all together, and it’s brilliant so far.

I’ve only had the Pixel Tag for a week and, frankly, it’s impossible to properly review a tracker in that time. There are only so many ways to artificially test out how a tracker works, as most cases where you’ll find value in this sort of product can only occur in real life.

So, with that said, let’s focus on the fundamentals.

Google Pixel Tag pairs to your Android phone just like any other Find Hub tracker – though much faster compared to some others I’ve tested – but the differences are obvious towards the end of that process. The final screen shows options for setting ringer volume and an option to set up “Ring this phone.”

Those new features are what make the Pixel Tag so good, and so appealing compared to all of the competition. A quick double-tap on the Tag’s button rings whichever phone you connected it to, assuming it’s in range, and it works pretty reliably. You can also set up “left behind” alerts (now available on other Find Hub trackers too) for when the phone leaves the tracker behind – you can set up exclusion zones such as your home or work address.

One of my favorite examples of the added polish from Google is the ability to adjust the ringer volume on the page where you actually want to ring the tracker. In a crowded but quiet space where you know the tracker is close by, being able to quickly set the volume to low is a great addition. In my book, it’s the reason to buy Pixel Tag over any other Android tracker.

UWB, of course, only makes up-close finding all the better. I found this decently reliable on my Pixel 11 Pro XL, but it is a little bit frustrating that the directional cues vanish within about 10-12 feet. Fine for a backpack or something like that, potentially a problem if your Tag is attached to a set of keys.

On that note, my biggest hardware complaint is that Google took the Apple route of having no built-in mounting mechanism. The super thin and light hardware of Pixel Tag is wonderful, don’t get me wrong, but being forced to buy a separate accessory just to attach it to my bag is frustrating! One of Google’s partners, Bellroy, built one of these accessories and it’s simple enough – a silicone case with a rope. I wish I didn’t need it, but it works, and at least you get two of them in a pack for $25.

The hardware itself is pretty good across the board, really, with the battery door also being slightly easier to open compared to the Moto Tag. Inside is a standard CR2032 battery that Google says will last “over one year.” I’d personally still prefer a rechargeable battery with USB-C or wireless charging, but this is a good enough solution given the amount of time the battery lasts – hopefully Google’s claim lives up.

Rounding out some of the key aspects here, it’s worth saying that the built-in speaker is more than loud enough at its highest setting, but the value for me so far has really come in that the low setting is actually low enough to not be a nuisance. I do find it a little strange that there’s no visual indication of where the Tag’s button is, but the packaging and app both do a good enough job of letting you know.

I really just wish it would have a rechargeable battery, preferably via USB-C. It would have been the only tracker on the market to support UWB and be rechargeable.

I’m looking forward to seeing how Pixel Tag performs as the travel season spins back up, so stay tuned for a later long-term review of Google’s tracker in the coming months. Initial impressions, though, are solid. Sound off in the comments below if you have any questions around Pixel Tag, I’ll answer everything I can!

Google Pixel Tag is now available at the Google Store and Amazon.

The Made by Google 2026 lineup is finally complete with tomorrow’s retail launch of the Pixel Tag. You can find our review here, while there are some additional details about the device since the August announcement.

The Pixel Tag is the first Find Hub tracker with NFC. Google did not mention this connectivity specification in August, with Near Field Communication letting you tap the tracker to the back of your phone to immediately open device settings. The NFC area on the Pixel Tag is below the circular battery door, which you hold down and twist counterclockwise to open.

On Android 17 QPR2, tapping immediately opens the details page. On QPR1, you first get a system notification that you need to click. NFC joins Bluetooth 6.0 with Channel Sounding and Ultra Wideband (UWB).

It wraps everything but the face of the Pixel Tag (and its speaker cutout), while giving you a hole in the corner and color-matching cord.

Getting your hands on fast NVMe storage for your PC or laptop has become extremely challenging. That said, the Samsung 990 SSD is currently available at a discounted price of $189.99, against its original list price of $229.99 on Amazon. Although the $40 saving might not seem that impressive, deals on high-performance internal SSDs are becoming harder to come by amid the ongoing NAND and DRAM crisis. If you've been holding off on a storage upgrade, this could be a good opportunity to pick up a reliable, high-speed SSD.

The Samsung 990 is a PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD that uses Samsung's latest V9 QLC NAND flash memory and a DRAM-less controller. It was introduced earlier this year with MSRPs of $269.99 for the 1TB model and $529.99 for the 2TB model. The 1TB model offers sequential read and write speeds of up to 7,150 MB/s and 6,450 MB/s, making it an excellent option for everyday computing, gaming, and handling large files. Samsung rates the drive for up to 400TB of written data, although it offers just three years of warranty. It features a single-sided M.2 2280 design, which should make it compatible with a wide range of desktop motherboards, laptops, and even mini-PCs.

Samsung's 990 is rated for read speeds of up to 7,150 MB/s and write speeds of up to 6,450 MB/s, offering plenty of bandwidth for modern games, large files, and everyday applications.

In our testing of the 2TB variant, we found that the Samsung 990 delivers reasonably good all-around performance, particularly for gaming and everyday applications. It offered similar performance to the Samsung 990 EVO Plus in some tests. However, it fell behind competing drives such as the Crucial P310 and WD Blue SN5100 in others, particularly during file transfers. One of its biggest advantages is its large write cache, which allows it to maintain speeds of nearly 6,100 MB/s for more than 57 seconds before performance drops once the cache is exhausted. Its power efficiency may not be the best, but overall it is a competent budget PCIe 4.0 SSD.

For anyone upgrading from an older SATA SSD or a traditional hard drive, the Samsung 990 should offer a noticeable improvement in boot times, application loading, and overall system responsiveness. At its current price of $189.99, it is also a suitable option for expanding game storage without spending a fortune.

Google Fi Wireless is rolling out a big update today with the return of network switching thanks to a “secondary” partner.

Google Fi is now bringing back a second partner as part of its new “super network.” Most users will be on the “Primary network,” but Google Fi will automatically switch users to the “Secondary network” if it meaningfully improves performance with so-called “smart thresholds” for doing so. Google is not naming the second network today, but did share that Ultra Wideband is supported. Officially, you are switching between “two of America’s fastest 5G networks.”

The Google Fi app gains a “Your super network” card in the Home tab that shows whether you’re connected to the Primary or Secondary network. “See activity” lets you view switching history and when it last occurred. Google will also note if you’re in range of W+ networks.

Google today is also expanding its Wi-Fi Auto Connect+ network beyond Pixel phones to select Samsung Galaxy (S23, Fold/Flip 5, and newer) and modern Motorola phones. The final update today sees the companion app gain “Ask Fi.” This AI-powered chat is meant to quickly provide answers and guided troubleshooting for common issues. You can request human support with seamless handoff that keeps the chat context.

#10418. From User Feedback to a Better Prompt: 4 Tools Tested in TypeScript

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

When an LLM app gives a wrong answer, nothing in your logs shows it. The request returns 200, the JSON is valid, and no exception fires. Usually the user is the only one who notices. A thumbs-down button records that moment, on the exact trace that went wrong, while the user still remembers why.

That button is easy to add. The hard part is what comes after: turning the thumbs-down into a reviewed test case, a judge score, and a better prompt.

We ran that loop in TypeScript in four tools: LangSmith, Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore. All four handled the first four steps, which are user feedback, reviewer comments, a dataset and an LLM judge. Only AcruxCore rewrote the prompt from TypeScript. On 15 support tickets that no tool had seen, the rewritten prompt routed 13 correctly, against 7 for the original.

Our test app is a support-ticket router. It reads a ticket and returns JSON with a category (account, billing, bug or feature_request) and a priority (P0, P1 or P2). The first version of the prompt describes only the output format:

The support team has a policy that this prompt never states. Sign-in problems are always account. A customer who can't use the product at all is P0. Any billing error is P1, even when the customer says there is no rush. Feature requests are P2, however angry the customer sounds.

Without that policy, the model guesses priority from the customer's tone. Here are three real replies from the first version:

Every reply is valid JSON, so no schema check catches the mistake. A person has to read the reply and say it is wrong. The loop in this article takes that judgement and turns it into a better prompt.

All four tools cover evaluation. We compared the self-hosted ones on tracing in Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent, and on prompt registries in Prompt Management in TypeScript. For a broader comparison of self-hosted options, see this LangSmith alternatives roundup. This article covers the feedback loop only.

We wrote 30 tickets. Fifteen are the "production traffic" that each tool's app processed. The other 15 are a holdout set. No tool saw them, and we used them only for the final before-and-after check.

Each tool ran the same sequence from one TypeScript script:

The reviewer comments follow one template, so the wording is identical in every tool:

The comments name one rule each. The full policy appears nowhere in the data any tool received.

The app model isn't fully deterministic at temperature 0. Each tool's run got between 6 and 8 of the 15 traffic tickets right, so the tools received 7 to 9 thumbs-down each. The holdout check below repeats every measurement three times.

All four tools accept feedback on a trace from TypeScript. They differ in how a second person, the reviewer, adds the correct answer.

LangSmith stores both as feedback on a run. The thumbs-down runs go into an annotation queue, where a reviewer adds feedback with a comment:

Langfuse stores both as scores. An annotation queue needs a score config first:

Phoenix stores both as span annotations. The reviewer's comment goes in explanation:

Phoenix stores spans asynchronously. Our first run annotated a span before Phoenix had stored it, and the API returned a 404. The script now waits until all 15 spans are visible.

AcruxCore stores both as feedback rows on the trace. The source field separates the end user from the reviewer:

This is the first step where the code differs a lot. Each tool can make a dataset, but only one builds it from feedback in one call.

In LangSmith, a run query finds the thumbs-down runs. Then createExamples copies them into a dataset. You decide where the reviewer's comment goes. We put it in the reference output:

LangSmith can also do this without code. An automation rule in the UI can add runs that match a filter to a dataset.

In Langfuse, the scores API finds the thumbs-down traces. Two details cost us a run each. A boolean score is filtered with value: "false", not 0. And the trace ID is returned only when you ask for the subject field group:

In Phoenix, getSpans can't filter by annotation. So the script lists the app's spans, reads their annotations, and keeps the ones with a thumbs-down. Then createDataset takes the examples. We kept the source span ID in the metadata.

In AcruxCore, buildFromFeedback takes the reviewer's feedback IDs. Each comment becomes that example's grading criteria, and the input comes from the variables captured on the trace:

Each tool scored the first version of the prompt on its own dataset. The judge read the reviewer's comment and the router's reply, and returned 1 for a match and 0 for a mismatch.

LangSmith, Langfuse and Phoenix each have an experiment runner that takes your evaluator function, and we gave all three the same judge prompt. AcruxCore grades with its built-in judge inside the optimize run. All four used the same judge model.

The first version fails almost every reviewed case. That is expected, because these are the cases users marked wrong. A score of 1 means the app model got that case right on the second call, or the judge accepted a wrong reply. We didn't check which.

The judge can also run without your code. Besides the in-code evaluator we used, Langfuse has a managed LLM-as-a-judge that runs on production traces and on experiments, with your own judge prompt. LangSmith has online evaluators, which you set up in its UI, for the same job.

An optimizer reads the failing cases and the reviewer comments, writes new versions of the prompt, and scores each one with the judge. This is the step that turns feedback into a better prompt, and it's where the four tools differ most.

LangSmith's API reference lists an optimize prompt job (POST /api/v1/repos/optimize-job). It takes a prompt name, a dataset name, evaluator IDs and an algorithm, promptim or demo. No method in the TypeScript SDK wraps it, so we called it with fetch. We gave it a code evaluator that checks the reply against the reviewer's correct answer.

The job was accepted and reported successful about ten seconds later. It ran no experiment on the dataset. With auto_commit set to true, it added no new commit to the prompt. We found no guide for this endpoint, so we may have configured it wrongly, but the job record and its logs gave no error to act on.

LangSmith's documented route to prompt optimization is promptim, which its README calls an experimental library. It is a Python package with a CLI, and it can add a human review step through LangSmith annotation queues.

Langfuse has no optimizer. Its blog shows a workflow with Claude Code agent skills that reads Langfuse data and edits the prompt. That workflow runs in a coding agent, not in your app's code.

Phoenix's Optimize Prompts Automatically tutorial uses Arize's prompt-learning package, which you clone from GitHub and install with pip. The Phoenix TypeScript client has no optimizer export, and the tutorial runs outside Phoenix. Arize's commercial platform, Arize AX, has prompt optimization built in.

For Python teams, there are more options: Opik's Agent Optimizer and DSPy both rewrite prompts from a dataset and a metric. This article covers TypeScript.

Its optimize run takes the dataset and drafts three rewrites of the production prompt. It runs each rewrite and the current production version on every example, and the judge grades all of them:

The three rewrites tied, so we took candidate A. Its rationale: "Added explicit priority rules for each category and clarified that access-blocking issues are P0, billing errors are P1, and feature requests are P2, overriding tone/urgency." The Improve a prompt from feedback guide covers the dashboard version of this step.

A rewrite that passes the cases it was built from can still fail on new tickets. So we ran both prompts on the 15 holdout tickets, three times each, outside every tool. The script calls the model directly and checks the category and the priority against the expected answer. No judge is involved.

Both come from one line in the rewrite: "P1 for bugs without workaround." That rule isn't in the team's policy, and no reviewer wrote it. The optimizer made it up to explain the examples it had. There was also no outage in the traffic set's thumbs-down cases, because the first version routed that one correctly. So no comment ever said that a full outage is P0.

The optimizer learns only from what users marked wrong. Anything they never marked stays a guess, and the rationale won't tell you which rules are guesses. Read the rewritten prompt before you promote it.

In LangSmith, Langfuse and Phoenix, shipping a new version is a tag or label move. We showed those calls in the prompt-management article. Here there was no rewrite to ship, so the step didn't apply.

In AcruxCore, promotion commits the candidate as a new prompt version and moves the production alias to it. Nothing else moves:

The app renders production on every call, so the next ticket used version 2 without a deploy.

Use LangSmith if your team already works in it and writes Python. Feedback, queues, datasets and experiments all work from TypeScript, and promptim covers optimization from Python.

Use Langfuse if you want a managed judge that runs on live traces with your own prompt. Plan to write the dataset glue code and the rewrite step yourself.

Use Phoenix if you already trace with OpenTelemetry and annotate spans. Plan to move to Python, or to Arize AX, for optimization.

Use AcruxCore if you want all six steps from TypeScript in one tool, including the rewrite. Keep a human on the promote button.

#10417. Nemotron-Personas-India: Synthesized Data for Sovereign AI

A compound AI approach to Indian personas grounded in real-world distributions

India represents one of the world's largest AI opportunities — with over 700 million internet users, a multitude of languages, and a rapidly growing developer ecosystem. Yet, most open datasets reflect Western norms and English-only contexts, creating a data gap that limits AI adoption in India's multilingual, multi-script environment.

Built with NeMo Data Designer, NVIDIA's enterprise-grade synthetic data generation microservice, Nemotron-Personas-India extends our global collection of Sovereign AI datasets. It builds on the success of our US and Japan persona datasets and includes new features designed specifically for India's culturally rich landscape.

This dataset integrates seamlessly with Nemotron models and other open-source LLMs, making it easy to fine-tune AI systems for Indian use cases—from multilingual chatbots to culturally-grounded specialized copilots.

This release complements our earlier suite of Hindi evaluation datasets — including ChatRAG-Hi, IFEval-Hi, MT-Bench-Hi, GSM8K-Hi, and BFCL-Hi — supporting a complete pipeline from synthetic data generation to rigorous model evaluation for Indian AI systems.

Produced using NeMo Data Designer, NVIDIA's microservice for synthetic data generation. This compound AI system enables generation with complex Jinja templating, Pydantic validation, structured outputs, automated retries, and supports multiple generation backends – the necessary tooling to scale a synthetic dataset of this size. We also leveraged the following models:

This dataset was aligned to India’s official demographic distributions from the 2011 Census and expanded to include attributes essential for trustworthy AI training:

No real names. No re-identification risk.

Nemotron‑Personas‑India is designed for developers building Sovereign AI systems for the Indian market, as well as global teams looking to adapt models to India’s unique linguistic, cultural, and social context.

Most open datasets today reflect English-speaking, Western norms—limiting AI performance in India’s multilingual, multi-script, and demographically complex environments.

India's 1.4 billion people speak hundreds of languages and live across vast cultural, economic, and geographic divides. India's National AI Portal estimates over 7,000 AI startups and research institutions are working to build locally relevant AI systems, and the Digital India initiative and government programs like IndiaAI are accelerating adoption.

But progress is constrained by a fundamental gap: high-quality, culturally grounded training data that reflects India's demographic reality. Without representative datasets, AI systems struggle with code-switching between English and Hindi, fail to understand regional occupational categories, and miss cultural context essential for trust and adoption.

The dataset improves diversity of synthetically-generated data, mitigates biases, and prevents model collapse (degradation caused by uncurated training on another model's outputs) by reflecting India's real geographic and demographic distributions.

Nemotron-Personas-India supports Indian model builders in developing Sovereign AI systems that incorporate important region-specific demographics and cultural context.

Want to build AI systems that understand India's culture, languages, and people?

Download it. Fine-tune it. Build AI that understands India. If you’re ready to go deeper, an extended version of Nemotron-Personas-India (which includes e.g., first/last names, religion, and synthetic addresses) is available in NeMo Data Designer.

Wyze is today launching its new “Lever Lock,” a smart lock for your front door that has a year of battery life and fast fingerprint recognition, all for an affordable price tag.

Available starting today, the Wyze Level Lock is not your typical deadbolt smart lock. #10415. Get your VLM running in 3 simple steps on Intel CPUs

With the growing capability of large language models (LLMs), a new class of models has emerged: Vision Language Models (VLMs). These models can analyze images and videos to describe scenes, create captions, and answer questions about visual content.

Small models like SmolVLM are built for low-resource consumption, but they can be further optimized. In this blog post we will see how to optimize your model, to lower memory usage and speedup inference, making it more efficient for deployment on devices with limited resources.

To follow this tutorial, you need to install optimum and openvino, which you can do with:

First, you will need to convert your model to the OpenVINO IR. There are multiple options to do it:

Now it’s time to optimize your model. Quantization reduces the precision of the model weights and/or activations, leading to smaller, faster models. Essentially, it's a way to map values from a high-precision data type, such as 32-bit floating-point numbers (FP32), to a lower-precision format, typically 8-bit integers (INT8). While this process offers several key benefits, it can also impact in a potential loss of accuracy.

Optimum supports two main post-training quantization methods:

Weight-only quantization means that only the weights are quantized but activations remain in their original precisions. As a result, the model becomes smaller and more memory-efficient, improving loading times. But since activations are not quantized, inference speed gains are limited. Weight-only quantization is a simple first step since it usually doesn’t result in significant accuracy degradation.

Since OpenVINO 2024.3, if the model's weight have been quantized, the corresponding activations will also be quantized at runtime, leading to additional speedup depending on the device.

In order to run it, you will need to create a quantization configuration OVWeightQuantizationConfig as follows:

With Static Quantization, both weights and activations are quantized before inference. To achieve the best estimate for the activation quantization parameters, we perform a calibration step. During this step, a small representative dataset is fed through the model. In our case, we will use 50 samples of the contextual dataset and will apply static quantization on the vision encoder while weight-only quantization will be applied on the rest of the model. Experiments show that applying static quantization on the vision encoder provides a noticeable performance improvement without significant accuracy degradation. Since the vision encoder is called only once per generation, the overall performance gain from applying static quantization on this component is lower than the gain achieved by optimizing more frequently used components like the language model. Nevertheless, this approach can be beneficial in certain scenarios. For example, when short answers are needed, especially with multiple images as input.

Quantizing activations adds small errors that can build up and affect accuracy, so careful testing afterward is important. More information and examples can be found in our documentation.

You can now run inference with your quantized model:

If you have a recent Intel laptop, Intel AI PC, or Intel discrete GPU, you can load the model on GPU by adding device="gpu" when loading your model:

We also created a space so you can play with the original model and its quantized variants obtained by respectively applying weight-only quantization and mixed quantization. This demo runs on 4th Generation Intel Xeon (Sapphire Rapids) processors.

To reproduce our results, check out our notebook.

We ran a benchmark to compare the performance of the PyTorch, OpenVINO, and OpenVINO 8-bit WOQ versions of the original model. The goal was to evaluate the impact of weight-only quantization on latency and throughput on Intel CPU hardware. For this test, we used a single image as input.

We measured the following metrics to evaluate the model's performance:

This benchmark demonstrates how small, optimized multimodal models, like SmolVLM2-256M, perform on Intel CPUs across different configurations. According to the tests, the PyTorch version shows high latency, with a time to first token (TTFT) of over 5s with a decoding throughput of 0.7 tokens/s. Simply converting the model with Optimum and running it on OpenVINO drastically reduces the time to first token (TTFT) to 0.42s (x12 speedup) and raises throughput to 47 tokens/s (x65). Applying 8-bit weight-only quantization further reduces TTFT (x1.7) and increases throughput (x1.4), while also reducing model size and improving efficiency.

#10412. Google Cloud C4 Brings a 70% TCO improvement on GPT OSS with Intel and Hugging Face

Intel and Hugging Face collaborated to demonstrate the real-world value of upgrading to Google’s latest C4 Virtual Machine (VM) running on Intel® Xeon® 6 processors (codenamed Granite Rapids (GNR)). We specifically wanted to benchmark improvements in the text generation performance of OpenAI GPT OSS Large Language Model(LLM).

The results are in, and they are impressive, demonstrating a 1.7x improvement in Total Cost of Ownership(TCO) over the previous-generation Google C3 VM instances. The Google Cloud C4 VM instance further resulted in:

GPT OSS is a common name for an open-source Mixture of Experts (MoE) model released by OpenAI. An MoE model is a deep neural network architecture that uses specialized “expert” sub-networks and a “gating network” to decide which experts to use for a given input. MoE models allow you to scale your model capacity efficiently without linearly scaling compute costs. They also allow for specialization, where different “experts” learn different skills, allowing them to adapt to diverse data distributions.

Even with very large parameters, only a small subset of experts is activated per token, making CPU inference viable.

Intel and Hugging Face collaborated to merge an expert execution optimization (PR #40304) to eliminate redundant computation where every expert processed all tokens to transformers. This optimization directed each expert to run only on the tokens it is routed to, removing FLOPs waste and improving utilization.

We benchmarked GPT OSS under a controlled, repeatable generation workload to isolate architectural differences (GCP C4 VMs on Intel Xeon 6 processors (GNR) vs GCP C3 VMs on 4th Gen Intel Xeon Processors (SPR)) and MoE execution efficiency. The focus is steady‑state decoding (per‑token latency) and end‑to‑end normalized throughput with increasing batch size while keeping sequence lengths fixed. All runs use static KV cache and SDPA attention for determinism.

Visit Google Cloud Console and click on create a VM under your project. Follow the steps below to create a 176 vCPU instance.

Visit Google Cloud Console and click on create a VM under your project. Follow the below steps to create a 144 vCPU instance.

Login the instance with SSH and then install docker. Follow the steps below to set up the environment easily. For reproducibility, we list the versions and commits we are using in the commands.

We are in container now, do following steps.

Run numactl -l python benchmark.py for the following codes.

Across batch sizes up to 64, Intel Xeon 6 processor‑powered C4 consistently outperforms C3 with a 1.4x to 1.7× throughput per-vCPU. The formula is:

normalized_throughput_per_vCPU=throughput_C4/vCPUs_C4throughput_C3/vCPUs_C3 \text{normalized\_throughput\_per\_vCPU} = \frac{\text{throughput\_C4} / \text{vCPUs\_C4}} {\text{throughput\_C3} / \text{vCPUs\_C3}} normalized_throughput_per_vCPU=throughput_C3/vCPUs_C3throughput_C4/vCPUs_C4​

At batch size 64, C4 provides 1.7× the per‑vCPU throughput of C3; with near parity in price per vCPU (hourly cost scales linearly with vCPU count), this yields a 1.7× TCO advantage (C3 would require 1.7× the spend for the same generated token volume).

Per‑vCPU throughput ratio: throughput_C4/vCPUs_C4throughput_C3/vCPUs_C3=1.7⇒TCO_C3TCO_C4≈1.7 \frac{\text{throughput\_C4} / \text{vCPUs\_C4}}{\text{throughput\_C3} / \text{vCPUs\_C3}} = 1.7 \Rightarrow \frac{\text{TCO\_C3}}{\text{TCO\_C4}} \approx 1.7 throughput_C3/vCPUs_C3throughput_C4/vCPUs_C4​=1.7⇒TCO_C4TCO_C3​≈1.7

Google Cloud C4 VMs powered by Intel Xeon 6 processors (GNR) provide both impressive performance gains and better cost efficiency for large MoE inference over previous generation Google Cloud C3 VM (powered by 4th Gen Intel Xeon processors). For GPT OSS MoE inference, we observed combined higher throughput, lower latency, and reduced cost. These results underline that thanks to targeted framework optimizations from Intel and Hugging Face, large MoE models can be efficiently served on next-generation general-purpose CPUs.
