#10410. Friendly Fraud Prevention for Developers: What to Log, Block and Automate

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Friendly fraud prevention comes down to three jobs you can do in code: log the right checkout data, block risky payments before they settle, and automate your response when a dispute still lands. Get the first one wrong and you can't win the dispute later, no matter how good your case is.

In this tutorial, we'll build each piece in Node.js in a way that works with any payment service provider (PSP). Your code owns the data and the logic, and a thin adapter talks to Stripe, Adyen, Checkout.com or whoever processes your payments.

Friendly fraud happens when a customer makes a real purchase, then disputes it with their card issuer. They might claim they didn't authorize it, that it never arrived, or that they canceled. Sometimes it's honest confusion. A spouse used the saved card, or the charge showed up under a name they didn't recognize. Sometimes it's a free refund with extra steps.

Either way, the money leaves your account. A dispute (also called a chargeback) reverses the payment, and your processor charges a dispute fee on top. Lose too many, and the card networks put your account into a monitoring program with higher fees.

It's also common. Visa puts friendly fraud at around 20% of fraudulent disputes globally, and up to 30% for high-volume online merchants. Mastercard goes further: it says first-party fraud makes up 75% of the fraud online businesses experience.

So why is this your problem and not finance's? Because the evidence that wins these disputes is created at checkout, by your code. If your app never stored the customer's IP address, device ID or login history, nobody can produce it three months later when the dispute arrives.

Friendly fraud can be stopped at four points, and each one is a different piece of code:

Most guides only cover stages 1 and 4. The rest of this tutorial walks through all four.

Log four things on every order: the customer's IP address, a device ID, their account ID and the shipping address. Those are the data elements Visa's Compelling Evidence 3.0 (CE3.0) rules check when you fight an "unauthorized" fraud dispute.

Here's how CE3.0 works. You win the dispute if you can show two earlier, undisputed purchases on the same card, made 120 to 365 days before the disputed one. All three purchases must share at least two data elements, and one of them must be the IP address or device ID. In plain terms: same card, same person, same device, and they never complained before.

Most PSPs support CE3.0, including Stripe, Adyen, Checkout.com and Airwallex. But none of them can submit data you never captured. And because the window reaches back a full year, you need to keep these logs for at least 13 months (Mastercard's rule, below).

Mastercard has its own version, called First-Party Trust, for disputes filed under reason code 4837 (no cardholder authorization). It asks for one data point from each of three categories: a device factor (IP address, device ID or fingerprint), a delivery factor (shipping address, email or phone) and a different identity factor (such as account login ID or billing address). On the dispute route, Mastercard calls a lookup service that you host, with named fields such as deviceIpAddress, orderDeviceId, orderEmail and userIdName. That service has to answer in about 2.5 seconds on average and search 13 months of sales data.

First-Party Trust is live in the US. Per Mastercard's October 2026 announcement, it reaches Eastern Europe, the Middle East and Africa from October 2026 and the rest of Europe from July 2027. If you sell into Europe, the logging work is due now.

The good news: one evidence table serves both networks. Capture the data once, then keep the eligibility checks for Visa and Mastercard separate.

Start with a table that stores this data per order, separate from your PSP:

Then capture it in your checkout route. If your app sits behind a proxy or CDN, set Express's trust proxy so req.ip returns the customer's address, not your load balancer's:

The psp object is your adapter: one small module per provider that maps its API to the same shape. Swap providers, and this route doesn't change.

For digital products and SaaS, log usage too. Login timestamps, downloads and feature activity prove the customer used what they paid for, which beats "I never received it" claims.

The cheapest dispute is the one that never happens. Three checkout changes do most of the work: 3D Secure on risky payments, a billing descriptor customers recognize, and a few rules that stop obvious abuse.

Use 3D Secure where risk is higher. 3D Secure (3DS) asks the cardholder to confirm the payment with their bank, often through an app prompt. For authenticated payments, liability for fraud disputes generally shifts from you to the card issuer. Every major PSP supports it, and most let you request it per payment instead of forcing it on everyone. Forcing it everywhere adds friction and costs conversions, so trigger it on risk signals.

Make your billing descriptor obvious. The descriptor is the text on the customer's card statement. If it reads PMT*SRV 8812 instead of your product name, expect "I don't recognize this charge" disputes. Use the brand name customers know, and add a support URL or phone number where your PSP allows it. If you sell several products, use a dynamic descriptor that names each one.

Add a risk check before you charge. Most PSPs include a rules engine, but a small check in your own code keeps the logic portable:

Store the signals array with the order. If a dispute arrives later, you'll know whether the payment looked risky at the time, which helps you decide whether to fight it or accept it.

Keep the rules few and specific. A rule that blocks 5% of good customers to stop 1% of bad ones costs more than the disputes it prevents.

Yes, if you ship physical goods. The window between a successful payment and the moment an order ships is the cheapest place to stop friendly fraud: nothing has left the warehouse, so canceling costs you nothing but the sale. Most fraud tools decide at checkout and never look again.

The pattern is a fulfillment gate. Instead of sending every paid order straight to your warehouse or 3PL, route it through a decision step first:

The verify path does two jobs. Legitimate buyers confirm and their order ships. Buyers planning to dispute see that the store is watching, and a confirmed verification becomes evidence if they dispute anyway.

The hard part is screenOrder. Your own data only shows how a customer behaved with you. A buyer who has filed "item not received" disputes at 10 other stores looks brand new on their first order with yours. That's why post-purchase screening works best on shared data across many merchants.

Chargeflow Prevent is one example of this kind of friendly fraud prevention. It scores each order after checkout and before fulfillment, links device, IP, email and payment behavior across a network of 20,000+ merchants, and returns approve, verify or cancel. Today it runs as a Shopify app, with no checkout changes. A public Prevent API isn't available yet, so on other stacks you'd build the gate above with your own rules and data.

Build an order lookup endpoint. When a cardholder taps "I don't recognize this" in their banking app, the issuer can now ask the merchant for order details before a dispute is filed. Visa does this through Verifi Order Insight, and Mastercard through Ethoca Consumer Clarity. Show the customer a receipt with your logo, the items and the delivery date, and many disputes are never filed.

One endpoint can serve both networks, plus Mastercard's First-Party Trust dispute route. Mastercard's published service levels for this kind of lookup are strict:

The tricky part is matching. Issuers often send partial data, so match on whatever arrives: acquirer reference number (ARN), authorization code, date, amount, currency, and card BIN plus last four digits.

On top of lookups, Visa and many PSPs offer rules-based auto-refunds. Verifi's Rapid Dispute Resolution (RDR) and Visa Resolve refund pre-disputes that match rules you set, such as "refund anything under $25". You don't write code for these, but you do pick the thresholds, so treat them like the REFUND_THRESHOLD below.

If you sell subscriptions, many friendly fraud disputes aren't about stolen cards at all. The customer forgot about a renewal, couldn't find the cancel button, or thinks they canceled. Each of these has a code fix.

Here's a daily job that sends renewal reminders and records that each one went out:

That evidenceLog row matters. When a customer later claims they never knew about the renewal, you can show the exact date you told them.

Automate two things: refunding payments that get flagged before they become chargebacks, and building evidence packets for the ones you fight. Both run off webhooks, and both have hard deadlines that humans miss.

Card networks can warn you before a dispute is filed. Visa runs this through Verifi and Mastercard through Ethoca, and many PSPs pass these alerts or their own early fraud warnings to you by webhook. Refunding at this stage costs you the sale, but you skip the dispute fee and the dispute doesn't count against your ratio.

The threshold is a business call. Refunding a $20 order is cheaper than fighting it; a $900 order with strong evidence may be worth contesting.

When a fraud dispute arrives, check whether it qualifies for CE3.0 by looking for two earlier undisputed orders on the same card that share data with the disputed one:

If you get two matches, pass them to your PSP's CE3.0 evidence fields. On Stripe that's evidence.enhanced_evidence.visa_compelling_evidence_3; other PSPs have their own equivalents. Your adapter handles the mapping. If not, fall back to standard evidence: the IP, receipt, usage logs, renewal reminders and terms acceptance you've been logging all along.

Always submit before the deadline your PSP returns with the dispute. A late response is an automatic loss.

The code above covers the basics. A production system also needs evidence templates per reason code, network deadlines per card brand, retries, and win-rate tracking. That maintenance multiplies with every PSP you add.

PSP-native tools only see that PSP's data, so they miss the usage logs, renewal reminders and support threads in your own app. A dedicated platform connects to your PSPs and lets you send that data in.

Here's what the buy path looks like with the Chargeflow API. Chargeflow ingests disputes from connected PSPs (Stripe, PayPal, Adyen, Checkout.com, Braintree and 20+ others), fires a dispute.created webhook, and you enrich the dispute with the evidence you logged:

Chargeflow then builds the response and submits it to the PSP before the deadline. Pre-dispute alerts work the same way: Chargeflow can refund flagged transactions for you, or send alerts.created and alerts.transaction.linked webhooks so your code issues the refund and reports the result to POST /alerts/{id}/outcome.

Using Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor to build this? Chargeflow publishes its whole developer documentation as one machine-readable file, docs.chargeflow.io/llms-full.txt. Point your assistant at it and it can write the webhook handler and field mapping against the real API, not a guess.

Then your merchants get the disputes, and you need to give them a dispute product without building a dispute team. Chargeflow Connect is built for this. It exposes the same prevention, alerts and recovery engine to your platform in a few delivery models:

EaaS is the most developer-friendly entry point. You POST /public/2025-04-01/evidence with a merchant account_id and a dispute, get back an in_progress record, and receive an evidence.ready webhook with the PDF link, typically in about 30 seconds. Store the evidence id, not the URL, because the download link expires after 7 days. You can run it on auto-pilot (Chargeflow generates and submits) or co-pilot (your merchant approves first).

Don't wait for a customer to dispute a charge to find out your evidence pipeline is broken. Most PSPs give you test cards that create disputes on demand.

One more check before launch: confirm your webhook endpoints verify signatures and return 200 fast. PSPs and Chargeflow retry deliveries that fail, and a slow handler can process the same dispute twice.

If you only do one thing this week, start logging IP address and device ID on every order. Everything else builds on that data.

True fraud is when a criminal uses a stolen card. Friendly fraud is when the real cardholder makes a purchase, then disputes it. Prevention differs: true fraud is stopped at checkout with risk checks and 3DS, while friendly fraud is won with evidence after the fact.

Mostly, yes. Both describe a real cardholder disputing a legitimate charge. "Chargeback fraud" usually implies the customer did it on purpose, while friendly fraud also covers honest mistakes, like a forgotten subscription or a family member's purchase. Visa calls it first-party misuse, and Mastercard calls it first-party fraud.

Check the reason code first. For "unauthorized" fraud claims, submit Visa CE3.0 or Mastercard First-Party Trust evidence if the customer qualifies. For "not received" or "canceled" claims, submit delivery proof, usage logs and your cancellation records. For low-value orders, accepting the dispute or refunding on an alert is often cheaper than fighting it.

Partly. 3DS generally shifts liability for fraud disputes to the issuer, so "I didn't authorize this" claims on authenticated payments rarely cost you. It doesn't help with "item not received" or "I canceled" disputes, which need delivery proof and cancellation records.

No. CE3.0 needs two undisputed purchases on the same card made 120 to 365 days earlier, so it only protects returning customers. For first-time buyers, rely on 3DS and standard evidence.

Yes. Mastercard's First-Party Trust program covers reason code 4837 disputes. It needs one device, one delivery and one extra identity data point, and Mastercard checks them against the cardholder's past purchases. The same evidence table you build for Visa feeds both.

It depends on the stage. At checkout, your PSP's 3D Secure and rules engine. After payment, post-purchase screening such as Chargeflow Prevent holds risky orders before they ship. Before a chargeback, Verifi Order Insight and Ethoca Consumer Clarity show cardholders the order details, while Verifi and Ethoca alerts (offered by many PSPs and by Chargeflow Alerts) and RDR let you refund early. After a chargeback, Visa CE3.0, Mastercard First-Party Trust and dispute automation tools submit the evidence. For developers, the Chargeflow API covers the alert and dispute stages across PSPs, and Chargeflow Connect does the same for platforms.

Microsoft is celebrating this quarter-century anniversary with a 25-game bundle free with new Windows PCs.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Microsoft’s first games console hit North America 25 years ago today. Effectively a PC in a box, the original Xbox was powered by an Intel Pentium III CPU and an Nvidia GPU inside a bulky black and green case. This first-gen device would sell 24 million units and be succeeded by the sleek PowerPC/ATI-powered Xbox 360 in late 2005.

The Xbox arrived on Nov 15, 2001, during the sixth generation of consoles, facing stiff opposition from the legendary Sony PlayStation 2, Nintendo GameCube, and Sega Dreamcast. However, it established a very respectable foothold in the console market thanks to its formidable hardware and a killer app in the shape of Halo: Combat Evolved. It would end up outselling Nintendo and Sega rivals, only living in the shadow of the PS2.

It is interesting to weigh up the performance hardware that was a big reason behind the OG Xbox’s success. Though the contemporary PC parts it used probably made it one of the biggest and ugliest consoles ever, powerful hardware is a great foundation for cutting-edge gaming experiences. The key components behind the Xbox were the Intel Pentium III 733 MHz CPU and an Nvidia NV2A 233 MHz GPU. Systems came with 64MB of DDR SDRAM and accessed games via optical media through its DVD drive. Perhaps most unusual for the time, the system included a built-in HDD (8GB), as well as offering 8MB memory cards for removable storage.

Another hardware advantage of the Xbox and key to connected gaming fun during the early broadband proliferation era was the inclusion of an Ethernet jack as standard. Xbox Live online gaming would launch in 2002. Microsoft used a heavily modified controller-friendly version of Windows 2000 for the system’s OS.

Setting the foundation for the next 25 years of Xbox, the original console was clearly a success. However, as the games industry prepares for a new generation of hardware, Microsoft’s strategy looks less certain than ever before. Even more so than with Sony, it seems less clear where the Xbox business is headed.

Microsoft couldn’t pass such an important anniversary without a celebratory promotion, and it looks like a very attractive one. If you are buying a new pre-built PC for gaming, you should keep an eye out for the 25-year Xbox bundle. This bestows new system purchasers with “25 fan-favorite Xbox games.” You’ll find the following games in your Microsoft Store Library, under the ‘Included with device’ tab on qualifying machines:

The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim Special Edition

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Game of the Year Edition

Those who aren’t getting a new gaming PC can still harvest a few commemorative freebies from Microsoft. On the dedicated page about the 25th anniversary, I spied free wallpapers, free in-game anniversary items for various titles, and an Xbox account badge. Fans are asked to check back at the linked page for “updates, freebies, exclusive experiences and the latest news throughout the year.”

#10406. 23 ways to handle tasks that trigger dread

Everyone has them: Tasks they dread. They can range from mundane or routine items that clog the calendar to difficult conversations and meetings that cause stress. Avoiding them doesn’t make them go away. It just makes the dread heavier. Figuring out how to get through them frees up the time and headspace they take up. 

We asked members of the Fast Company Impact Council how they handle tasks they dread. Here, 23 of them provide their best tips for getting them off your to-do list.

1. BODY-DOUBLE THE TASK

I don’t tackle them alone. We call it body doubling: pulling in a teammate for a focused session to knock out the task neither of us wants to face solo. It depends on the task at hand too! My default is our incredible chief of staff. She’s the left brain to my right brain. From there it’s our executive team if the task requires finance, operations, technology, etc. Consistently routing the task with the right team members keeps the business moving forward. — Cody Barbo, Trust & Will

2. JUST DO IT AND DO IT NOW

Dread is what you feel when you aren’t just doing it. Just do it. And when you do, more often than not you enter flow state, and you just keep doing stuff. — Eric Simons, Bolt.new

3. APPROACH IT LIKE AN ATHLETE

When I face a task I’d rather avoid, I try to tackle it right away, before I give myself a hundred reasons to postpone it. I approach these situations like an athlete: Discomfort is part of progress, not a reason to stop. Whether it’s a challenging negotiation or a difficult decision, I’ve learned to take action even when I don’t feel ready. Years of daily training and building at my company have taught me that motivation comes and goes, and discipline is the key to keeping you moving forward. You can’t always control how you feel about a task, but you can train yourself to show up and get it done anyway. — Victoria Repa, BetterMe

4. TAKE ONE SMALL STEP

In my mind, most dread comes from a task that has no clear definition or parameter. I’ve found it helpful to jump on the first physical step, small enough to finish in a few minutes (e.g., open the file, draft the subject line, pull last month’s numbers) and physically stop there to build next steps. This creates a sense of internal accountability. Once the task has a shape, the rest usually goes faster than the dread predicted. Also, if it still sits there after a week, that’s useful information: It may belong to someone else, or it may not need doing at all. — James Chester, WVN

5. CHIP AWAY EACH DAY

Momentum beats motivation. I start small and chip away a little each day. Procrastinating doesn’t buy you time, it just weighs you down, and eventually it crowds out the work you love. — Tami Rosen, executive board and advisor to technology and finance companies

6. TACKLE THEM FIRST, EARLY IN THE DAY

I do them first, and I make them smaller. Dread grows in the gap between knowing a task needs doing and starting it. So I close that gap early in the day, before anything else competes for my attention. If it’s big, I commit only to the first part. Momentum handles the rest. I’ve also learned to ask what the dread is telling me. Sometimes it’s a sign the task needs a conversation, not more effort, and the fastest way through is a call to the right person. — Megan Noel, Covista

7. NAME WHAT YOU DREAD AND WHY

Usually, people dread something because it is uncomfortable, ambiguous, or carries some sort of emotional weight. I try to name what I dread and why, instead of pretending the task itself is the problem. If it matters, do it and do it now, because avoidance compounds just like progress does. The things we put off usually get heavier, not lighter. — Ethan Braden, Texas A&M University

8. TAKE OUT THE TRASH DAY

A colleague once inspired me with her “take out the trash day,” dedicating a chunk of time each week to knock through dreaded tasks. With all the noise on Slack, texts, and email, I block an hour at the end of the week, mute my notifications, and cruise through. It’s how I take care of budgets, expenses, and the general paperwork, so I can get back to the creative work where I’m in my flow. Sometimes there’s a snack reward waiting at the end. — Courtney Brigham, Typeface

9. SET A REWARD FOR YOURSELF

I break it down into chunks, set a target date and time to complete each chunk, and then block out time and get it done. I also set a reward for myself after doing it. For example, I’ll get to have this great lunch after I finish it. It sounds silly, but it’s nice to have rewards after doing a project that is not enjoyable! — Felicia Curcuru, Binti

10. RELY ON PREPARATION

During dreaded high-stakes situations like meetings with multiple stakeholders or delivering sensitive performance-based feedback, I rely on preparation. Coming armed with a brief outline of mission-critical points ensures you stay on track and helps you recover if the conversation gets derailed. If I’m ruminating on a complex problem that I just can’t seem to crack, I put everything down and do something completely unrelated. Taking a walk, listening to a podcast, or even washing the dishes allows my brain to marinate, discover hidden connections, and eventually the solution becomes clear. — Celia Jones, FINN Partners

11. PRIORITIZE ACCORDINGLY

Tasks I dread are rarely the most important for our business, so I prioritize them accordingly. However, they tend to bubble up to the higher end of the list of less critical tasks. The longer they remain on my to-do list, the more days they get to impact my morale, so I’m motivated to get them done. — Brad Weber, InspiringApps

12. CONNECT IT TO OUTCOME

I try to stay positive by focusing on the value the task will create once it’s completed. I put it in the broader context of the goal it supports and the impact it will have. As a big-picture person, details can be challenging, but connecting the work to a meaningful outcome helps me stay motivated and push through with a positive mindset. — Chris K Bailey, Bailey Brand Consulting

13. TAKE THE MEDICINE ALL AT ONCE

I put them off. Then I bundle them up and take care of them all at once. Like medicine. It tastes bad but works. Sort of like Buckley’s cough and cold medicine. — Phillip Haid, Public Inc.

14. STOP AND MAP IT OUT

If I catch myself spending real time on something where I’m just going through the motions, I stop and map it out. What are the inputs, what am I doing with them, and what does the output need to look like? Once the process is clearly mapped, it’s usually pretty obvious that a lot of it doesn’t need me. Then I build an automation around it. I still get the result; I just skip the mundane part. — Mike Sewell, Gresham Smith

15. ASK WHETHER YOU’RE THE RIGHT PERSON TO DO IT

I try not to spend too much time negotiating with myself. If something needs to be done, I focus on the next step and start. Usually, the anticipation is worse than the task itself. As a CEO, I’ve also learned to ask whether I’m the right person to do it. There are many things I can do, but I don’t need to do all of them. Sometimes leadership means taking something on yourself. Other times it means trusting someone else to own it. What I try to avoid is letting something I don’t enjoy become something the organization has to wait for. — Yuping Huang, Quantum Computing Inc.

16. CARVE UP YOUR DAY

Technology marketing is constant context switching and rapid decision-making. If you’re not careful, a whole day passes without a minute of real thought or creativity. You give in to the “critical” transactions, and eventually the work that’s most critical to your job disappears entirely. So I carve up my day. Mornings are for content, strategy, and creative problem-solving. Midday is the transactional work. The last couple of hours go to administration and anything that wasn’t urgent. And if something that needs real creativity slips through until late in the day, it gets the first look the next morning, with fresh eyes. — Colby Proffitt, Seekr

17. DIVIDE IT INTO MANAGEABLE STEPS

When I face a task I dread, I focus on understanding what makes it difficult and what depends on completing it. This matters because postponing an uncomfortable responsibility does not remove it. It can affect decisions, relationships, and other people’s work. I divide the task into manageable steps, establish a clear deadline, and begin with the first action. For me, discipline is not about enjoying every responsibility. It is about addressing what needs to be done before hesitation becomes a larger problem. — Manuel Freire-Garabal, Gioya HEI

18. DO THE WORST THING FIRST

Do it first. I was told once that you should always do the worst thing on your to-do list first because the day then only gets better. Have stuck to it ever since. And never overlook the power of reward: For every annoying task give yourself a little treat in return. The promise of a future good thing coming your way works every time. — Helen Andrews, Johannes Leonardo

19. AUTOMATE THE MUNDANE

Recently, I’ve unlocked a new cheat code in chipping away at those dreaded tasks. When walking to work, I’ll start talking with my favorite large language model of the moment and we can hammer out 10 open items from unanswered Slack messages and emails to meeting recaps and other nagging tasks that can quickly pile up. When all the right connectors are in place, the efficiency unlock is tremendous and has been a game changer for knocking out those dreaded to-dos. — Matt Conlin, Fluent

20. KNOW WHEN THE TASK BELONGS TO SOMEONE ELSE

I like to understand every aspect of my business, even the things that don’t come naturally to me. I’m always open to learning something new, but I also recognize when something falls outside my skill set. I believe in knowing your strengths and surrounding yourself with people who bring expertise you don’t have. If it’s something I can tackle, I get it done. If someone else can do it better, I delegate. My time is best spent where I can make the greatest impact. — Kim Wileman, No Makeup Makeup

21. USE THE HEADWIND AS A TAILWIND

I once heard Jimmy Iovine, co-founder of Beats, talk about using a headwind as a tailwind, and it’s stuck with me ever since. If there’s something you hate doing, run towards it, not away from it. Delay is a false economy because it just extends the dread. Then I break it into tiny actions and get the first one done. Momentum beats motivation every time, and most tasks are never as bad as the story you’ve told yourself about them. — Emily Kortlang, Meaco

22. MEET IT AT YOUR COGNITIVE PEAK

I use power hours. I know my brain is sharpest late in the evening or early in the morning, so I save the tasks I would normally procrastinate on for that window. I don’t do it every day. The idea is simple: Dreaded work takes far less energy when you meet it at your cognitive peak, so an hour or two of focus can clear what would otherwise linger for weeks. — Muneer Panjwani, Engage for Good | The Halo Awards

23. ATTACK THE FIRST FIVE MINUTES

I try to attack the first five minutes rather than the whole task. Dread grows in the space between knowing you have to do something and starting it. Once I take action, the task usually gets a lot less intimidating. — Ran Mullins, Psympl

#10405. What AI Gets Wrong About the Front End, and Why You Still Need to Know

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The product carousel looks finished. The image fills the card, the price sits under the product name, and the arrow on the right takes you to the next item. The demo goes smoothly.

Then you put the mouse down. You press Tab, and focus skips the arrows entirely. If you rely on a keyboard, the first product is the only one you can reach.

That’s a front-end bug hiding in plain sight. It’s also a good illustration of where AI fits into front-end development. A prompt can describe what a component should look like and what should happen on click. The implementation still has to account for how people reach that control, activate it, and understand what changed.

Imagine asking an AI coding assistant for this:

Build a React product carousel with previous and next arrows. Show one product at a time and wrap around at the ends.

Here’s an illustrative excerpt from the sort of implementation that can satisfy a quick mouse-driven demo:

With some CSS, this can look exactly like the arrow in the design. The click handler advances the slide. A screenshot shows the right layout.

But a plain div sits outside the normal Tab sequence and has no native button semantics or keyboard activation. Adding tabIndex={0} would make it reachable while leaving Enter and Space behavior to be implemented separately. The browser already provides those behaviors through a native button.

The real omission was in the requirement. “Show arrows” described the visual design. “Let someone reach and operate both controls with a keyboard” describes behavior you can test.

Here’s a small version of the same carousel. The product data is fixed for the example, and the slides change only when the user requests it.

The buttons have visible labels and work with both Enter and Space. When a slide changes, focus stays on the button you pressed, so you can press it again to keep browsing. The status message gives assistive technology a way to announce the new product and its position. Only the current product link is rendered, so Tab never lands on a link from a hidden slide.

Those are deliberate interaction choices. W3C’s carousel pattern provides guidance on using native buttons, keeping focus on the slide controls after activation, and handling automatic rotation when a design requires it. W3C Carousel Pattern

I’d revise the original prompt like this:

Build a manual React product carousel. Use native Previous and Next buttons. Both must work with Tab, Enter, and Space. Keep focus on the activated button after a slide change. Announce the new product name and position through a status message. Keep only the current product link in the Tab sequence. Show what happens when the user advances past the last product.

The extra detail also gives you a review plan. For this carousel, I’d use four checks:

AI can help draft automated tests for the active link and wraparound behavior. I’d still run the keyboard and screen reader checks on the integrated page. A global stylesheet can erase a visible focus outline. A surrounding component can introduce an extra tab stop. The experience depends on the page the customer actually uses.

A checkout form can look complete with sample data and lose the customer’s entries when a request fails. A responsive header can match the design at two widths and overlap when a translated label is longer. A component can render correctly in isolation and shift the page when a slow image loads.

Each example gives AI a concrete job. Ask it to preserve form values after a failed request, check the header with longer labels, or reserve space for the image. Then reproduce the condition yourself. Knowing which conditions matter is part of knowing the front end.

The next time AI gives you a carousel that looks ready, start the review with your hands off the mouse. Tab to Next, press Space twice, and see where focus lands. That short test gives you evidence about how the component works for someone who relies on a keyboard.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It looks like AMD is trying to get back into the good graces of gamers, with its CEO, Dr. Lisa Su, joining the grand opening of Micro Center Austin. The company shared official photos of AMD’s chief executive cutting the ribbon to mark the store’s opening on its Instagram page, while a Redditor shared a short clip showing her making the rounds among the people waiting to get inside the shop and signing a Gigabyte Radeon RX 9070 XT GPU, one of the best gaming GPUs you can buy today.

AMD has been saying that it is a data-center-first company repeatedly since 2024. Dr. Su reiterated the stance in an interview earlier this month, at which point some in the press finally decided to notice. The reporting naturally enraged gamers who supported AMD and Nvidia for decades and are now feeling left behind as these companies pivoted towards more lucrative AI hardware. This has become apparent with the paper launches of Nvidia’s latest RTX 50-series chips in 2025 and the purported production cuts of powerful RTX 5080 and RTX 5090 GPUs, even as demand for Nvidia’s AI GPUs continues to rise.

A post shared by Micro Center (@microcenter)

However, it seems that this outrage has been drowned out by the unfolding scandal at Nvidia, which saw the dramatic fall from grace of the company’s legendary founder. It’s unclear if this plan to have the AMD chief at the Micro Center Austin’s grand opening has been in place for some time or if it was an attempt to smooth the ruffled feathers of the gaming community, but Austin is home to one of AMD's largest hubs, so it's likely an organic and planned event. But whatever the case, it was a treat to the people who were on the ground during the event — Micro Center said that AMD gave away 300 swag bags and had a couple of prizes for the people in the store.

The opening of Micro Center’s Austin brick-and-mortar store is actually a good sign for the people in the area, especially now that we’re at the age where almost everything can be bought online. While the AI shortage has made RAM, GPU, and many other things more expensive, physical retailers remain one of the best places where PC builders can find deals on parts and components. We even saw Walmart honor a $2,299 CyberPowerPC mistakenly displayed for $1,099 each, allowing a Redditor to secure two relatively powerful gaming PCs for more than half off.

#10401. Is another crypto winter upon us? Why Bitcoin, XRP, and Ethereum fell more than 20% in a month

The crypto markets are down again today, with major tokens suffering significant losses over the past 30 days.

As of this writing, Bitcoin is trading below $65,000, Ethereum is nearly down to $1,800, and XRP is below 96 cents.

Those are more than 20%, 25%, and 26% drops, respectively, over the past month.

Bitcoin hit an all-time high of more than $126,000 a token in October 2025, meaning its value has roughly halved since then.

Those falls are causing some to wonder whether another crypto winter is upon us. The term describes extended bear markets across cryptocurrencies, in which digital tokens drop significantly in value and stay down. Major crypto winters previously hit in 2018–2019 and 2022–2023. 

It may be too early to tell whether this is the start of another one, but several factors have been driving cryptocurrencies lower in recent weeks. Here’s what you need to know.

Expected Federal Reserve interest rate hikes

One of the greatest factors likely weighing on cryptocurrencies is the expectation that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December. As Reuters reported, a majority of economists expect the Fed to hike rates next month. The hike is expected to be by 25 basis points, to a range of 4.00%–4.25%.

Rate hikes make money more expensive to borrow. This can encourage people to save, which can dampen spending and thus help fight inflation.

But when money is more expensive to borrow, those who lend it can earn more. So, when rates are higher, investors tend to pull their money from non-interest-bearing assets, like crypto, and put it into interest-bearing assets like U.S. Treasury bills.

This reallocation leads to a selloff in crypto, driving the basket of digital currencies lower.

AI stock rut

Cryptocurrencies aren’t the only assets having a tough time lately.

Big Tech stocks—especially AI-adjacent ones—are having a rough few weeks. Last week was perhaps the worst thanks to the Jensen Huang scandal that sent shares of Nvidia Corporation (Nasdaq: NVDA) down more than 12% during the last five trading days.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq is also down about 1% during the same period.

AI stocks and cryptocurrencies often tend to move in tandem. Both are highly volatile and act as speculative assets. When one falls, investors tend to get jittery and sell off the other class in an effort to prevent further losses and lock in gains.

The 2026 midterm elections

A blue tsunami swept across America in early November’s midterm elections. In some ways, that is very good for the markets, as a large political majority brings a certain amount of certainty.

Investors may or may not like that party’s policy positions—but knowing what’s coming can help them plan financially.

Unfortunately for crypto, the incoming Democratic Congress may be much less friendly to the industry.

Crypto investors fear that this new political leadership could propose stronger regulation, which may stymie the industry’s growth—or at least impose checks it otherwise wouldn’t have had if the GOP had retained control of Congress.

Crypto Fear and Greed Index falls to “Extreme Fear” level

Unsurprisingly, after a 20-plus percent selloff in major tokens over the past month, investors are fretting about crypto’s future—at least in the near term. 

And nowhere is that worry more evident than when you take a look at CoinMarketCap’s Crypto Fear and Greed Index. The index tracks investor sentiment surrounding the crypto markets. It ranges from 0 to 100.

The higher the index, the more optimistic (and potentially greedy) investors tend to be about Bitcoin and other tokens. The lower the index, the more fearful they tend to be.

Right now, the index stands at a paltry 13, placing it in the “Extreme Fear” range—its lowest range. It has not been at this level since February 2026, when Bitcoin fell from around $87,500 to around $60,000 in the first few days of the month.

Of course, despite the index’s low rating—and the many factors weighing crypto down over the past month—it’s still too early to tell whether the crypto markets are on the cusp of another prolonged downturn. But the longer the rout lasts, the more the specter of another crypto winter will weigh on investors’ minds.

#10400. Nike spent years reinventing Air. Meet the new Tuned Air (exclusive)

For half a century, Nike has been synonymous with Air. The cushioning—developed at NASA, then incorporated inside a 1978 running shoe and the Air Max 1—came to represent Nike’s commitment to cutting-edge innovation. Now, with Nike on its back foot after several years of missteps, the company is counting on a new version of Air to help pull it out of its slump.

Today, a day before it announces its financial results, Nike is unveiling Tuned Air, a high-tech evolution of Air that has been in the works for years. It’s debuting this technology in a running sneaker that will come out within a year. But Nike sees Tuned Air as a broader platform that can be incorporated into other sports and even its apparel lines.

It’s one way Nike hopes to restore its credibility as an innovator and win back runners who have drifted to rivals. Given how much ground Nike has lost in recent years, it’s unclear whether this strategy will work. But the company is optimistic.

“There’s no better innovation that speaks to our formula than Air,” says Phil McCartney, Nike’s chief innovation, design, and product officer.

McCartney has spent three decades at Nike, where he ran the footwear business from 2016 until last year, when CEO Elliott Hill put him in charge of innovation, design and product across Nike, Jordan, and Converse. Speaking to me from the LeBron James Innovation Center at Nike’s campus in Beaverton, Oregon, McCartney explained that his team has a motto borrowed from two Nike legends: “Create epic shit. Make athletes better.” (The first comes from Kobe Bryant, the second from Nike’s cofounder, Bill Bowerman.)

McCartney says Nike is translating that slogan into a formula, “athlete, science, solution,” that will guide the company’s approach to innovation. His teams gather insights from athletes, then tests ideas at the Nike Sports Research Lab in Beaverton and through field teams in Eldoret, Kenya; London, and Shanghai.

Introducing Nike Tuned Air

The original Air technology created tough pockets of nitrogen using two sheets of plastic. In that case, the air was evenly distributed, creating cushioning throughout the pocket. With Tuned Air, Nike adds nuance. Before the plastic sheets are pressed together, Nike adds a chemical that allows it to create a pattern; it can now fine-tune where the gas is located and how much air is in each pocket. In doing so, it can make one part of the cushion soft and springy, and another part firm and stable. “It allows us to completely change the relationship between cushioning and support, and precision-tune the experience,” says McCartney.

Nike has given this technology to runners over the last few years. “The feedback that we’ve had from the runners who have been trying this for a couple of years now is it feels like no other cushioning system out there,” he says. “Incredibly well cushioned, but also has stability. That’s the sort of holy grail that we’ve been trying to unlock in Air.”

While Nike’s approach to achieving this balance might be distinct, many other running brands are also trying to balance cushioning with structure with their own innovations. Brooks’s DNA Tuned foam uses a dual-cell construction, with large cells in the heel to cushion landings and smaller cells in the front to make the toes more responsive. Hoka’s H-Frame features a firm strip of foam in the midsole, surrounded by softer cushioning. On’s CloudTec technology uses hollow tubes of foam molded to the bottom of the sole to absorb impact, along with a steel plate in the midsole.

With this newfound ability to modulate how much air is in each pocket, Nike can now explore “wildly different expressions” of the technology, McCartney says. Besides running, Tuned Air will be incorporated into other sports, like soccer, and into clothing like the Air Milano jacket, creating air pockets that improve temperature regulation.

Nike can even integrate Tuned Air into lifestyle shoes, like vintage sneakers, creating more comfort. “How could we make an Air Force 1 using a sock liner that is Tuned Air, so you get comfort and support?” McCartney says.

Nike has streamlined the manufacturing of Tuned Air so that it can move 70% faster than it typically does from idea to product. This is crucial to allowing Nike to be nimble as it seeks to compete with the many rivals that are also spinning out innovative new products quickly.

Nike Needs a Win

Nike needs this innovation to resonate with consumers. Last quarter, revenue declined 4% to $11.2 billion, and the company expects full-year sales to fall by a high single digit percentage. Sportswear, which accounts for nearly half the business, fell by double digits. Sales in China dropped 26% and Converse sank 28%. Nike has announced a restructuring plan that will cut more jobs after several rounds of layoffs in recent years.

Nike’s rivals have been closely observing its missteps, and taken advantage of the opportunity to steal market share. In running, a category Nike once dominated, it’s now in third place, trailing Brooks and Hoka. In the lifestyle sphere, Adidas has had hit after hit by bringing back its classic Samba and Gazelle, and New Balance has turned its retro styles like the 550 into bestsellers. Meanwhile, Nike hasn’t had a lifestyle sneaker hit in years.

Nike’s running business is starting to recover. It’s grown by double digits for more than a year, helped by the successful Vomero line. “We’re seeing market share gains almost daily right now,” says McCartney.

Historically, Nike has built running technology for elite athletes that tries to shave seconds off on their race times. But that technology takes a long time to trickle down into running shoes that the average person can lace up.

Nike doesn’t have the luxury of time anymore. That’s why its Tuned Air is designed for the everyday runner. “The entry point will be that everyday run,” McCartney says. “When you’re just trying to log your Tuesday morning run, you want the maximum amount of running with precision-tuned support.”

Nike is making a big bet on Tuned Air. But whether enough consumers get excited about the technology—and the forthcoming sneakers—to boost Nike’s fortunes is unclear. Tomorrow, when Nike lays out its long-term financial plans, we’ll get a better glimpse into how much ground it has yet to make up.

A letter demanding the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO has been circulating online and has already garnered more than 91,000 signatures at the time of writing. Elon Musk said on X that he signed a petition, but it is unclear which one he has signed. At least one large online petition has circulated, with other big names supposedly among the signatories, ostensibly including Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and several prominent shareholders, partners, and current and former Nvidia employees. However, the signatories on this petition apparently aren't verified. Regardless, this petition has gathered over 130,000 signatures.

@yunta_tsai A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it tooNovember 13, 2026

However, not everyone is keen on bringing Jensen back; Nvidia Vice President for Applied Deep Learning Bryan Catanzaro said on X that an online letter purportedly circulated at Nvidia is fake, and he had no involvement and wouldn’t sign it if it were real. He also reiterated his support for Colette Kress, the newly appointed interim CEO who would run the company while the board looked for a suitable replacement for Jensen.

There is a made-up letter circulating online asking NVIDIA’s board to reinstate Jensen, claiming my involvement. This letter is obviously fake, and even if it were real I would not sign it. I am grief-stricken that Jensen is no longer with NVIDIA. At the same time, I fully support NVIDIA’s board and have confidence in their decisions. I’ve worked with Colette for years and know her as an extraordinary leader. She has my full support.November 13, 2026

Jensen Huang’s fall was sudden and dramatic — he went from being one of the leading figures in the hardware needed to run AI to completely resigning from the company he built in under two weeks. It all started when U.S. intelligence sources claimed that Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, apparently close to the former CEO, was passing information to Chinese intelligence. The company initially denied this story, saying, “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

But a little over a week after that story, more news came out alleging that Jensen had an affair with the Megaspeed executive, forcing him to finally admit his relationship with the alleged spy. This led to a flurry of investigations by his own company’s board, the U.S. Congress, and the FBI. Just as things were already escalating, another alleged affair surfaced — this time with an Nvidia executive. Amid this whirlwind of scandals and rumors that Jensen would be ousted from the company, Elon Musk said it would be an honor to hire Jensen. Nvidia announced Jensen’s resignation just hours after Musk made the X post.

Despite the nature of his departure, it seems that there is still widespread support for Jensen from Nvidia’s employees, with thousands reportedly rallying behind him and calling for his reinstatement in an internal forum. The Stand with Jensen petition isn’t directly related to Nvidia, but it echoes comments from people inside the company that the former CEO was removed without meaningful due process. “Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen’s leadership,” the public letter said. “The inquiry must establish the facts, not merely justify an outcome already imposed.”

Jensen Huang’s larger-than-life persona will be difficult to replace, with the board considering candidates including Arm CEO Rene Haas and Apple Chief Hardware Officer Johny Srouji. It’s probably harder for interim CEO Colette Kress, who’s temporarily stepping into the position while the company is in the midst of massive turmoil, especially with the allegations that Huang was removed because of the mass smuggling of up to 1.5 million Nvidia AI GPUs, and who has the job of reporting its third-quarter results as CEO for the first time on November 17.

#10396. Santa with a cause: Amazon Prime teams up with Arnold Schwarzenegger for its latest holiday campaign

After more than five decades in Hollywood, Arnold Schwarzenegger finally feels fit to play his most iconic role yet. And he’s taking the reins just in time for the holiday season.

The Terminator and Total Recall actor is suiting up in bright red and white for Amazon Prime’s new holiday creative campaign, “Santa Schwarzenegger,” which debuts on Monday.

The advertising spot begins with Schwarzenegger looking a little forlorn as the paparazzi chase him around New York. He then orders a Santa suit from Prime, allowing for anonymity as Schwarzenegger donates snacks to a dog rescue center, watches a basketball game, and heaves a Christmas tree onto the roof of a car.

“I’m at that age now and it’s believeable”

Throughout his career, Schwarzenegger has played plenty of iconic roles. He’s portrayed a killing machine from the future, Batman’s nemesis Mr. Freeze, both Hercules and his father, Zeus, and an undercover cop teaching kindergarteners.

But Schwarzenegger says no role he has ever played has been as worldwide as this one.

“This is the perfect time for me to play Santa, because I’m at that age now and it’s more believable,” Schwarzenegger tells Fast Company. “With all the interesting characters that I played in my career—from Conan to Terminator—I thought that Santa is the ultimate.”

For Amazon, the Schwarzenegger spot fits neatly into two goals: driving sales and attention to Prime, a core pillar of the online retail giant’s Black Friday, Cyber Monday, and other holiday sales events throughout the season.

But it also ties in neatly with Amazon Prime’s The Man with the Bag, an upcoming holiday film that debuts on December 2, starring Schwarzenegger as Santa for a second time.

Alan Ritchson, Awkwafina, and Ken Jeong are also featured in the film’s cast. The film also ties into Amazon’s 2026 holiday campaign, which is called “Joy Delivered.”

“Arnold is the king of the kids, we saw that when he made Kindergarten Cop,” Jo Shoesmith, Amazon’s vice president and global chief brand officer, tells Fast Company. “There is a warmth and charm to him that lives outside of the character of Santa.”

Santa “has to be in shape”

“Santa Schwarzenegger” will run through December 23 across several channels including television, digital, social, and streaming audio. Yet another component of the campaign that Amazon is promoting is Schwarzenegger’s curated holiday gift guide, which includes plush dog toys, supplements, toys intended for children and grandchildren, and dumbbells.

“Think about it, Santa has to fly all the way from the North Pole, he has to be in shape to hand out the gifts at every single continent to go to every single house,” says Schwarzenegger. “It is a lot of work. He has to be in shape.” 

There are also two books: Better Every Day, a self-help book penned by Schwarzenegger that’s due to be published in January, and Arnold, which is written about him.

There’s also a cigar lighter, which may seem counterintuitive for the fitness enthusiast, but apparently he’s smoked them for over 40 years, including during his interview with Fast Company.

“We never want to twist the arm of the personality to put something in their mouth that doesn’t come across as authentic,” says Shoesmith. “It’s very driven by his holiday ordering list.” 

As an Austrian, Schwarzenegger says his holiday traditions differed from how he raised his children in America. The holiday is celebrated on December 24 and the gift giver is a baby Jesus called Christkind, not Santa, though Schwarzenegger says the latter has become more popular there in recent years. 

“I always question with every script I get: is this something that would just be good for America, or just good for Europe, or is this something that can play in every continent,” says Schwarzenegger.

Santa, he says, is a role that can “entertain the whole world.”

The rise of star-powered Santas

While Santa has been “the face” of the Christmas holiday for marketers for more than a century, the celebrity angle has been a more recent development.

John Travolta has played the role in multiple ad spots for Capital One, while Jon Hamm did so for Fox Sports, Steve Carell for Comcast, and Brent Bailey for Target.

“He’s kind of just this joyous, universally loved figure,” adds Shoesmith. To be clear, Shoesmith was talking about Schwarzenegger at this moment, not Santa, though she says both have cross-generational appeal.

Schwarzenegger is also a safe casting choice for the retailer at a time when the American consumer isn’t optimistic. Unease about the economy was a central theme in the recent midterm elections, and the sales projection forecasts for the upcoming holiday season look fairly mixed.

Research firm Circana says average holiday spending will total $779 this year, down from $796 in 2025. The trade association the National Retail Federation is more bullish, expecting retail sales in November and December to increase 4.2% to about $1 trillion, compared to a year ago.

“We’re a brand whose logo is a smile, so joy is inherently part of who we are as a brand,” says Shoesmith of the tone approach for Amazon Prime’s campaign. “We really make sure that we have a great selection of brands at a really great price, and that’s really important for customers right now . . . they’re very price conscious.”

#10394. How to Reduce Hallucinations in LLMs

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Ask one of the newest language models whether a backpack comes in green, and it'll usually admit it doesn't know. Ask it how to return that backpack, and it may send the customer to a returns page, an account screen, and a return label that the store has never had. That's still a hallucination: an answer that sounds right, comes with total confidence, and isn't true.

Whatever you're building, the fix is the same: stop trusting the model with the parts it can get wrong, and check its work before anyone sees it.

In this tutorial we'll build a small support bot for a made-up outdoor gear store, three times over. The first version is the prompt plenty of bots start with. Then we'll apply five fixes, run six tricky customer emails through every version, and finish with a bot where the model can't slip a made-up price, date, or product past the code.

An LLM hallucination is output that's fluent and confident but not backed by the facts: a product that doesn't exist, a policy nobody wrote, a date that's a week out, or a citation to a paper that was never published. The word covers two different failures:

Each one needs a different fix, so it helps to keep them apart.

A language model writes by predicting likely text, one token at a time. It has no separate store of facts it checks against, and nothing in that process says "stop, you don't know this". Training adds to the problem. OpenAI's research on why language models hallucinate points out that when models are graded only on how many answers they get right, a guess scores better than "I don't know", so they learn to guess.

Newer models are much better at the first one. They'll often say they don't know a price rather than invent one. But they still fill gaps with what's typical, and what's typical isn't always what's true for your business. You can't train that out of a model you call through an API. What you can change is what you ask it to do, what you give it, and what you check.

A made-up answer costs more than one bad reply. Some of the costs are already on the record:

In a support inbox, the cost is quieter but adds up: a refund you didn't owe, or a customer who goes looking for a live chat button that isn't there and doesn't come back.

Northwind Outdoor sells four things: two packs, a rain cover, and a tent. It has two orders on file and three short policies. Here's all of it:

Six emails come in, and each one is there to trip the bot in a different way:

The traps: the 40L pack doesn't come in green, but the 28L does. The 40L is water-resistant, not waterproof. There's no 60L. Whether the return is allowed depends on a membership, a sale price, and a count of days since delivery. The tracking details are in one order record. And the store has no price match policy at all.

Make a folder, add "type": "module" to its package.json, and install the Anthropic SDK and Zod:

Every version calls the model through one small helper:

We're using Claude Opus 5.5 at low effort. These are short, simple replies, so the model doesn't need to think for long. Swap in any model you like, because none of the fixes depend on it.

Opus 5.5 didn't invent a single price, colour, or delivery date across the six emails. Every reply said it couldn't see the store's details. That's real progress compared with older models, but look at what it said instead. Here's the reply to the email about a pack the store doesn't sell:

It treats the Ridgeline 60L as real and offers to help pick a fit. The other replies made up the store around the customer:

Northwind has none of those. None of it is a wild guess: it's what a typical online store has. That's exactly why it's dangerous. A customer who goes looking for the live chat or the newsletter discount won't find it, and the bot never answered the question anyway.

The model can't know Northwind's prices, so give them to it. This is the idea behind retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): find the records that matter and put them in the prompt. Our store is small enough to send all of it.

Two things changed. The store data goes in the system prompt, wrapped in tags so the model can tell data from instructions. And the prompt tells it to answer only from that data. Here's the green pack email again:

Right on all three counts, and it even pointed to the pack that does come in green. The return, which needs four facts from two places, came back right as well:

Delivered October 6, a Trail Club member, so 60 days, so December 5. Bought on sale, so store credit for what was paid, not the list price. Version 2 got all six emails right.

The last line of that prompt matters as much as the data: "If the answer isn't in the data, say you don't know and that a team member will reply by email." Without it, a model that can't find the answer has to choose between letting the customer down and guessing, and training has taught it to guess. With it, "I don't know" is a right answer, not a failure.

The price match email is the test, since the store data says nothing about price matching:

It said it didn't know, passed the question to a person, and answered the parts it could from the data.

If version 2 got everything right, why build a version 3? Because "right on this run" isn't the same as "right every time":

The next three fixes take the facts and the rules away from the model completely.

Version 3 splits the work into three steps. First, the model reads the email, but instead of writing a reply, it fills in a form. Every field is a choice from a list, a yes or no, or text copied from the email:

Zod describes the form, and z.toJSONSchema() turns it into a JSON schema for the API's structured outputs. The API holds the model to that schema, so product can only be one of our four product IDs, not_sold, or none. There's no way for it to answer ridgeline-60. Zod then checks the answer again, so the rest of the code gets a typed object. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema goes deeper on this pattern.

The model is still reading natural language, which it's very good at. It just isn't trusted to know what the store sells anymore.

A form also makes the model's mistakes easy to see. The first time I ran this, the form had no asks_something_else field, and the model filed the price match email under product. The reply didn't make anything up, but the email never reached a person. In version 2, a mistake like that would be hidden inside a paragraph. Here it was one wrong value in a JSON object, and the fix was one more field.

If all you need from this step is decisions like these, a model built for typed answers can do it faster and for less. Our typed AI pipeline tutorial builds the same kind of email sorter with Jev and Clairic.

Second step: plain code takes the form, looks up the product and the order, applies the rules, and does the maths. What comes out is a list of facts in plain sentences:

Every number in there was worked out by code that does the same thing every time, and that you can unit test. The 34 days, the December 5 deadline, and the $151.20 in store credit come out the same on every run, whatever the model does.

The last rule in decide() matters most. If an email asks something the rules don't cover, the facts say so and the email goes to a person. Code decides when to say "I don't know", not the model.

Third step: the model writes the reply from the facts and nothing else. Writing is the one job here it does better than code.

Even with the right facts, a model writing a reply can still add something: a helpful "ships in 1–2 business days", or a price it remembers from somewhere. So the last step checks the reply. Anything that looks like a number, an order number, or a product name has to appear in the email or the facts:

It's simple on purpose. It doesn't understand the reply. It just refuses to let through a value that came from nowhere, and that covers the hallucinations that cost money: prices, dates, quantities, and products. Nothing in the reply can talk it out of a result.

The writer runs the check on every draft:

If a draft fails, the model gets one retry and is told exactly which values weren't in the facts. If the retry fails too, the customer gets the facts as a plain list. That's less charming, but it's true.

A check like this will raise false alarms, and that's fine. On my first run, it read a line about the tent's 2.1 kg weight as a product called "Weighs 2" and sent the draft back for a retry. The weight was right, and it was the only thing flagged. A false alarm costs a few seconds. A missed one costs a customer. I tightened the patterns (the version above has the fix), but I'd still rather it flag too much than too little.

It's the same thing that separates the better agentic AI coding tools from autocomplete: they run the tests and read the errors instead of trusting their first draft. Model output isn't finished until something other than the model has checked it.

This script sends each email through all three versions, saves every reply, and runs the check from Fix 5 over all of them. Versions 1 and 2 are checked against everything the store knows:

The check caught one thing in version 1: the "1–2 business days" it made up for processing an order. It missed the "up to 24 hours" for tracking in the same reply, but only because $24 is the rain cover's price, so 24 counted as a known number. And it couldn't catch the invented returns page or live chat at all, because they aren't numbers. That's why the check is the last fix, not the only one.

Reading all 18 replies, here's how each version did:

Version 3 was less helpful than version 2 in one place. It couldn't give the rain cover's price, because decide() only adds facts about the product the email names. Version 2 had the whole store to look at. In version 3, the fix is a rule you write once: when a product has an add-on, include the add-on's facts too.

Here's version 3's reply to the price match email:

No model is free of hallucinations, so you can't stop one from ever making something up. What you can do is build so a made-up detail can't reach a customer: let code own the facts, and check the model's output against them before it's used. Where it matters, send anything your rules don't cover to a person.

It cuts them a lot, because the model no longer has to guess facts it was never given. In our test, putting the store's data in the prompt took the bot from no useful answers to six right ones. It doesn't stop the model misreading what it retrieved, mixing up two records, or filling a gap the retrieved text leaves. Pair it with a way out and a check on the output.

Not really. Temperature controls how random the wording is. A low temperature makes the model give the same answer more often, including the same wrong answer.

Collect inputs that have tripped your app (or are likely to), write down the right answer for each, and run every version of your prompt or pipeline over the same set. Automated checks like the one in this tutorial catch made-up values. Read the replies yourself for the rest, because the made-up returns page above would pass any number check.

Hallucinations come from asking a model to do jobs it isn't built for: knowing facts it was never given, and running small programs in its head. The five fixes take those jobs away:

The model still does what it's best at: reading messy text and writing a friendly reply. It just isn't trusted with the facts anymore. From here, try a seventh email that asks two things at once, add the add-on rule to decide(), or extend the check to catch colours and sizes as well as numbers.

#10391. What is the FAA’s SMART AI system? Officials are denying a link to the nationwide ground stop

The airline ground stop that wreaked havoc on travel since Friday was not related to the FAA’s new, $875 million AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky, according to government officials and the artificial intelligence company behind the technology.

But the timing of the ground stop, so close to the national rollout of the Federal Aviation Administration’s SMART system, has raised questions about what the system does, its benefits and risks compared with the existing human system and what guardrails there are to address potential problems.

Officials say no connection to ground stop

The SMART system is based in a single location near Washington where a team of experts analyzes flight schedules, weather forecasts and hundreds of other streams of data. Then that office sends recommendations to the FAA’s command center, which relays them to air traffic controllers across the country for consideration.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday there’s no indication the communications issues that caused the ground stop are linked to the new computer system, and the top officials at the Transportation Department and FAA reiterated that Saturday.

The startup that designed the system, Air Space Intelligence, or ASI, said the ground stop wasn’t caused by “the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.”

But lawmakers and outside groups raised questions about the SMART system before Friday’s ground stop. Last month, House Democrats sent a letter to the U.S. Government Accountability Office requesting an audit of the new software, raising concerns about safety and guardrails.

“Concerningly, the nation’s front line aviation safety workforce apparently had little to no input into SMART’s development and have received limited training and information during the current deployment process,” the Oct. 13 letter said. “The use of artificial intelligence within SMART has rightfully raised serious questions about its reliability and safety benefits, particularly on its potential to interfere with decision-making by experienced air traffic controllers or to hallucinate safety-critical information.”

SMART, however, is not — at least not yet — set up for AI to be in charge of flight control. Rather, it is making recommendations to humans who do so.

What is the SMART system?

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford unveiled the system in September, calling it a “cutting-edge tool that centralizes 200 data streams — including weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow, and controller staffing metrics — into one platform.” SMART stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories.

The system’s AI-supported engine synthesizes the data systems and shows a “comprehensive visualization” of where planes are going, how much traffic the system can handle and where congestion or weather could cause problems, according to the announcement. The idea is for specialists to then use the platform to fix problems before they arise.

The FAA says that during the initial test of the system in the Washington area this fall, the system helped reroute 180 flights and saved an average of 10 minutes and 80 gallons of fuel per flight by diverting around weather or other issues. The agency said that one flight cut 42 minutes off its trip from Tampa, Florida, to Dallas thanks to the system’s recommendations.

So SMART was expanded for use nationwide on Nov. 10 for the airspace of all 22 air traffic control centers. That was three days before the ground stop.

According to a government fact sheet on the tool, SMART can predict where air traffic is headed and identify other routes before an area becomes too congested. The system can also help reopen restricted airspace faster and better manage airport arrivals.

SMART is also supposed to help with weather-related issues faster.

Currently, the FAA blocks off portions of airspace affected by weather as “large, rectangular boxes,” according to the fact sheet, which doesn’t reflect how weather actually looks, with quick-moving thunderstorms and storm systems that are “often irregular in shape, with narrow gaps or corridors that aircraft could safely fly through.”

To help with this, SMART gives the FAA and airspace operators a “clearer picture of how weather will affect air traffic over time,” allowing air traffic controllers to plan around storms and use available airspace instead of unnecessarily shutting down large areas.

No other country has a working AI air traffic tool like the SMART system, according to Michael McCormick, a former FAA airspace manager and an associate professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Eurocontrol, the European air traffic authority, has a system in testing and several manufacturers are prototyping similar tools.

Concerns around relying on AI

While government officials and ASI, the company behind SMART, have stressed that its AI system is designed to assist humans and not run flight control, its deployment has raised concerns about relying on artificial intelligence when human lives are at stake, given that even the most advanced models are prone to hallucinations — when models fabricate false information and present it as fact.

Mike O’Donnell, a former top FAA official who worked for the agency for 17 years and now does aviation safety consulting work, said the agency “has got to make sure that this is just a tool in the toolbox and not the actual machine that’s doing the work.”

The FAA, he said, “cannot afford to be wrong on this.”

“It’s good to use it with the proper guardrails and backstops to ensure that they’re not giving wrong information to controllers based on what (AI) has come up with,” O’Donnell said. “There’s got to be a way to verify and validate what it’s doing to make sure that it’s not the wrong information.”

He cautioned against putting too much trust in AI “until we know for sure that it’s proven itself time and time again. And that’s going to take a while.”

The AI system’s launch comes amid a longstanding shortage of air traffic controllers around the country. The National Air Traffic Controllers Association has been raising concerns about this for more than a decade, telling Congress in 2015 that the shortage was at a crisis level. It said then that the FAA had missed its hiring targets for five years in a row. The union represents about 14,000 controllers, roughly 3,000 of them trainees. That said, experts say no AI system can replace the human air traffic controllers who spend years training for this highly demanding and stressful job.

In an October interview with NPR, ASI co-founder and CEO Phillip Buckendorf said the SMART tool is designed for traffic managers who manage the entire U.S. airspace.

“The AI does the math, the AI does the computation,” Buckendorf told NPR, but it’s ultimately up to the human operator whether to take the system’s recommendation. “They make the decision, they are the decider, they are the judge.”

—Barbara Ortutay and Josh Funk, Associated Press
