#10368. Stressful jobs do, in fact, pay more. But there’s a catch

Do more stressful jobs come with a bigger paycheck? It depends.

According to a recent study conducted by online resume building platform Resume Genius, the most stressful jobs pay an average of 62% more than the least stressful jobs. And yet, not everyone is enjoying a high-pressure premium.

Workers with a high school diploma or postsecondary certificate typically see a 24% pay premium for taking on a more stressful job; those with a Master’s earn 27% more in high-stress roles, while those with a doctoral or professional degree earn a whopping 78% more.

Among bachelor’s degree holders, however, higher work stress doesn’t pay. In fact, bachelor’s degree holders in high-pressure roles earn 1% less on average than bachelor-holding colleagues in lower-pressure positions.

“Not all forms of workplace stress are rewarded equally,” says Resume Genius career expert Nathan Soto. “The data we found suggests that a stress premium exists, but it’s concentrated in particular educational and occupational groups, rather than being a universal feature of the labor market.”

The study is consistent with other research that suggests workers are less willing to take on more stressful jobs, even if they come with a higher salary. A survey of 14,000 workers by emotional insight platform Hint App, for example, found that 58% would reject a promotion that required them to be available after hours.

Putting a price on workplace pressure

Soto says Resume Genius developed a “Stress Index” to help quantify workplace pressure across 754 occupations.

One-third of that 100-point scale is based on the role’s “Stress Tolerance” level, according to the U.S. Department of Labor’s Occupational Information Network (or O*NET) database. The agency defines “Stress Tolerance” as “a tendency to cope and function effectively in stressful situations at work.”

The remaining two-thirds were based on seven stressful job attributes: time pressure, workplace conflicts, dealing with unpleasant or angry people, the consequence of errors, responsibility for others’ health and safety, competition and long working hours. Stress Index scores were then compared against the latest pay data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

“Among six-figure occupations, workers in high-stress jobs were much more likely to deal with unpleasant or angry people, handle conflict regularly and face time pressure every day,” Soto says. “Responsibility for other people’s health and safety and the seriousness of potential mistakes were also major factors.”

Soto explains that high-paying, highly stressful jobs that don’t require a bachelor’s degree often involve physical risk, demanding work conditions or significant responsibility. For example, electrical power-line installers earn an average of $95,320 and have a Stress Index level of 97. Detectives and criminal investigators, who also aren’t required to earn a bachelor’s, scored 100 on the stress index and earned an average of $93,790.

High-paying jobs that require a professional or doctorate degree, meanwhile, often require specialized training or expertise, come with greater responsibility as well as higher stakes. For example, anesthesiologists scored 100 on the Stress Index and earned an average of $391,490 per year.

But: “Jobs that require bachelor’s degrees follow a different pattern,” Soto says. “Many of them pay high salaries without necessarily rewarding additional workplace stress with higher pay.”

More than half of the six-figure jobs included in the study scored above 67 on the Stress Index, but the researchers did identify 19 high-paying low-stress jobs. They include electronics engineer, software developer, statistician, data scientist, computer and information research scientist and actuary.

A high tolerance for stress has a dollar value

Many workers look to avoid stress, and are even willing to take a pay cut for it. But those who can take the heat can often earn more.

According to a 2025 study conducted by researchers at the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg in Germany, workers are willing to take a 9.6% wage cut to avoid frequent, tight deadlines, and earn about 6% less to avoid having to multitask often.

“Avoiding pressure comes at a price. So you have to think whether you’re willing to pay that price,” explains economics professor Markus Nagler, who co-authored the study.

Swapping a low-pressure job for a high-pressure job within the same occupation, according to the study, came with a 12% earnings premium on average, though half of that raise was due to an increase in working hours.

The researchers, however, also found that those who didn’t mind certain stressful job aspects were more likely to find jobs that paid them for that sacrifice. For example, those who take on jobs with tight deadlines may be able to stomach the pressure more than the average worker.

“The kind of people who select into these jobs and remain in these jobs typically are those who have the highest tolerance for these kinds of working conditions,” Nagler says. “The problem is that you choose a job, but you don’t get to choose specific aspects of the job.”

Not everyone gets to choose a lower-stress job

The research suggests that workers in higher-stress jobs tend to earn more. But other research finds that workers in low-wage jobs are more likely to face harsher working conditions.

According to a 2023 study published in the American Economic Review, workers earning lower wages were less willing to give up part of their earnings to enjoy non-work amenities like schedule flexibility, more paid time off and less heavy lifting. The study also found that higher-wage workers are more likely to enjoy those additional perks than workers in lower-wage jobs.

“The people that are getting paid more are also getting better working conditions,” explains one of the study’s co-authors and an associate professor at Penn Medicine, David Powell. “People who are compensated better want a combination of higher wages and better amenities, so when you look at disparities, and you include amenities, they typically widen.”

That is not to say that high earners aren’t dealing with difficult working conditions. However, Powell’s research suggests those with higher earnings are in a better position to sacrifice some of their earnings for a lower-stress role. Those struggling to make ends meet, however, are typically less willing to forfeit some of their pay for better working conditions.

As a result, lower earners tend to enjoy fewer of the amenities that make work less stressful, while higher earners can more easily swap a high-stress job for a more laid-back alternative, even if it pays less.

#10367. Why Transactional Emails Fail After Deployment: A Practical Debugging Guide for Developers

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Transactional emails are easy to overlook during application development. A registration form works, the database stores the user's information, and the backend successfully triggers an email. Everything appears to be functioning as expected.

Then a user reports that their password-reset message never arrived.

The problem might not be in the email template or the sending function. It could involve DNS configuration, authentication failures, message formatting, queue processing, recipient-server policies, or an incorrectly configured production environment.

For developers building SaaS applications, ecommerce platforms, and web services, reliable email delivery is an important part of the user experience. An account-verification message that never arrives can prevent someone from accessing an application, while a delayed security notification can create unnecessary confusion.

Understanding how to investigate these problems requires looking beyond the email-sending function. This guide explores a practical debugging workflow, the technical layers involved, and the tools developers can use to identify common email delivery failures.

One of the first mistakes developers make when troubleshooting email is assuming that a successful API response means the message has reached the recipient.

When an application submits an email through an SMTP server or an email service provider's API, the provider may accept the request and return a successful response. However, the receiving mail server still needs to process the message.

Depending on its configuration and policies, the receiving server might:

Accept the message and place it in the inbox.

Accept the message but classify it as spam.

Reject the message because of authentication or policy issues.

Accept the message but place it in another folder.

A successful request therefore confirms only that a particular stage of the process completed.

Developers should distinguish between three important states:

Submission: The application successfully handed the message to its sending provider.

Acceptance: The receiving mail server accepted responsibility for the message.

Inbox placement: The message became visible in the recipient's expected inbox.

These distinctions make troubleshooting considerably easier. Instead of immediately rewriting an email template, developers can identify which stage is actually failing.

Before investigating external email infrastructure, examine the application's own implementation.

A common example is a password-reset workflow. The application receives a request, generates a temporary token, creates a reset URL, and sends an email containing that URL.

Several problems can occur before the message even reaches an email provider.

The application generates an expired token.

The reset URL points to a staging environment.

An asynchronous task fails before processing the message.

The email service credentials are incorrect.

An API request times out without being retried.

The application records success before confirming the provider's response.

Start by logging the important stages of the process.

For example, a Node.js application might use structured logging:

This example assumes that the email provider returns a message identifier. Adapt the response fields to the actual SDK being used.

Notice that the logs identify the recipient through an internal ID rather than exposing their complete email address.

Avoid logging passwords, authentication tokens, reset URLs, or other sensitive information.

The objective is to establish a traceable record of what happened without introducing additional security risks.

Email authentication is another important area to investigate when messages are rejected or consistently classified as spam.

Three commonly used mechanisms help receiving servers evaluate whether a message is authorized to represent a particular domain.

Sender Policy Framework (SPF) allows a domain owner to specify which servers are authorized to send messages using that domain.

This information is published through DNS.

A simplified SPF record might look like this:

The actual record must reflect the sending services authorized by the domain owner.

Forgetting to authorize a new email provider.

Publishing multiple SPF records for the same domain.

Leaving outdated sending services in the record.

Remember that SPF evaluates the sending infrastructure against the envelope sender domain. It does not automatically guarantee that the visible From address is aligned.

DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing messages.

The receiving server can retrieve the corresponding public key through DNS and verify that the signature is valid.

A mismatch between the configured selector and published record.

Developers integrating multiple email providers should verify that each provider has the correct signing configuration.

Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) builds on SPF and DKIM.

It allows domain owners to define how receiving servers should handle messages that fail authentication and alignment requirements.

A basic monitoring-oriented DMARC record might look like this:

This is an illustrative configuration. The reporting address must be valid, and the domain should have an appropriate monitoring and policy-enforcement plan.

Developers can use MXToolbox to inspect DNS records and investigate common authentication problems.

For additional technical background, SitePoint's guide to HTML email development explains why email environments require different implementation considerations from ordinary web pages.

An email template that looks perfect in a browser can behave differently when rendered by Gmail, Outlook, Apple Mail, or another email client.

This happens because email clients do not implement HTML and CSS in exactly the same way.

A layout may break because of unsupported CSS properties, image restrictions, unexpected font rendering, or differences in how tables are handled.

For this reason, email testing should be part of the development process rather than something performed only after users report a problem.

HTML validation: Check the markup for malformed elements, missing attributes, and unnecessary code.

Rendering tests: Preview the email across desktop and mobile email clients.

Link verification: Confirm that buttons, links, and personalized URLs point to the correct destinations.

Image testing: Check whether the message remains understandable when images are blocked.

Content inspection: Review subject lines, sender information, and the plain-text alternative.

Deliverability checks: Examine authentication, content-related warnings, and potential inbox placement problems.

Developers can also incorporate pre-send diagnostics into their release workflow to identify potential deliverability problems before a message is sent to a larger audience.

The important point is to treat these checks as one part of quality assurance, not as a guarantee that every message will reach the primary inbox.

For more information about email rendering differences, SitePoint's article on essential HTML email coding tips provides useful examples of client-specific behavior.

Testing transactional emails with real customer addresses during development can create unnecessary problems.

A better approach is to use a dedicated testing environment that captures outgoing messages without delivering them to actual recipients.

For example, Mailpit provides a local SMTP server and web interface for inspecting messages during development.

The final output generated by the application.

Another option is Mailtrap, which provides email testing capabilities for development workflows.

Consider a registration feature that sends a welcome message whenever a new user creates an account.

Instead of sending hundreds of test messages to real addresses, developers can configure the development environment to capture them in a testing inbox.

This makes it possible to repeatedly test different templates without affecting actual customers or generating unnecessary email traffic.

A separate testing environment also reduces the risk of accidentally sending development notifications to production users.

Applications that send large numbers of emails often use background workers instead of processing every message during the original HTTP request.

This approach helps keep the application responsive, but it introduces another potential source of failures.

Imagine an ecommerce application that sends order confirmations after checkout.

The application creates an order successfully and places an email task in a queue. However, the background worker becomes unavailable before processing the task.

The customer receives an order confirmation much later than expected, or perhaps not at all.

To investigate these problems, developers should monitor:

Retries are particularly important, but they need to be implemented carefully.

A temporary network failure may justify another attempt. A permanent rejection caused by an invalid recipient address usually does not.

Exponential backoff can help prevent repeated requests from overwhelming an unavailable service.

In a production system, add random jitter to avoid having multiple workers retry simultaneously.

Also consider idempotency. If a worker processes the same task twice, the application should avoid sending duplicate transactional messages whenever possible.

A reliable queue architecture should distinguish between temporary failures and permanent failures rather than retrying every error indefinitely.

Testing before deployment is important, but it cannot reveal every issue that may occur in production.

Real email traffic introduces changing conditions, including recipient-server behavior, sender reputation, invalid addresses, and differences between email providers.

Developers should therefore establish ongoing monitoring.

For Gmail-related monitoring, Google Postmaster Tools provides information about domain reputation, spam rates, and authentication.

It is particularly useful for teams sending enough email to generate meaningful reporting data.

Another useful resource is Can I Email, which documents HTML and CSS feature support across email clients.

These tools address different problems. Monitoring sender reputation will not fix a broken password-reset URL, just as validating HTML will not resolve a DNS authentication failure.

The best approach is to monitor each layer independently.

A repeatable checklist helps developers investigate problems without overlooking important details.

Before releasing a new email feature, review the following:

Confirm that the application successfully submits the message.

Verify that provider credentials and environment variables are correct.

Inspect SPF, DKIM, and DMARC configuration.

Validate the HTML and plain-text versions.

Preview the message on desktop and mobile email clients.

Verify that development and production configurations are separated.

Check delivery events and provider error reports.

Monitor bounce and complaint rates after deployment.

Not every application needs an expensive testing platform or a complicated monitoring stack.

A small project might only require a local email testing environment, basic DNS checks, and structured application logs.

A larger SaaS platform may benefit from automated integration tests, provider webhooks, queue monitoring, authentication reports, and dedicated deliverability testing.

The right setup depends on the application's sending volume, complexity, and the importance of its email workflows.

Reliable email delivery requires more than calling an SMTP function or integrating an email API.

Developers need to understand the complete process, from application logic and message construction to authentication, queue processing, recipient-server acceptance, and inbox placement.

The most effective troubleshooting strategy is to isolate these layers instead of treating every missing message as a template problem.

Start with application logs, inspect provider responses, validate authentication records, test email rendering, and monitor production behavior.

By incorporating these checks into development and deployment workflows, teams can reduce avoidable failures and build applications that communicate more reliably with their users.

Update 11/16/2026 2:40pm PT: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has now clarified the nature of the failure in an interview on CNBC, saying the HPE routers were not at fault. Instead, older infrastructure from 2001 was at fault:“[...]as we did one of those switchovers in El Dorado, Arkansas, that server or that router started to flood our network. Well, all of the work that I had done to put in new equipment, those routers in my system didn't go down. But we also use a lot of 2001 Cisco servers that went out of commission in 2006. It's those old servers that were flooded and started to give us inconsistency in our network.”Original article: Air travelers in the U.S. were in for a nasty surprise last Friday night after the Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) called for a nationwide ground stop. According to the Wall Street Journal, the issue started after a newly installed Juniper router, built by HP Enterprise, started broadcasting to a wide part of the network. This, in turn, overloaded the established and antiquated system, resulting in communications glitches and interruptions between air traffic control and pilots.

Thankfully, this did not affect other safety services, like Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS), which primarily relied on hardware in aircraft that communicated with other transponders to help prevent accidents. Still, air traffic’s inability to communicate with high-flying aircraft made it impossible to coordinate the thousands of airborne aircraft at any given time, forcing the agency to call for an emergency ground stop. A nationwide ground stop order is quite a drastic move, and it has only been invoked twice before. The first such event was on September 11, 2001, when terrorists infamously used hijacked airliners as weapons. The second was on January 11, 2023, when the agency’s Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system, which sends warnings to pilots and air crews of important information crucial to flight safety, suffered from an outage for about a couple of hours.

The problem first became apparent at Indianapolis Center, which monitors the airspace in northern Kentucky, southern Indiana, southern Ohio, and parts of West Virginia, when the personnel working at the site had trouble communicating with flight crews. The agency then went on a nationwide hunt for the glitch, and it soon found two possible sources — an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. Upon deeper inspection, the agency discovered that new routers recently installed in both places have begun sending out a high volume of data across the entire FAA communications network.

“We saw two places that were actually pinging our network at a very high rate, a thousand connections over every four to five seconds,” FAA technology chief Rebecca Guy said in a press conference. This might seem like a minor hiccup for any modern network, which could typically handle connections in the hundreds of thousands, or even millions, per second. For example, one of the largest recorded DDoS attacks for 2026 saw traffic spike to 31.4 TB/s, which is enough to takedown an entire country’s web infrastructure.

However, the FAA still uses an antiquated copper network, which was easily overwhelmed by the amount of data that the routers sent. This network is already several decades old, so the agency is currently in the process of upgrading everything to fiber, which is costing taxpayers billions of dollars. Even as the agency is in this period of transition, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford has raised several questions. “Was it a faulty installation? Was it a faulty configuration? Or was it just a bad piece of router technology that we put into this system that propagated these errors?” Bedford said in statement on Saturday. He also added that the agency is investigating the incident. As for the Juniper router, an HPE spokesperson said that they appear to be working as intended and that “They did not fail.” It was eventually discovered that a specific feature on the router caused the system overload, with FAA employees turning it off across the entire network on all Juniper routers.

It took about four hours for the FAA to return its communications network to normal, but repercussions go way beyond that. Passengers aboard all those canceled and diverted flights needed to be served, even as new passengers kept on arriving for their scheduled flights. It’s been estimated that airlines needed a few days to recover after the CrowdStrike crash of 2024 forced United, Delta, and American Airlines to cancel flights (except for Southwest, which avoided the chaos because it used an antiquated OS from the 1990s), so we expect passengers unlucky enough to be in transit during this incident to suffer waits between a few hours to a day or two before their journeys could continue.

#10363. Your marketing approval process is spending your budget

“Can we get one more person to weigh in?”

If you work in marketing, you know where this can lead. The campaign is ready, the team has worked through the feedback, and the launch date is approaching. Then another reviewer joins the conversation and questions a decision everyone thought was already settled.

Back it goes. New copy, updated graphics, another round of approvals. Meanwhile, the next project is waiting.

No one approved a bigger budget. But the team is spending more time on the same work.

In June 2026 research from Bloomberg Media and Lippincott, nearly eight in 10 CMOs said bureaucracy frequently interferes with decision-making. Corporate leadership was the primary source of delays for major marketing initiatives.

As leaders, we need to look at our part in that. We expect teams to deliver on time, but every additional review affects their ability to do it.

“ONE MORE REVIEW” IS MORE WORK THAN IT SOUNDS

Changing a headline might take a few minutes. Updating it across a landing page, emails, ads, and a sales deck takes longer. Someone also has to check those changes and send the updated materials back for approval.

That rework has to fit somewhere, and it’s rarely planned for in the workback schedule. So it takes time from a campaign already in production. It forces the creative department to stay late (again), or pushes the deadline to next week. Your team feels overworked and stressed, so it may appear to be a resource problem. But the real problem is in the process.

The solution is to take a hard look at your marketing workflow, both documented and unspoken.

START WITH APPROVALS

If you find your campaigns are consistently missing deadlines, look at how many review rounds you typically have, and how many stakeholders must sign off. Understand who is involved, why they are involved, and how you can make sure they’re providing that value at the right time.

Is the CMO signing off on the campaign messaging before any creative is designed, or are they seeing the campaign messaging the night before launch? Is legal being asked to approve photos from the expensive product shoot without being asked to provide any legal guardrails in the brief? 

Carefully sequencing sign-offs based on dependencies, and allotting time in your workback schedule for their review, will ensure you’re setting your team up for success from day one.

GIVE REVIEWERS CLEAR EXPECTATIONS

Often, the root of friction is in how we request feedback. Send a draft with “Let me know your thoughts,” and you may get a rewrite when you just needed someone to check the facts.

Be specific about each person’s role. Product experts review accuracy. Legal reviews claims. The marketing lead evaluates whether the message speaks to the audience and aligns with the campaign goal.

Establish who makes the final call when those perspectives conflict. A project manager can gather comments and chase responses, but someone with decision-making authority needs to resolve any disagreement. Asking the team to satisfy incompatible feedback just sends it around again.

RANK FEEDBACK BY ITS IMPACT

There are good reasons to reopen approved work. A product feature changes, a claim turns out to be inaccurate, or legal identifies a concern.

If someone wants a late change, bring the conversation back to the campaign’s goal. Will it help the audience understand the message or correct something important? If it doesn’t clear one of those hurdles, stick with the approved version.

As a reviewer, before requesting a change, find out what that change will impact. That includes who must review it again and what will have to move or be sacrificed to accommodate it. You need to understand its impact on the schedule, the team capacity, and ultimately the budget. Make sure it’s worth the cost.

As leaders, we need to trust our team to make the right decisions. But when there are too many decision-makers on a project, nothing gets resolved. Before asking your marketing team to move faster, look at how approvals are handled in your organization. Every review has a cost, and those review cycles may be eating up your budget.

Lisa Larson-Kelley is president and CEO of Quantious.

Nvidia Board Director Mark Stevens sold about 4.2 million of his shares, netting him around $1 billion in cash, almost exactly two months before Jensen Huang was accused of having “close ties” to an alleged Chinese spy. According to Moneywise.com, Stevens started the sale from August 31 to September 2, when Nvidia stock hovered between $220 and $226, which made him $411 million. The next tranche, totaling $236 million, came in the next couple of days as Nvidia traded from $227 to $234. The final sale happened on September 18 at around $220 per share, making Stevens approximately $300 million. These three transactions would have made him somewhere around $947 million.

Last year, Jensen Huang sold up to six million Nvidia shares, netting him around $925 million. However, unlike Stevens, who had no plan, this move was announced six months earlier in a Rule 10b5-1 trading plan to help avoid accusations of insider trading.

Nvidia’s stock price has taken a beating since the scandal broke, with the company trading at $162.85 at the time of writing, its lowest level in the past 12 months. When the story first broke at the end of October, Nvidia shares were at around $205. It then started sliding, with the price at $178.67 after Jensen admitted to the affair last Sunday, although he did not name the involved party.

A second affair was revealed a few days after the former Nvidia chief’s confession, leading to his resignation from the company a few hours after that. The news sent Nvidia stock down to $151.09 — a nearly 25% drop from before the scandal. It recovered somewhat after the initial shock, climbing to nearly $170 before Friday’s trading, but took a beating again soon after the market opened.

Despite the sale, Stevens still holds about 27.5 million Nvidia shares, making him the second-largest shareholder after Jensen and Lori Huang. The price difference between today and September 18 is around $57, meaning he would have lost 25% of the value if he had sold after the scandal broke. Furthermore, his remaining Nvidia shares have lost more than $1.5 billion in value in just one quarter. Still, selling one’s holdings in a company as a board director does not constitute a crime. After all, it's unlikely that one could have predicted how hard Jensen Huang would fall in such a short time.

#10359. The ‘recession indicators’ visible at your workplace

People all over the U.S. have been sharing their “personal recession indicators” in recent months, from only being able to afford Goldfish crackers and water for lunch to filling up their cars with a few dollars’ worth of gas at a time.

According to employment attorney Craig Levey, a partner at Bennett & Belfort, there are recession indicators at your workplace, too—you just have to take a look around. And they could be a sign that bigger cutbacks, or even layoffs, could be around the corner.

Levey makes content on TikTok, where he tracks patterns in his comments and feed that highlight how people feel about the world of work.

“Over the last few months, I noticed that a lot of companies were suffering financial issues. There was a downturn in their numbers,” he tells Fast Company. “People were trying to assess whether a recession was happening in the United States.”

Levey posted a video about workplace recession indicators that employees should look out for, including companies slashing expenses on business trips, bonuses, holiday parties, and even office snacks. Companies often start with the little things when tightening their belts, he says, and these cuts could be an early signal that a business is preparing for tougher economic conditions.

“Upper management and leadership, they probably get together and they say, ‘Okay, we need to cut costs. What can we do? Let’s cut the low-hanging fruit,’” he says.

Cutting now to save later

Companies do this, Levey says, because they’re looking six, 12, or even 18 months ahead, and taking preemptive steps to put themselves in a better position for the next fiscal year.

These cuts may seem trivial to some. But for other employees, they can be incredibly important. Levey says he regularly hears from people who have full-time jobs but have to live in their cars because they can no longer afford rent.

“A lot of employees are really struggling because the day-to-day costs are so high that they can’t pay their bills,” Levey says. “If you’re somebody who can’t pay their rent, trying to figure out how you’re going to get your next meal, and you can go into your company’s kitchen and get a snack—that makes a big difference.”

According to Chris Marvel Davis, cofounder of Pivot, a training and development provider that runs workshops on wellness, burnout, and leadership, snacks may be what people notice first. But there are other, less obvious signs that a company is becoming more cautious with its spending. 

Travel and conference requests getting denied or delayed may not be immediately apparent, he tells Fast Company. Other signs include open roles staying unfilled, job postings disappearing, backfills for departed employees being paused, and contractors being let go before full-time employees.

“Small purchases need bigger approvals,” he adds. “When a $200 expense suddenly needs a director’s sign-off, someone in finance is watching cash closely.”

Is it routine or a sign of something bigger?

Companies make these kinds of cuts first because they’re easier to reverse, Davis says. On their own, they may simply suggest that leadership is being careful.

“They buy leadership time to see how bad things might get without alarming employees or customers,” he says. “One sign by itself doesn’t tell you much, but several at once are worth taking seriously.”

People should also pay attention to what happens the next time someone leaves, Chiquita Hall-Jackson, an employment attorney at Hall-Jackson & Associates, tells Fast Company.

“If the company leaves the position vacant, divides the work among the remaining team, and still expects the same output, that tells you more about its staffing plans than a cut to the travel budget,” she says. “When that pattern shows up across teams, it’s worth asking whether leadership is planning to operate with fewer people.”

According to Hall-Jackson, it’s also a good idea to look at what’s being cut and how long the cuts last. A canceled off-site meeting may save money once, but a hiring freeze changes how the business operates.

“One budget decision can have plenty of explanations,” she says. “Several decisions that consistently reduce staffing or hours are more meaningful.”

Another potential warning sign is a change in the company’s management structure. If there are fewer middle managers than there used to be, and larger teams are now reporting to more senior supervisors, that could suggest the company is looking to operate with fewer people, Levey says.

It’s more important than ever to have leverage

Of course, many of these signs could just mean that an individual company isn’t doing well and may not indicate a wider, looming recession. 

But in this tough economy and job market, employees should consider being more sensitive to changes at work that may hint at something bigger happening, Levey says. He adds that it’s important to maintain a sense of where you stand within the company, how secure your position is, and what the general temperature is when it comes to potential layoffs.

“You want to pay attention to messages from the CEO or upper management. Because if you think that your job is in jeopardy, then while you’re still employed there and making a wage, you’ve got to start looking elsewhere to see what your other options are,” Levey says.

The worst thing is being blindsided, so it’s always a good idea to make sure you have some leverage, he notes. “It doesn’t mean you need to microanalyze every single thing that happens with the company. But be a realist. Keep your eyes open, really understand what’s going on. That way, you’re less surprised if these things happen.”

#10358. What Actually Happens When a Kafka Region Fails?

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most Kafka deployments in the industry plan to survive the loss of a single Kafka broker or an availability zone. But that's not enough for critical Tier-0 infrastructure where downtime or data loss of even a few seconds could have a massive business impact.

In such scenarios, the failure model should consider not just the loss of a broker or a zone, but the loss of an entire region. The business is expected to operate without interruption even when a whole region goes down, and it should be possible to also roll the cluster safely while operating in that state, to apply any break-glass changes.

But what actually happens inside Kafka when an entire region goes down? What happens to the replicas, producer writes, and KRaft quorum? And what happens when that region comes back?

Let's walk through these scenarios using a Tier-0 multi-region Kafka architecture.

For a Tier-0 multi-region Kafka cluster, we need three different regions with isolated failure domains and a minimum of two brokers in each region.

Brokers in each region should be configured with rack awareness to indicate their failure domains as follows:

For Tier-0 workloads, each topic's partitions should be configured to have a replication factor (RF) of 6. Kafka's rack-aware replica assignment will spread the replicas across the three regions. If the automatic replica assignment doesn't allocate two replicas per region, we have to explicitly reassign replicas immediately after topic creation to meet our availability guarantees.

This way, if one region goes down entirely, we still have four replicas surviving and the cluster would still continue to operate.

But just running brokers in multiple regions is not the solution here. In fact, that's the easy part. The hard question is, what guarantee remains when one of those regions disappears, and does it solve the business needs?

The two brokers in that region become unavailable, leaving four surviving replicas across Regions B and C.

For any partitions whose leaders were in Region A, Kafka needs to elect new leaders from the surviving in-sync replicas.

But having four surviving replicas alone does not determine whether Kafka will continue accepting writes.

The next step is to define what is considered a successful write in this Kafka setup. For this, we need two configs:

min.insync.replicas determines the minimum number of replicas that should be present in the in-sync replica set (ISR) of a partition for Kafka to accept writes when producers use acks=all.

acks=all is a producer-side config that ensures that the producer will get an acknowledgment only when the write has been successfully replicated to the required in-sync replicas.

These two settings work together to satisfy the durability guarantees we want.

When all three regions are healthy, ISR would include all six replicas. Let's say one region goes down, then the ISR would drop down to four.

Since minISR is three, writes will still continue to work.

There may be temporary interruptions while Kafka detects the failure, elects new leaders, and clients reconnect to them. But once the surviving leaders are available, the cluster can continue accepting writes as long as the ISR requirements are met.

The goal isn't availability at any cost, but rather the system should be available as long as the durability guarantees that we designed for can be maintained.

Now let's make the scenario more interesting.

Region A is still down. We have four replicas surviving across Regions B and C.

What if we need to roll the cluster one broker at a time, to apply any break-glass changes?

During that time, the ISR can go down from four to three. But since minISR is three, writes will still continue to work.

Let's look at how the cluster behaves under different failure scenarios.

Kafka will stop accepting writes only when the surviving ISR drops below three.

This is an important distinction for Tier-0 workloads.

It's not sufficient to design a cluster that survives a region failure. We also need to consider whether the cluster can continue operating safely while already in that degraded state.

So far, we focused on the data plane. Now switching gears, the KRaft controllers have a completely different availability model.

They form the metadata quorum, and a majority is needed to continue operation.

For our setup, five controllers could be distributed as 2 + 2 + 1 across the three regions, requiring a majority of three to maintain quorum.

If either of the regions containing two controllers goes down, three controllers remain. If the region containing one controller goes down, four remain.

So, the controller quorum survives the loss of any one region.

But, unlike brokers, we cannot necessarily roll the controllers at that point because taking one controller down could cause the quorum to drop below three.

With a static quorum, one way to solve this is to use more controllers, and a 3 + 3 + 3 distribution would provide this. Losing one region would leave six controllers with room to still roll the controllers, as we only need five to maintain quorum.

On the flip side, an increase in quorum size also increases the coordination overhead. The official Kafka documentation typically recommends three or five controllers, which tolerate one or two concurrent failures respectively.

Alternatively, with dynamic KRaft quorum (KIP-853), introduced in Kafka 3.9, we can add or remove controllers from the voting quorum without restarting the cluster.

For example, with our 2 + 2 + 1 setup, if a region containing two controllers goes down, the remaining three controllers can still maintain quorum. We can then remove the failed controllers from the voting membership, one at a time, reducing the quorum size to three. This allows us to roll one of the surviving controllers while still maintaining the new majority of two.

However, dynamic quorum reconfiguration is not automatic. The surviving controllers must be able to maintain quorum and successfully commit the membership changes before we can proceed with the controller restart.

You need to consider whether you want the same availability guarantee for the controllers as that of the data plane, and whether dynamic quorum reconfiguration during a regional outage is acceptable for your Tier-0 workloads.

So far, we assumed that a region either works or goes down completely.

But the WAN itself becomes a failure mode.

In this setup, a partly working WAN between two regions can be more dangerous than a link that's completely down.

Increased latency, packet loss, or intermittent connectivity issues between regions can cause replication to lag, ultimately resulting in replicas falling out of ISR.

The three regions might be independently healthy, but if the connectivity between them is not, then the availability of the cluster might be impacted.

Going back to the CAP theorem, to tolerate a network partition, we must choose between consistency and availability.

So, if a partition's ISR falls below the configured min.insync.replicas of three due to a network partition, Kafka stops accepting writes with acks=all rather than weakening those guarantees.

Similarly, if the KRaft controller quorum is lost, then no metadata changes, like leader elections, can happen in the cluster, even though existing data-plane traffic may continue for some time.

The availability guarantees we discussed also come with their own costs.

The first cost is client latency. With cross-region replication and acks=all, the network latency between these regions directly affects producer latency. Consumers can also pay the WAN latency cost when consuming from partition leaders located in a different region.

The second cost is replication overhead. With RF=6, there is additional storage, network traffic, and replication-related coordination cost in the brokers compared to a smaller number of replicas.

So, in an architecture like this, monitoring the health of the network paths between these regions is as critical as monitoring the Kafka brokers and controllers.

Metrics like round-trip latency (RTT) between regions, packet loss, TCP retransmissions, connection errors/timeouts, and network throughput/bandwidth utilization are a good start.

When one region goes down, all the partition leaders in that region would move to the two other surviving regions.

This implies that those two regions would have to handle more producer and consumer traffic, network throughput, and disk I/O.

Even if the cluster is designed to satisfy its ISR and controller quorum requirements, if it's not sized to handle these failures when one region goes down, the surviving regions would be overloaded, resulting in higher latencies, timeouts, and operational instability.

So, for Tier-0 infrastructure, capacity planning should always be done for failure states and not stop at normal operations.

Now let's say Region A comes back online.

The brokers in the recovered region might have to catch up on a significant amount of data before they become fully in sync again.

This can result in a sudden burst of cross-region network traffic and disk I/O across all regions.

Region recovery needs to be controlled so that it doesn't overwhelm the healthy part of the cluster.

This can be achieved by throttling the replica catch-up, with the trade-off of longer recovery time to minimize the impact on live production traffic.

Replication throttling needs a deeper discussion of its own, so we won't go into details here.

The important point is that bringing a failed region back online is not simply a matter of restarting its brokers. We need to make sure that the recovery process itself doesn't impact the business.

Before putting a Tier-0 multi-region Kafka cluster into production, validate these scenarios:

There is no shortage of ways to deploy Kafka across multiple regions. The challenge here is to pick the right architecture that addresses all our durability guarantees.

For Tier-0 workloads, this means designing the architecture around failures first.

What happens when a region goes down? Can we still roll the cluster? What continues to work, and at what point do we deliberately stop accepting writes?

Lastly, can we safely bring back the region that was down without impacting the business?

That is ultimately the difference between simply running Kafka across multiple regions versus actually supporting a mission-critical Tier-0 workload.

#10356. Make money or make a difference

Early in your career, you’ve probably been told you have to choose: Make money, or make a difference. Do well first. Then, once you’ve earned it, do good through philanthropy.

I believed that for most of my career. I spent decades on Wall Street, eventually becoming a partner in one of the country’s leading alternative investment firms, where I oversaw its real estate business.

Simultaneously, I spent years as a philanthropist. Both paths left me unsatisfied. Growing net worth felt hollow, and many of the charities I funded treated symptoms without “curing the disease.”

A FALSE CHOICE

What I’ve learned since is that the choice is false. Some of the best investment opportunities for the next generation sit inside society’s hardest problems. They start with the foundations every community depends on: housing, education, and healthcare. That’s where my firm invests, because when those foundations are strong, everything built on them gets stronger too. The investors who see this opportunity first will do well, and they’ll help reshape our world. They will build economic success and solve societal problems at the same time.

When Magic Johnson and I launched our first urban real estate fund in 1998, I thought raising the capital would take six months. It took two-and-a-half years. Investors believed then, as many still do, that attaching a social goal to an investment means sacrificing returns. We proved them wrong. Over 15 years, those funds raised $2 billion, facilitated $6 billion in urban revitalization, and created tens of thousands of jobs while generating strong returns. Potential investors also didn’t believe that an athlete could be a financial success of this scale. Yet today, Magic is a billionaire and proved those doubters wrong. 

WHAT IMPACT INVESTING LOOKS LIKE

Done right, impact investing can deliver better risk-adjusted returns than traditional strategies. This type of investing targets large, growing, unmet needs in markets less tied to the broader economy, where government and philanthropy have historically been the only players.

Take workforce housing. In 2023, over 21 million renter households (49.7 percent of renter households) spent at least 30 percent of their income on housing. Households spending more than 50 percent are considered severely cost-burdened. I’m talking about teachers, police officers, firefighters, and healthcare workers who earn too much for subsidized housing but not enough to buy a home. They don’t need a handout. They need housing that’s within reach.

Building new affordable housing at market-rate returns without public incentives is nearly impossible. Meanwhile, existing affordable units keep disappearing as investors buy them, renovate, and raise rents on the people who can least afford it.

We flipped the model by buying existing properties and keeping rents affordable. Then we offer reduced rent to teachers, law enforcement officers, and healthcare workers who live on-site and provide tutoring, community safety, and health programs in return. 

The result is pride in rentership. When residents feel invested in where they live, they stay longer and treat the property better. In our first housing fund, lease terms increased 32%, crime fell 48%, and economic loss dropped 37%. Net operating income grew 13%, and the fund delivered a 25% internal rate of return, all without raising rents.

The social outcome drove the financial outcome.

IMPACT MARKETING

As impact investing grows, so does impact marketing. Plenty of funds now put “impact” on the label without changing anything underneath. Here are four things to look for.

1. Ask where the impact shows up in the financials. If the social goal could be cut without touching returns, it’s an add-on, and it will be the first thing cut when times get tight. Real impact drives the business. In our housing, the community programs are why tenants stay longer, which is why the numbers work.

2. Look for measured outcomes, not good intentions. Lease duration, crime rates, graduation rates, patient outcomes. If a fund can’t show you the data, the impact is a story, not a strategy.

3. Follow the demand. Durable impact investments meet an existing and growing need. Be wary of anything that depends on creating demand or on a single subsidy that could disappear.

4. Look at who’s on the team. Ask whether the people making decisions understand the problem firsthand. Our team includes former teachers, physicians, law enforcement officers, and frontline workers alongside recovering bankers. That expertise is how we spot financial and social risk before it costs anyone.

FINAL THOUGHTS

Too many Americans have their health, education, and economic outcomes determined by where they were born. That isn’t sustainable, and government and philanthropy can’t solve it alone.

If you’re early in your career, you have something my generation didn’t: proof that you don’t have to choose. You can build a career and a portfolio around solving the problems that matter most, and get paid for doing it.

That’s the conversation I want to have with the next generation of investors. Impact investing has never been more critical, and it has never been more rewarding.

Bobby Turner is founder of Turner Impact Capital.

#10353. What’s happening with banks today? Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo customers report widespread outages

If you’re having trouble accessing your bank account today, you’re not alone.

Customers at several U.S. financial giants reported problems accessing their accounts on Monday as widespread service disruptions appear to have hit Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and other financial institutions.

The problems started Monday morning, November 16, when thousands of customers began reporting trouble logging in to their Chase accounts, checking their balances, and completing transactions.

According to outage-tracking website Downdetector, Chase appeared to be the hardest hit, with more than 4,000 reports by early Monday afternoon. But Chase wasn’t alone: Bank of America and Wells Fargo also saw spikes in customer complaints, along with U.S. Bank and payment service Zelle.

Reached for comment by Fast Company, a Chase spokesperson said that a technical issue impacted not only Chase but also other banks it does business with.

“JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems—there is no evidence this is cyber-related,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “It is taking longer than usual to service some customers. This is not a systemic issue—other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us. Customers still have access to their accounts and funds. We’re working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today.”

Fast Company has also reached out to the other banks for more details.

The banking troubles come after multiple separate major technology disruptions in recent days, including a widespread Microsoft Outlook outage on Thursday and a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop Friday, disrupting air travel across the country.

There’s no confirmed connection between those incidents and Monday’s banking problem.

Is Chase down?

Chase customers began reporting problems around 9:48 a.m. ET Monday, according to Downdetector.

Logging into the website was among the most common complaints, although some customers also ran into issues with the mobile app and viewing their account balances and transaction histories.

And the problems are not limited to online banking.

Some customers on Reddit reported trouble accessing services at physical Chase branches, suggesting the disruption could extend beyond the bank’s website and app.

At one New York City branch visited by Fast Company on Monday, Chase associates were alerting customers as they entered the door that systems were down.

Issues at Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and other financial giants

While possibly the worst hit, Chase wasn’t the only bank having a rough Monday, though Chase indicated that those issues were related to its own technical issues.

Downdetector also recorded a jump in outage reports involving Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank, and Truist. Some customers said they were unable to view transactions or complete payments and transfers.

Zelle, the popular person-to-person payment service used by many major banks, also saw more outage complaints.

It’s worth keeping in mind that Downdetector relies on reports submitted by users. A spike in complaints doesn’t necessarily mean a bank’s entire system is down, and the numbers don’t reflect the total number of customers affected.

The Pentagon has been testing packs of autonomous ground vehicles (UGVs) in simulated combat situations. In mid-October, at Fort Knox’s St. Vith Range in Kentucky, four UGVs “worked as a team, negotiating and surveilling the rolling landscape in search of enemy forces,” recalls a DARPA blog post. These UGVs are highly modular and can be kitted out with a wide range of tactical add-ons, but target engagement was controlled by a human operator. This latest exercise was prompted by the request of European allies.

“Out here at Fort Knox, we’re looking at how autonomous mobility technology can be paired with payloads to enable new warfighter capabilities,” explained Jason Gregory, technical advisor at DARPA. The blog notes that this location was also chosen as it represents a similar landscape to the European theater.

During the demo an operator received a tip about a simulated threat alongside some satellite imagery. They then sent the pack of UGVs to the area to surveil the landscape and identify targets. Smartly, a sole UGV went ahead of the pack to scout, with the three others waiting behind. The scout UGV was equipped with a flying drone. In a real-world scenario this could have been flown for better visuals or to strike the targets from the sky. “Soldiers can mount anything and everything onto – 240 Bravos, drones, rockets,” said a technician attending the demo, as they are “super modular platforms.” The blog says three of the four UGVs in the exercise had drones.

After the designated area was scouted by the leading autonomous ground vehicle, other UGVs followed on “to provide cover and support.” A simulated rocket was fired at a target identified about 300 yards from the robot pack. Finally, the last robot came out of cover, higher up over a ridge, to assess the field of conflict.

It was emphasized that during the exercise, a human operator was controlling any kinetic engagement. “All the mobility, all the movement, all the detections, all of that is autonomous,” explained Gregory. “But they don’t pull the trigger until a human says pull the trigger.”

This exercise was part of DARPA’s Robotic Autonomy in Complex Environments with Resiliency, or RACER program. Expertise required for RACER’s success includes vehicle design, algorithm technologies, super intelligence, and secure communications.

After five years of work, these UGVs can now be instructed to complete tasks on the battlefield, instead of being manually driven, notes Gregory. They roam off-road as fast as any human driver could manage, at a minimum.

#10349. Nearly half of Americans are making the same gamble with their holiday travel plans

Air travel is getting more and more expensive. And as prices continue to soar, American travelers are becoming desperate for deals on flights. Oftentimes, they’re even delaying bookings or totally altering holiday travel in order to score reasonably priced plane tickets.

The findings come from a new report from the online travel agency and flight consolidator CheapOair, which surveyed 1,000 U.S. consumers to understand how travelers are making decisions around holiday travel promotions. The survey found that modern day fliers are more willing to book flights at the last minute, often waiting for promotions that happen on Black Friday, Cyber Monday, and Travel Tuesday. In fact, nearly half (49%) of the survey’s respondents said they have delayed bookings in order to shop holiday travel deals. Another 60% say they are likely to consider doing so in the future.

Still, while fliers are perhaps more deal-driven than ever before, they’re not consistently convinced that they’ll be able to find true savings. More than a quarter (26%) said they believe holiday deals are mostly marketing hype, whereas 17% believe the savings are totally legit. Another 57% say the deals are a mixed bag of both savings and hype.

It’s not all that surprising that consumer confidence is fading when it comes to shopping for deals, however. As companies increasingly utilize tactics like surveillance pricing—which relies on using consumer data and algorithms to adjust prices on things like groceries, home items, and even flights—many people worry about how transparent modern businesses are being with their marketing tactics. 

Last year, Delta Air Lines announced it would more widely deploy the method of price-setting. “The practice of dynamic pricing is certainly not new in the airline industry,” Kerry Tan, professor of economics at Loyola University Maryland, previously told Fast Company of the announcement. “Certainly, Delta, as with any other company, is profit-driven and stands to gain” from the tactic,” he said. 

Tan added: “As an economist, we assume that companies are profit maximizers, and so in a way I see this as companies really making a push toward that objective of profit maximization.”

It’s also not that surprising that customers are increasingly worried about the cost of air travel. That’s true because prices are undoubtedly reaching staggering new highs. According to federal data, airfare was up 22% this past September when compared with the year before. A September 2026 report from Hopper media also found that round-trip domestic airfare for Thanksgiving travel is up 31% from 2025, while Christmas travel is already up by 23%.

As prices keep climbing, cost is by far the biggest concern consumers have when it comes to holiday travel. Per the CheapOair survey, 39% say it’s their biggest worry compared with other concerns like flight delays and cancellations (18%), crowded airports (15%), and winter weather disrupting their plans (10%).

Still, savvy shoppers aren’t just sitting back and fretting. Some are altering their holiday travel plans altogether. While changing their travel destinations is an unpopular choice, with only 7% saying they’re open to the change, 43% will change their preferred travel dates in order to land a better price.

While it’s not unheard of to book flights on cheaper travel days, holiday travelers who do so risk missing out on family traditions or planned events. However, with soaring energy costs making travel less affordable than ever, missing the family football game or even the whole turkey dinner might be what it takes to go home for the holidays.

#10348. How to Build an Accessible Gold Value Calculator in Vanilla JavaScript

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Ask anyone selling an old chain or a broken ring what they want to know, and it's one thing: what is this worth? A small calculator can answer that in a second, but most of the ones you find online get the details wrong. They ignore troy ounces, treat 14K as 58.5% one day and 58.3% the next, or show a "value" that no buyer will ever pay.

In this tutorial, we'll build a gold value calculator that gets those details right. It runs on plain HTML and JavaScript, updates as the user types, works with a screen reader, keeps its state in a shareable URL and pulls a live spot price through a small Node.js endpoint. The calculation lives in one pure function, so we can test it in a few lines.

Every gold calculator comes down to three inputs: how much the item weighs, how much of that weight is actually gold, and what pure gold is trading for today.

Purity is measured in karats, out of 24. A 14K ring is 14 parts gold and 10 parts other metals, so it's 14 ÷ 24 = 58.3% gold. You'll also see 14K stamped as "585", which is the hallmark many manufacturers use for the same alloy. For a calculator, the karat fraction is the safer default:

The second detail most tutorials miss is the unit. Gold spot prices are quoted in USD per troy ounce, which is 31.1035 grams, not the 28.35-gram ounce on a kitchen scale. Jewelers also use pennyweight (dwt), which is 1.5552 grams. If your calculator multiplies grams by a per-ounce price without converting, every result is wrong by a factor of 31.

Put together, the formula looks like this:

For example, with gold at $2,400 per troy ounce, 10 grams of 14K gold contains 5.83 grams of pure gold, which is worth $449.85 at melt.

That $449.85 is the value of the gold content alone. Refiners and buyers pay a percentage of it, because refining, assaying and handling cost money. Depending on the buyer, the item and the market, the payout can sit well below melt value.

That gap is why good production tools separate the two numbers. A dedicated scrap jewelry gold calculator, like the one The Alloy Market offers, lets sellers estimate what their gold is worth from its weight and karat before they send anything in. Our calculator does the same job with a payout field: leave it at 100% to see melt value, or enter a buyer's rate to see a realistic offer.

Start with real form controls and a visible

A few choices here matter more than they look:

A little CSS gives touch-friendly controls. Keeping inputs at 16px (1rem) also stops iOS Safari from zooming in when a field gets focus.

The biggest problem with most calculator snippets is that the math is buried inside an event handler, mixed with getElementById calls. You can't test it, and you can't reuse it on a server. Put the calculation and validation in their own module instead:

Both functions take plain values and return plain values. They don't know a DOM exists, which means the same file can run in the browser, in Node.js and in your test runner.

Notice that we don't round inside the calculation. Rounding happens once, at display time. Rounding in the middle of a chain of multiplications is a classic way to end up a few cents off.

Now connect the form to the module. Listening for the input event on the form itself catches changes from every field, including the dropdowns, so there's no need to wire up each control separately.

With the markup, CSS and script in place, here's the finished calculator showing our 10 g, 14K example with an 80% buyer payout:

Asking users to type the spot price works, but prefilling it is friendlier. Don't call a metals price API straight from the browser, though. Your API key would be visible to anyone who opens DevTools, and every visitor would spend one of your API calls.

Instead, put a small endpoint in front of your price provider and cache the result. This example uses Express and the fetch built into Node.js 18 and later:

Three things keep this endpoint dependable:

On the page, the loadSpot() function from Step 3 fills the field and shows the time of the price. The field stays editable, so a seller who has a quote from a specific buyer can type that instead.

A seller comparing offers might want to send their numbers to a family member, or come back to them tomorrow. Because every input has a name, turning the form into a query string is one line with URLSearchParams.

The syncUrl() function in Step 3 runs on every change and uses history.replaceState instead of pushState, so typing doesn't fill the back button with dozens of entries. On load, restoreFromUrl() puts the values back. A link like this opens with the form already filled in:

This is also the progressive enhancement story. If JavaScript fails to load, the form still submits as a GET request. Your server can read the same parameters, import the same gold.js and render the result in HTML.

Because goldValue() is a pure function, testing it needs no browser and no mocks. Node.js ships with a built-in test runner, so there's nothing to install:

Run it with node --test. (Add "type": "module" to your package.json so Node treats the files as ES modules.) The troy ounce test is the one worth keeping forever: if anyone "simplifies" the conversion later, it fails immediately.

A quick checklist for putting this calculator on a real store:

A gold calculator looks like a ten-line script, but the details are what make it useful: converting troy ounces properly, separating melt value from payout, keeping the math testable and making the result accessible and shareable. The same pattern of a pure calculation module, a thin DOM layer and a cached server endpoint works for any calculator where the price depends on several inputs, from shipping estimates to currency conversion.

Mathematically, 14K is 14 ÷ 24 = 58.3%. Many manufacturers stamp 14K jewelry "585" and alloy it to that standard, so both numbers are common. Pick one, state it in the dropdown, and use it consistently.

Let the user choose. Most people weigh jewelry in grams, but spot prices are quoted per troy ounce, so the calculator should accept either and convert internally.

Yes. Drop Step 4 and let users type the spot price, or have a scheduled job write the current price into a static JSON file. Everything else runs entirely in the browser.

An app engineer has showcased his homemade breadboard 486 DX2 PC running Doom. The intricate explosion-of-wires system build appears to have taken just 16 days, with the first appearance of the legendary Intel CPU on @nagakurage’s timeline on October 24, and a video demo of some fragging in Doom published on November 9. Moreover, the Tokyo-based app engineer behind the project also developed and made a bezelicious ‘CRT monitor’ to go with the homemade early-90s-era gaming beast.

はじめてDOOMで遊びます、自作のi486 PCで https://t.co/feosWgd6deNovember 9, 2026

This project’s first signs of life were seen towards the end of October. On October 24, @nagakurage showcased the legendary Intel i486 DX2 CPU that he had acquired. It was the sought-after DX2 66 model, which meant it ran at a blistering 66 MHz internally, and 33 MHz externally (2x multiplier). On the other side of this gray made-in-Malaysia chip, you can see its 168 pins, which look incredibly tree-trunk-like by today’s standards.

The enthusiast next bought a Colorlight i9 v7.2 FPGA board to attach the CPU to and to cover chipset duties. We know this is a breadboard PC, but there are limits… Every pin of the 486 CPU appears to have been connected separately to an experimental ‘socket’ made using a baseboard.

i486 CPU実験用ソケット完成 低クロックで動かなければ基盤発注する https://t.co/cXCnvPtkQ5October 24, 2026

A significant milestone was reached on October 26, when the finished form of the breadboard system started to come into view, and the dev managed to get the CPU to blink an LED using x86 code. RAM was added on October 31, and tweaked to be error-free. Then, on November 3, the enthusiast managed to add microSD storage to the system. That same day @nagakurage enjoyed seeing the breadboard 486 boot FreeDOS 1.3 for the first time [machine translation].

The app developer then took a 3D printing diversion and used his Bambu Lab A1 mini to output the parts necessary for a custom CRT-style enclosure. This was designed by Claude and was assembled with a 5-inch 800×480 Elecrow Raspberry Pi panel inside.

Finally, on November 9, @nagakurage showcased his breadboard PC and era-matching design beige-shelled monitor side-by-side and powered up. The seminal shooter looked smooth enough on the vintage 1992 silicon, as it should do.

Going forward, the enthusiast wants to refine this breadboard-based project and make it fully PC-98 compatible, in line with the dominant NEC PC-9800 series in Japan in the early 90s.

#10344. Benefits need to change with the times

Over the next five years, AI will change the people companies need and the work they do. At the same time, medical costs will keep taking more of the benefits budget. Employers will have to rethink what it means to take care of their people.

The change is already underway. Agents write code, run tests, and carry out research assignments. OpenAI reports that an internal model has resolved more than 100 long-standing math problems.

For many companies, though, there’s still a gap between giving individuals better tools and changing how the business runs. Agents need access to company information, permission to act, and a way to get help when something goes wrong. Research co-led by Chicago Fed economist Ezra Karger points to uneven adoption as a reason technical progress takes time to reach the economy.

Here’s what I anticipate: By 2028, expect more tasks to be handed to AI, with people checking the results. By 2030, companies will reorganize around that work. By 2032, agents will carry assignments across departments, bringing people in when a decision or approval is needed.

WORK CHANGES AT DIFFERENT SPEEDS

Software, law, and consulting will move fastest. As coding, research, and drafting take fewer hours, people will focus more on deciding what matters and checking the work. Firms will have to figure out how people learn to become experts when the work that used to teach them has been automated. Stanford research already finds weaker hiring for young workers in AI-exposed jobs, although it does not establish causation.

Physical work will change more slowly. Better planning helps a manufacturer, but someone still has to maintain the equipment. Patients still need nurses, and homes still need electricians. Anthropic’s scenarios show how cheaper knowledge work can support demand for hands-on work.

MEDICAL COSTS KEEP CLIMBING

Meanwhile, healthcare keeps getting more expensive. Aon expects costs to rise 9.5% in 2027 before employers take steps to offset the increase. CMS projects health spending growing faster than GDP through 2034. KFF finds workers’ contributions toward family coverage rose 9% this year.

Employers can spend considerably more and still deliver bad news at open enrollment. Employees see a bigger deduction from their paycheck. Explaining that the increase would otherwise have been worse doesn’t make it feel like a better benefit.

Routine assignments will take fewer hours, and companies will depend more on people with experience. Losing someone with hard-earned judgment or trusted customer relationships will be harder for a lean team to absorb.

Good medical coverage remains essential. But competing on medical alone is becoming a losing proposition.

Employers are trying to get medical spending under control through allowances for individual insurance, higher-deductible plans, and medical captives that pool large-claim risk. These approaches change how costs and risks are shared. They don’t stop medical inflation.

LIFE NAVIGATION GIVES PEOPLE PRACTICAL HELP

Non-medical benefits offer more room to make each dollar count. In MetLife’s survey published earlier this year, 73% of employers called them the most cost-effective way to support employee well-being.

One way to put that support into practice is life navigation: someone who helps find care for a parent, sort out a disputed bill, or handle a family emergency. The idea is simple. Give people one place to turn. Someone will do the research, make the calls, and stay with the problem until it’s sorted out.

AI can handle routine legwork, but human support still matters when life gets complicated.

Leave and PTO, housing assistance, income protection, and financial well-being support helps employers stand out. So does life navigation. People remember who helped when life got hard. That matters when deciding where to work—and whether to stay.

Jon Cooper is CEO of Overalls.

#10343. How to replace the battery on Pixel Tag [Video]

The battery on the Pixel Tag is rated for about a year, but what happens when you need to replace it? Here’s how to replace it.

Due to the shape and design of the Pixel Tag, you might have a bit of difficulty getting the backplate off quickly to throw in a new battery when it’s time.

Having had a few problems myself (yes, a me problem most likely) due to the slick, smooth shape, I figured that, even though it might insult the intelligence of many, the process was at least documented so that anyone having issues has a reference to come to if they’re struggling to get that backplate off.

You will have difficulty if you try to do this one-handed. Instead, clasp the Pixel Tag with one thumb at the base or midframe, then with your other thumb twist anticlockwise until the backplate comes loose and the battery will drop out.

The first time you do this, it will be harder due to the tight factory seal. However, once it’s open, the process gets easier to replicate. Here’s a little demonstration of how to get it off without it slipping and being flung into the ether:

Be aware that you may need to open and reseat the battery if Find Hub does not recognize the Pixel Tag again when you’ve done this. Even with the factory-supplied battery, it can misalign if you don’t place it in the correct position and fully close the door when reassembling.

If you’re wondering what type of battery you need, CR2032 are the standard for watches and most Android trackers. They’re super cheap with a 10-pack of Amazon Basics batteries for just $10, Duracell offers a 4-pack for under $7 but you can even get unbranded 20-packs for around $9. All fairly cheap at various points in the quality spectrum.

It can’t hurt to have some on hand when you do eventually need to replace the battery in your Pixel Tag. You can get the tracker from Amazon and the Google Store right now.
