Non-planar 3D printing has mostly been experimental, but PancakeSlicer could finally make more people interested in trying it out and find more ways to improve it and use it practically.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Alpaca Engineering posted a YouTube video yesterday showcasing his self-hostable non-planar slicer. He explains that most non-planar 3D printing — printing across all three axes, rather than in 2D horizontal layers — demonstrations are usually for research purposes, for demonstration and experimentation, with no easy way for most 3D printer owners to try out non-planar 3D printing. His project, named PancakeSlicer, aims to fix this by making his non-planar slicing algorithm as easy to implement as existing slicing workflows, even improving upon it with 3D printer management features.

Alpaca Engineering explains that every few months, a non-planar 3D printing demonstration goes viral, but is rarely adopted practically by most 3D printer owners. Most non-planar experiments are for research, with half-abandoned GitHub projects. He further explains that non-planar isn’t widely adopted not because there aren’t any general-purpose non-planar slicers, but because it’s not accessible and easily implemented in a familiar workflow, with 3D printer owners spoiled by modern workflows and not needing to manually run G-code directly from an SD card.

Commercially available 3D printers are also not optimized for non-planar 3D printing. The challenge with printing at various angles is the clearance angle needed to bring a print head up and down without crashing into its own print. The slicer uses 3D models of various print heads from different 3D printer models to know how to slice the object to avoid collisions, thus having limited support; but Alpaca Engineering has listed a large number of supported 3D printers from Bambu Lab, Prusa, Creality, Voron, and many others. The varying shapes of the print heads also mean different printers will have different capabilities, with some managing less angle and curvature than others.

Alpaca Engineering also has great animations and practical demonstrations of the different slicing algorithms in the slicer, including how the algorithm slices the object for non-planar printing. We highly suggest you watch the video if you’re interested, as his animations explain non-planar slicing intuitively.

One of the best features of this slicer is its self-hosting features. Users can host the slicer from a desktop, NAS, or a home server and access it with a web UI, allowing multiple users to send print jobs from any device. It also has 3D printer management features, applying different profiles to different printer brands, unifying the experience without hopping from one slicer to another to operate multiple 3D printers — this is even available to Bambu Lab users, replacing Bambu Studio and Bambu Connect in LAN-only mode. The slicer can also manage two slice jobs at the same time in case other users happen to be slicing at the same time.

While PancakeSlicer isn’t the first to implement self-hosted 3D printer management features, it certainly levels up his initial goal of making non-planar slicing as easy to access as most modern workflows. We hope to see how more people can experiment with non-planar 3D printing, contribute their findings, and rapidly improve upon it as a genuinely practical slicing method.

#10339. Fed chair weighs AI’s economic impact, but sidesteps inflation risk

Artificial intelligence could accelerate innovation and usher in an era of faster economic growth, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said Monday in remarks that also acknowledged risks from the technology.

The adoption of AI could also lead to widespread job loss or a steep drop in the stock market if the healthy returns expected from the huge investments in AI infrastructure don’t materialize, Warsh said. But he did not mention inflation, even though many of his colleagues blame the buildout of data centers for accelerating price increases.

Warsh’s remarks kicked off a one-day conference on AI and productivity at the Fed’s San Francisco branch. The Fed chairman did not comment on what the Fed’s next steps would be on interest rates, nor did he say anything about recent government data showing that inflation accelerated last month. That data led many of Warsh’s colleagues on the Fed’s rate-setting committee to signal their support for additional interest rate hikes, including at the Fed’s next meeting in December.

“What might set SI apart, as an economic influence, is that it could supercharge idea generation,” Warsh said. “It appears to be changing the method—and, at least as important, the speed—of innovation. If idea generation broadens, growth could be sustained at a level substantially higher than the long-run average.”

The Fed refers to AI as “super intelligence” following an executive order issued by President Donald Trump requiring federal agencies to use the term.

Yet Warsh also spent more time in his remarks considering the downsides of AI than he has in previous speeches. The chairman has previously touted AI as a technology that could significantly boost the economy’s efficiency, which would enable it to grow without worsening inflation. In turn, the Fed could potentially lower interest rates under that scenario.

“As policymakers, we have to be mindful that great opportunities rarely come risk-free,” Warsh said. “And the risks in this case, if overlooked, can be highly disruptive and economically costly.”

For example, “after significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment,” he said. Fed staff has begun evaluating different scenarios for how AI’s impact may play out, Warsh added.

The conference Monday was part of a task force Warsh set up to evaluate AI and its impact on the economy’s efficiency. Warsh appointed five different task forces soon after taking the helm at the Fed.

Warsh on Monday did not address AI’s impact on inflation, a top concern of many of his Fed colleagues. Last week, several policymakers expressed concern that AI is fanning inflation because the buildout of AI infrastructure has sharply raised demand for computer chips, electronic components, electricity, and copper.

Those increases, in turn, have lifted the cost of smartphones, computers, and other consumer electronics. Smartphone prices rose last month at the fastest pace on record, the government said last week.

In addition, Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said Friday that if AI does accelerate economic growth, it could lead to higher interest rates over time, even if inflation declines.

“If the new technology leads to permanently higher levels of productivity growth, it may increase firms’ desire to invest and, hence, their demand for funding, raising the level of interest rates,” Jefferson said.

—By Christopher Rugaber, AP economics writer

#10337. Kevin O’Leary tells Gen Z: ‘Every generation has had whiners like you’

Shark Tank investor and businessman Kevin O’Leary is at odds with Gen Z, who say building wealth and success is harder for their generation than it was for his.

In Jubilee Media’s latest Surrounded video—an online series where a single public figure faces 25 individuals with opposing viewpoints—O’Leary, known as “Mr. Wonderful,” takes on a slate of questions regarding success and wealth.

But it’s one particular conversation in the nearly two-hour-long video that has gained traction on social media.

When the discussion turned to O’Leary’s assertion that “if you want to be successful, work-life balance comes second,” one participant pushed back on how realistic that advice is today.

“We used to have work-life balance—we don’t have that anymore,” one of the participants told O’Leary. “My question to you is, how do you believe that our generation is supposed to be successful and have a work-life balance if we can’t even afford what success would look like, which is owning a home and not being straddled by student loans and medical debt.”

O’Leary quickly replied, “Every single generation has had whiners like you in it. Each generation is surprised to find out things change in the economy all the time.”

Twenty years ago, O’Leary continued, a liberal arts or humanities degree could be considered an “economic disaster,” whereas today, videographers and storytellers are “making anywhere from $200,000 to $400,000 working for corporations.”

‘The kids . . . have totally given up’

As the clip made the rounds on social media, some agreed with O’Leary’s stance on the matter, echoing the age-old claim that younger generations are less willing to work than their older counterparts.

“Not a huge Kevin O’Leary guy, but the kids he’s speaking with have totally given up. They need to keep pushing, they break through or change careers,” one user said on X.

But for most, Mr. Wonderful’s comments came across as disconnected from reality.

“With a straight face, Kevin said “photographers, videographers are making $200-$400k a year.” Out of touch doesn’t even begin to describe this guy’s ignorance,” one user replied on YouTube.

“Kevin O’Leary needs to go walk in the shoes of a middle-class American for a week. He has no idea what he’s talking about,” another added on X.

For others, the conversation further highlighted the tensions between generations.

A user on X added: “Kevin’s generation got theirs, bought houses cheap, got money to build businesses, got cheap college, then changed the rules to fuck every other generation after them.”

The video and the discourse surrounding it also pointed to a larger problem: Neither side can reach consensus.

A user added: “Problem is, the truth is somewhere in the middle of both tales being told, and nobody wants to acknowledge that their respective sides are both overstating the opposing ends of the equation.”

#10336. What Breaks When a Self-Hosted LLM Gateway Hits 1,000 Concurrent Streams

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

We sent 1,000 streaming calls at the same moment through three self-hosted LLM gateways: the Langfuse AI Gateway, the LiteLLM proxy and AcruxCore. Each gateway was limited to 2 CPUs. As shipped, Langfuse finished 261 of the 1,000 streams and LiteLLM finished 403. Neither failure came from the gateway's own code.

Langfuse's failures came from Linux's open-file limit, which Docker sets to 1,024 by default. LiteLLM had that problem too, plus a second one: an empty key cache sent hundreds of database lookups at once, and the ones that waited longer than 10 seconds were rejected. This article shows how each failure looked, how we traced it to its cause, and the settings that fixed it.

This benchmark measured the resource consumption of three LLM gateways under scaling concurrent streaming loads.

Full latency, memory, and feature results are available in the Langfuse vs LiteLLM vs AcruxCore benchmark.

First-token times are medians of the streams that succeeded. Up to 250 streams, every gateway succeeded. Then the errors started, and they did not look alike:

A 502 and a 503 point at different layers, so we expected two different causes. Two of the three turned out to share one cause.

Linux counts every network connection as an open file, and it caps how many open files one process may hold. The cap has two values. The soft limit is the cap that is in force now. The hard limit is the ceiling: a process may raise its own soft limit up to that value, and no further.

A streaming gateway holds two connections for each stream: one from the client, and one to the model provider. That makes about 1,000 open files at 500 streams, and about 2,000 at 1,000 streams. A gateway also needs a few more files for its database, its logs and its own libraries.

Docker on our machine gave every container a soft limit of 1,024 and a hard limit of 524,288. All three gateways received the same two numbers. What differed was how each program treats them when it starts:

Node.js raises its own soft limit to the hard limit at startup. The Rust and Python services keep 1,024, and neither project's Compose file sets a higher value. So the two gateways ran out of open files near 500 streams, which is the point where the errors started.

The out-of-files error appeared as a failed connection, not as a clear message. The Langfuse gateway's logs showed failed connections to OpenAI, and also failed connections to Langfuse's own web service, which the gateway asks to check each key. Both come from one cause: a process that cannot open another file cannot open another socket. Its client then receives a 502.

Read the limit the process actually has, not the one you think Docker gave it. Process 1 is usually the main process in a container:

If the gateway runs under a supervisor or several workers, check each worker's process ID instead of process 1. To see how close a process is to its limit under load, count its open file descriptors:

Raise the limit for the gateway service in its Compose file. We used 65,536 for all three gateways:

The same ulimits block works on the LiteLLM service. On Kubernetes or another platform, check /proc//limits inside a running container rather than assuming a value.

With the open-file limit raised, the Langfuse gateway finished all 1,000 streams. LiteLLM still returned 503 errors. To separate the two causes, we ran LiteLLM with one worker and only the open-file limit raised. All 500 streams succeeded in that ladder, but 595 of 1,000 failed with 503.

The 503 message names the authentication database, so we read LiteLLM's logs and its source. The log gave the same reason for all 840 failed streams in these runs, 595 in that ladder and 245 in the cold-cache runs below:

When 500 calls arrive while the key is not in the cache, each call looks the key up in Postgres. All of those lookups queue for 10 connections. The worker was also using its whole CPU allowance at this point, which slows every query it sends and receives. We infer that this CPU load lengthens the queue, but we did not measure it separately. Whatever the share of each, the lookups at the back of the queue miss the 10-second deadline.

If that explanation is right, the failures should depend on whether the key is already in the cache. So we ran 500 streams four more times. Three runs started after 75 seconds with no calls, which is longer than the 60-second cache. One run started right after a single warm-up call:

The warm run had no failures. The cold runs failed by different amounts, 161, 84 and 0, because the result depends on how many lookups miss the deadline, and that changes from run to run. This probably explains why the earlier ladder succeeded at 500 and failed at 1,000. A run is a race between the lookup queue and the deadline, so a single ladder does not show where the limit is.

The warm-up result is the one we measured. Send one call with each virtual key after LiteLLM starts, and avoid quiet periods longer than 60 seconds before a traffic spike. A steady flow of traffic keeps the key in the cache.

LiteLLM also exposes three settings that act on this path. We did not test them, so treat them as places to look rather than proven fixes:

We raised the open-file limit to 65,536 for all three gateways and gave LiteLLM 2 workers, one per CPU, as its production guide recommends for a single machine. Then we ran the full ladder again:

The open-file errors were gone for every gateway, and the Langfuse gateway gave the fastest first token of the three. LiteLLM still returned 120 × 503 at 500. That level started about 60 seconds after the first call of the ladder, so the cached key had probably just expired. All 1,000 succeeded at the next level, which started within 60 seconds of the 500 level.

Once nothing failed, CPU decided the first-token times. LiteLLM used its whole 2-CPU allowance from 100 streams on, and its median first token took 19.2 seconds at 1,000 streams. AcruxCore also used both CPUs from 100 streams on, and its first token at 1,000 streams was 3.8 s at the median and 9.7 s at p95. The Langfuse gateway peaked at 1.65 CPUs and 168 MiB, with a first token of 1.7 s at the median and 9.6 s at p95.

Each gateway also needs the rest of its stack, and that stack uses CPU too. While the Langfuse gateway served 500 streams, its whole stack used up to 3.1 CPUs, because the web service checked keys and the worker and ClickHouse stored usage. AcruxCore's whole stack peaked at 4.0 CPUs, because its API writes a trace for every call to Postgres. Size the stack around the gateway, not only the gateway container.

Talha Anwar is a senior AI and full-stack engineer and writes about building and running AI systems at talhaanwar.com.

#10335. Google Voice appears to finally be working on RCS support

It might finally be happening. A new Google Voice update plants seeds of RCS support, though the exact details remain unclear.

About APK Insight: In this “APK Insight” post, we’ve decompiled the latest version of an application that Google uploaded to the Play Store. When we decompile these files (called APKs, in the case of Android apps), we’re able to see various lines of code within that hint at possible future features. Keep in mind that Google may or may not ever ship these features, and our interpretation of what they are may be imperfect. We’ll try to enable those that are closer to being finished, however, to show you how they’ll look in case that they do ship. With that in mind, read on.

Google Voice is an invaluable tool for accessing one phone number across a host of different devices, but to say it’s becoming less impactful without support for RCS is a bit of an understatement. Now that virtually every Android phone and iPhone supports the new messaging experience, Google Voice is less useful both for business and consumer users.

Google Voice for Android version 2026.11.01.1014278023 doesn’t enable RCS, but it does, for the first time, actually hint that the functionality might be on its way. In a teardown of the app, one simple string stands out:

That points to a new send button used for RCS messages rather than SMS. Google Messages similarly changes its send button to differentiate between the two standards.

This is great news. I can have both options now to text friends and businesses with RCS as a fallback option on Google Voice because I don't want to give out my Google messages number.

This update contains a host of other new strings around images, videos, and more, but none of them are directly tied to RCS support.

The folks over at Android Authority dug up some other tidbits about RCS including an “RCS chat preference” toggle and various RCS actions and messages. But, again, nothing is live just yet, and there’s no word on when it might arrive, if ever.

Google has been championing RCS support for over a decade now, so it’s long past due for Voice, a long-running Google product, to get on board. While the tidbits in this update don’t serve as any confirmation RCS if coming to Voice, it’s the most exciting update on the matter in years.

Judge Noël Wise, who presides over the proposed class-action lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, has denied the companies’ motion to have the case dismissed. According to the decision, the defendants’ argument that the legal action is just “a rerun” of the same antitrust case filed against the industry in 2018 was rejected as the plaintiffs have established that there’s some new evidence suggesting that there was collusion between the big three memory chip manufacturers.

Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix argued that they watch each other like hawks because of how tight competition is. Judge Wise disagreed with this characterization, though, saying that what they are accused of goes beyond that. “Their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation — an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do.”

The plaintiffs, which are made up of 17 individuals and small businesses, allege that the companies made four parallel moves that restricted DRAM supply and led to the current shortage, which saw prices jump by as much as 500% in one year. One of the events they cited included the “simultaneous DRAM production cuts” from October 2022 to April 2023, which was quickly followed by a “coordinated pivot to HBM.” They also said that the three companies announced the winding down of DDR4 production in a span of three months and have failed to expand the production capacity “despite these extraordinary prices — the single most powerful supply signal the DRAM industry has ever produced.”

Other factors that the suing parties brought to the table include the introduction of stringent customer vetting procedures in response to the shortage, the refusal to sign long-term contracts for DRAM customers, Micron’s decision to shut down Crucial (its consumer memory brand), multiple statements projecting the shortage, as well as their involvement in previous price-fixing scandals.

The big three memory chip makers argued that all of these are logical business moves so that they can maximize their revenue during a period of great demand and that they are “consistent with [their own] independent self-interest.” They also said that they appear to have similar behaviors because they’re in a highly concentrated market, and that they’re all “reacting to the same market pressures,” thus it would make sense for them to have a similar response.

Despite their rebuttals, the judge decided that the case is plausible enough to move forward. This isn’t a judgment, though — both sides would still have to show their evidence and speak their arguments before the court before getting a decision. Because of this, the three companies are given until December 7 to respond to the original complaint with the case management conference, which will determine the administrative matters on the case, set for January 2027.

#10332. The FAA’s ground stop has a simple culprit. Its causes may not

On Friday afternoon, L3Harris Technologies was doing what it has done at Federal Aviation Administration facilities month after month: moving a communications line off decades-old copper and onto fiber, work that federal auditors count as part of a $12.5 billion overhaul of the country’s air traffic control system.

Shortly after a technician installed a new router at an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, the device began pumping out data—so much that the flood disrupted communications at 17 of the 22 so-called en route centers that handle high-altitude traffic.

At 3:36 p.m. Eastern, with about 3,500 planes in the air, the FAA held all departures nationwide. The stop lasted more than four hours, until 8:15 p.m. Airlines canceled more than 5,000 flights by Saturday and about 1,500 more on Sunday as they repositioned crews and aircraft. It was the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when the system that sends safety notices to pilots failed.

“We haven’t determined what the fault was,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a Saturday news conference. Investigators are trying to establish whether L3Harris installed or configured the router incorrectly, or whether the equipment itself was at fault. Adam Bauer, a spokesperson for Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns router maker Juniper Networks, told Fast Company its devices appeared to have worked as intended. “Based on what we know and have been told by others, our equipment was working as configured.”

But the failure exposed weaknesses the FAA has been warned about for years: a contractor that has run the FAA’s network since 2002 and has a record of outages, an integrator the agency’s own staff rated a financial risk, a technician workforce the FAA admits is understaffed, and a $12.5 billion overhaul that auditors say is racing ahead without a master schedule. There is no evidence yet that any of them caused Friday’s failure.

Still, some critics see Friday’s chaos as years of warnings come true. “The sad fact is this has happened before,” Mary Schiavo, a former Transportation Department inspector general, told NPR’s Weekend Edition.

The sprawling network of copper and fiber that carries the country’s air traffic communications across roughly 4,400 FAA sites still runs largely on technology that dates back decades. Some older equipment, including radar, requires replacement parts that can only be obtained through online auction websites or made with 3D printers. In 2023, an FAA-commissioned panel of outside experts warned that the condition of the agency’s facilities and equipment was “elevating system risk to unsustainable levels.” The agency under President Joe Biden had commissioned another group of aviation experts to examine air traffic control in October 2024, but weeks after Trump took office, the group learned it was being disbanded, The Washington Post reported. 

Last May, Duffy said the FAA was speeding up its overhaul of the system under a program called BNATCS, or the Brand New Air Traffic Control System. Congress approved $12.5 billion for the effort, which aims to modernize the telecom network by the end of 2028, before the end of Trump’s term, and 21 months ahead of an earlier September 2030 target.

In September, the Government Accountability Office released its latest report on the overhaul. The FAA was moving at an unprecedented speed, auditors said, but without a reliable lifecycle cost estimate or an integrated master schedule. Instead, auditors counted 11,389 separate project schedules that had not been coordinated, so different programs were booked to visit the same sites repeatedly or in ways that risk “excessive disruptions to air traffic control operations” and could jeopardize the FAA’s “aggressive deployment schedule.” Delays, in turn, could leave controllers reliant on outdated systems that are prone to failure, and “lead to more system outages, ground stops, flight delays, and safety incidents.”

The GAO auditors also found the agency had exempted the effort from nearly all of its standard acquisition rules. Schedule pressure on federal programs can lead teams to skip or compress testing, they warned. “In essence, the FAA is buying delivery speed at the risk of cost uncertainty and potential disruptions,” the GAO wrote.

The incident has also drawn attention to Peraton, the Herndon, Va.-based defense contractor hired last December to manage the broader overhaul, under a contract with a $1.5 billion ceiling. Politico reported in June that one lobbyist—a former Duffy spokesperson who sits on the board of a nonprofit linked to the Transportation Secretary—lobbied for Peraton in the period when it won its FAA contract. (The FAA has said that Duffy played no role in the company’s selection.)

By August, FAA officials were frustrated with Peraton’s performance, according to a September Politico report, citing people familiar with the matter who described slipping schedules and a contractor that was not managing the project. Peraton was “not sophisticated with how the FAA works” and was being asked to sprint from the start, one person told Politico. The same person said the FAA was partly to blame, accusing the agency of blocking Peraton’s efforts to work with its own staff.

As the FAA began its investigation into the cause of the router issues on Saturday, Schiavo told NPR that uncoordinated schedules and a rush to patch the system had made such a failure predictable. “What did the GAO conclude? That it will result in air traffic outages and disruptions. And there we are.”

The FAA and L3Harris take different approaches to scheduling 

The trouble first showed up as interruptions at the FAA’s Indianapolis center, as a surge of data flooded the network’s older routers. A flurry of erratic radar feeds and communication drop-offs with aircraft led officials to order a ground stop. Soon troubleshooters traced the issue to the El Dorado router and to a second one at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas; when both were cut off from the network, the problems stopped. Officials have zeroed in on a feature on the new Juniper routers that broadcast data more widely than necessary. The FAA has since switched the feature off on all of its Juniper routers. The two suspect routers are being tested in Florida with help from Juniper and Cisco engineers, L3Harris and the FBI. 

“Was it a faulty installation? Was it a faulty configuration?” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford asked on Saturday, adding that the agency would have to rethink how it carries out upgrades.

Asked why the work was done on a busy Friday afternoon, Duffy cited the urgency of the upgrades and said the site was far from major flight corridors. But he added: “there will be a reevaluation of when we do this work.” 

The timing contrasts with how L3Harris describes its own method. In an interview published in March, Chris Collings, the L3Harris vice president who runs the business, said the company never switches network segments off. At critical sites with two paths, he said, crews upgrade one path, validate it, then upgrade the other, during low-traffic windows. The network is designed to contain a local fault, so why one remote radio site could disrupt most of the country’s en route centers remains unexplained.

Duffy repeatedly blamed the contractor. “We’re going to hold people accountable,” he said, adding that many contractors “take our money and provide really poor service.” He also told reporters he was “stuck with L3Harris.” 

In a statement, L3Harris said it was supporting the agency’s investigation, and that it “takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

The FAA said that one of its representatives helped an L3Harris technician gain access to an agency site on Friday. The union for FAA technicians, however, said its members had no part in the work. Historically, it said in a statement Saturday, contractors have relied on FAA employees to assess risk and coordinate maintenance, but its “technicians were not involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop.” 

The FAA has acknowledged that its technician workforce is understaffed and released a workforce plan in May 2026 calling for an increase of at least 750 more certified technicians by 2030. “However, little progress has been made on hiring those new technicians,” the union said. 

The FAA and L3Harris did not respond to a set of emailed questions for this story.

A push to shift from L3Harris to AT&T

L3Harris, based in Melbourne, Fla., specializes in defense, but it has run the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure network, known as FTI, since its predecessor Harris Corp. won the contract in 2002. The company says it has already converted 70% of the copper-to-fiber conversion. 

The agency has had warnings about the network for years, including a failure strikingly like Friday’s. On Nov. 19, 2009, an FTI outage hit 129 air traffic facilities. The inspector general concluded that configuration and procedural errors by Harris caused the outage and delayed restoring service. A Harris engineer had put a new router into service in Los Angeles that carried a configuration error. Even after fixes, the inspector general noted, FAA and Harris officials acknowledged a continuing risk of critical outages.

The FAA has since faulted the company publicly. After a September 2025 telecom outage at the Dallas approach-control facility halted flights at both of the city’s major airports for hours, the agency blamed failures in service from local carrier Frontier Communications. It added: “Oversight by L3Harris, an FAA contractor, failed to ensure that redundancies in the system functioned properly.” L3Harris responded that it and the carriers had warned the FAA for years that the circuits needed replacing, but the money never came.

This September, a primary circuit serving the Philadelphia approach-control facility failed, and after L3Harris advised switching to a backup fiber line, which turned out to have been cut by a construction crew in New Jersey. About 9,500 U.S. flights were delayed or canceled. “When it fails, we just don’t have the redundancy” of a modern architecture, Bedford said at the time.

The FAA is already moving to replace FTI. In August, using waiver authority tied to the modernization program, it made a single, undefinitized award to AT&T to lead the FAA Enterprise Network Services program, FTI’s successor. The award started with a $74.3 million task order for what the FAA expects to be a multibillion-dollar contract lasting up to 15 years. In September, Bedford called for an additional $10.5 billion from Congress for the project. On Saturday, Duffy said that Verizon and Lumen were also “ready to go” on the upgrade. Until that transition is done, L3Harris remains the operator, and the contractor converting the FAA’s copper lines.

The FAA network is a small part of a company that has become more central to the administration’s priorities. L3Harris, which reported $21.9 billion in revenue last year, converted a Boeing 747 donated by Qatar into an interim Air Force One this year. It worked against a July 4 deadline that, Democratic senators say, forced it to scale back the usual upgrade package. (The Air Force has said the work would cost less than $400 million; the contract is classified.) 

In January, the Pentagon agreed to invest $1 billion in L3Harris’s missile business, which the company plans to spin off—a rare direct federal stake in a major defense supplier. And in July, the Space Force awarded L3Harris up to $955 million to build 18 missile-defense satellites for the Golden Dome shield, bringing its orders for U.S. missile-tracking and defense satellites to at least 70. L3Harris shares fell tk percent on Monday, the first trading day after the ground stop, and are down [tk] percent this year after peaking in early March.

What the GAO found about the FAA upgrade

The GAO’s September report examined the FAA’s upgrade. Of the $12.5 billion Congress allocated, $9 billion is for systems modernization. Telecommunications is one of 13 programs in the overhaul’s first phase: replacing 5,170 copper lines with fiber and moving nearly 30,000 services to Internet Protocol. GAO figures show the program’s estimated cost rising from about $4.75 billion to about $5.91 billion. 

The auditors’ main findings:

  • There’s no reliable cost estimate. In June the FAA put phase one’s systems work at $10.6 billion, but officials could not produce the analysis behind the figure, telling auditors it would take a tremendous effort to find. The estimate omits government costs, most operating and maintenance costs and all of phase two. The FAA says it needs another $10.8 billion.
  • There’s no master schedule. Peraton, the prime systems integrator, delivered a preliminary integrated master schedule in April. As of May, though, the 11,389 project schedules had not been integrated, which risked inefficiencies and conflicts with airport operations. Officials said loading them all into their scheduling tool “would not be useful or helpful.” The FAA planned to use an artificial intelligence tool to flag conflicts, but as of May it was still being tested and rules for using it had not been set.
  • Rules were waived. In August 2025, Bedford issued a blanket waiver exempting the program from nearly all of the FAA’s acquisition management requirements, including the one that would require a lifecycle cost estimate. The GAO called that a key reason no such estimate exists.

The Transportation Department partly agreed with the GAO’s two recommendations: build a reliable lifecycle cost estimate and a detailed integrated master schedule. In its reply, the department said 12 of 13 workstreams, covering over 95 percent of project tasks, were on plan as of July. According to the FAA’s public Modern Skies dashboard, 11 out of 12 programs are at or ahead of plan. The exception is the replacement of analog protocol converters, devices that turn analog signals into digital ones, which stands at 8 percent complete, with just 45 of 69 planned sites completed in the most recent month recorded. 

The FAA has said it will answer the GAO’s September recommendations in detail within 180 days of the report, a deadline that falls in March.

Whose upgrade was it?

Bedford tried to separate Friday’s failure from the modernization program. “We’re conflating modernization with this upgrade at this particular facility. We spend $1 billion a year maintaining and sustaining the existing 1980s [legacy] telco network,” Bedford said. “This is not part of the Peraton-FAA $12.5 billion modernization effort.”

That contrasts with the GAO’s account, which lists the copper-to-fiber program as part of phase one of the modernization. And according to the GAO, existing program contracts were modified to give Peraton authority to manage the other contractors on the FAA’s behalf. “Peraton, think of them as an extension of me,” Bedford said in April. 

Peraton was seen as an underdog for the FAA job, in part because it had little prior experience working with the agency. The company itself grew out of the government IT services unit of Harris Corp., L3Harris’ predecessor, which private equity firm Veritas Capital bought and rebranded as Peraton in 2017. 

Before the FAA award, agency staff had rated the company a high risk for financial instability in an October 2025 presentation to Duffy, Bloomberg reported in September. When agency staff evaluated the bids last year, they graded Peraton and Parsons, which bid alongside IBM, on four technical criteria, according to the presentation. Parsons rated better on three and the same on the fourth. Staff wrote that Peraton’s answers to use cases and direct questions “often focused on matters irrelevant to the discussion topic.”

Peraton scored better on past performance, helped by a positive review from NASA. The FAA told Bloomberg that strong ratings from Peraton’s customers, including NASA, were among its reasons for the choice, along with what it called the company’s significant telecommunications experience. The presentation also showed that Peraton sought a higher award fee than Parsons; it is unclear whether that changed later in the process.

Politico reported in June that a former Duffy spokesperson, Mark Bednar, who now sits on the board of the nonprofit that paid for Duffy’s road-trip video series, Great American Road Trip Inc., had lobbied for Peraton in the period when it won its FAA contract. At a December 2025 congressional hearing, Bedford said career FAA staff ran the selection without interference from Duffy or Trump. The recommendation went from Bedford to Duffy and then to the president, he said, and Trump demanded a $200 million cut in the fee.

Concerns about Peraton’s work have since dogged the program. A few months ago, the FAA called Peraton in and told it to improve its performance, and the company blamed the agency in return, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. The FAA has said it hasn’t penalized Peraton or issued the company a formal warning about poor performance.

A Peraton spokesperson told Bloomberg in August that the program is on track. But the company said the schedule is among the largest and most complex in government history, covering 330,000 independent projects and half a million dependencies. Peraton did not respond to an inquiry for this story. 

Duffy used the outage to renew and even scale up his call for Congress to fund the larger telecom modernization effort, arguing the $12.5 billion already allocated is not enough. For weeks, he has been calling for $30 billion in additional funds—with only about $10 billion of that request specifically for air traffic modernization—but during the outage he raised the demand to $50 billion. Bedford said the FAA would review its upgrade protocols. Neither said whether copper-to-fiber cutovers would be paused while investigators work out why and how one router could halt the country’s air traffic.

Representative James Walkinshaw (D-Va.), a member of the House Oversight Committee, said on Saturday that Duffy must be questioned by Congress, including about why the work was being conducted “on a busy travel day, as opposed to in the middle of the night where a disruption wouldn’t have been so damaging because they’re rushing.”

#10327. How to Use Developer Time Tracking Data to Improve Sprint Planning and Estimates

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sprint estimates usually fail because development teams heavily rely on memory and assumptions instead of evidence. They assume similar tasks will take the same amount of time. Based on these half-baked assumptions, most managers plan around ideal sprint working hours. The backlog then fills with commitments that look realistic on paper but often end up delayed.

Actual development rarely follows that plan. There are always unexpected bugs and task dependencies that consume more time than teams account for in their estimates. Even the buffer time set aside for unexpected work may not be enough. This causes tasks to take longer than expected and pushes sprint commitments behind schedule.

Developer time tracking helps teams make better estimates with historical data. It shows how long previous tasks actually took, which provides managers with an evidence-based reference when they are planning similar work.

Reviewing this data before committing to a sprint scope turns estimation from guesswork into an evidence-based process.

Historical time data offers deeper insights, depending on how you collect and analyze it. Most importantly, it explains why planned work took longer than expected.

Before sprint planning, the following records should be reviewed.

Completed task duration: Check the time spent on finished tasks. Managers should compare similar work to understand typical development effort.

Actual versus estimated hours: Management should observe and identify differences between planned and recorded hours. If there are repeated delays, to some extent, it indicates inaccurate estimates.

Carryover work: Review unfinished tasks from previous sprints. Determine whether poor estimates or external delays caused the spillover..

Interruptions: Measure time spent on urgent requests and production issues. These activities reduce the development capacity that you had planned earlier.

Meetings and ceremonies: Review the time being spent on planning sessions and sprint reviews.

Bug-fix time: Examine hours spent resolving defects. You can also compare it to the time for developing new features.

Blocked tasks: Managers should account for the tasks delayed by missing approvals or technical dependencies.

Capacity differences: Compare team availability across sprints. Include leave and staffing changes in that time as well.

These records provide the most value when reviewed together. For example, a task may finish three days late even if the development work stayed within its estimated hours. The actual issue could be an external dependency.

Teams should understand these differences before using historical data to estimate future work.

Historical records provide a useful starting point for estimating new tasks. However, teams must interpret the data rather than simply copy previous estimates.

The following approaches can improve estimation accuracy.

The first step is to consider completed tasks that resemble upcoming work. Managers should compare their requirements and technical complexity. Moreover, the development environment should be considered.

For example, suppose a team needs to estimate a new API integration. Three previous integrations required 12, 15, and 18 hours of active work.

The average is 15 hours. This gives developers a reference point for the new estimate.

However, the average doesn't tell the entire story. The new integration may involve unfamiliar authentication methods or more complicated testing.

Review the reasons behind differences in previous task durations. Check whether developers encountered unexpected bugs or unclear requirements.

As a project manager, I'd consider these details before estimating for the next project. In my experience, they provide more context than an average alone.

Inaccurate estimates can happen; it doesn’t mean that there is a definite planning problem. However, repeated overruns across similar tasks may reveal an underlying issue.

Research suggests the pattern is widespread. A review of software estimation surveys reports that 60–80% of software projects encounter effort overruns, with the average overrun falling between 30% and 40%.

Start by calculating the difference between estimated and actual effort. Here is the formula for it.

Estimation variance (%) = [(Actual hours − Estimated hours) ÷ Estimated hours] × 100

Suppose a task was estimated at 10 hours but needed 14 hours. The actual effort exceeded the estimate by 40%.

You can compare the results across similar tasks.

For example, database migrations may repeatedly require more time than expected. This means that the team might be overlooking data validation or additional testing. Once the cause is clear, adjust future estimates accordingly.

Avoid increasing every estimate by the same percentage. Different types of work involve different risks. Teams can also break large tasks into smaller parts. This makes hidden development activities easier to identify.

The aim is to correct recurring estimation errors without unnecessarily increasing the entire sprint backlog.

Task duration doesn't always reflect the hours spent developing a feature.

A study of developer workdays by Meyer and colleagues, which tracked 2,197 hours of activity across 20 developers, found that coding accounted for around 21% of the typical day. Collaborative work such as meetings and email took up roughly 24%.

Consider a developer who starts a feature on Monday and finishes it on Wednesday. The task took three days to complete. This is pretty straightforward, and the estimation could be based on it; however, the developer may have spent several hours in meetings. Other than that, urgent support requests could also have consumed additional time.

The actual development effort could be much lower than three full working days. This distinction matters during estimation.

Teams should record focused development time separately from interruptions. They should also track waiting periods caused by blocked tasks. A more appropriate approach would be to use active development hours to estimate similar future work. They should also account for recurring interruptions when calculating sprint capacity.

For example, a task may regularly wait for security approval. Adding more development hours to its estimate won't resolve that delay.

Instead, the team should recognize the dependency and consider its effect on delivery.

If managers are able to separate these activities, it will help create better estimates without confusing effort with elapsed time.

A precise estimate can create false confidence when a task involves substantial uncertainty.

Suppose similar tasks previously required between 12 and 20 hours. If you estimate the next task at exactly 14 hours, it will overlook important differences.

A range of 12–20 hours provides a clearer picture of the possible effort. Developers can then discuss what might push the task toward either end of the range.

For example, the lower estimate can be directly applied to integration, and the upper estimate might be considered for unfamiliar code or additional testing.

In such scenarios, if the requirements stay unclear, consider a short technical investigation before finalizing the estimate. This can help identify dependencies and reduce uncertainty.

However, estimate ranges should still support practical planning decisions. Teams need to determine how much capacity to reserve for the work.

Choose a planning assumption that reflects the task's risk and available capacity.

As developers learn more about the task, they can refine the estimate.

Historical time data should affect how much work a team accepts during sprint planning. Better estimates offer little value if teams continue making unrealistic commitments.

If several sprints end with unfinished tasks, it is best that you first review why the team missed its commitments in the first place. Once you have identified the causes, use those findings to reduce the next sprint's scope.

Teams should prioritize work that supports the sprint goal. Moreover, avoid adding extra tasks just because they appear manageable during planning.

Production incidents and urgent requests can disrupt planned development. To get more reliable estimations, review how much time these activities consumed in previous sprints. Then reserve an appropriate amount of capacity.

Historical estimates become less reliable in case unfamiliar technology or additional dependencies are involved. It is best to break complex tasks into smaller components where possible. This helps developers assess the work more accurately.

Nominal capacity represents scheduled working hours, whereas actual capacity reflects the time available after accounting for other commitments.

The Scrum Guide identifies previous performance and upcoming capacity as important inputs to sprint forecasting.

When you are selecting backlog items, consider both. Additionally, avoid committing every available hour or deducting the same interruption twice.

Historical time data is useful for sprint planning. Most development teams already use project management tools that include basic time tracking features.

However, these tools don't always break down how developers spend their working hours. For clearer time data, a feature-specific time tracker is more useful because it provides more details about tasks and workloads.

TimeBee is one such developer time tracking tool I've used. It tracks working hours and time spent on projects and tasks. It also provides attendance records and workforce activity reports.

With this data, teams can review how much time previous tasks required. For example, developers can record hours spent building a feature. They can also track debugging and revisions separately. Later, managers can compare these records with the original estimates. This helps them plan similar work more accurately.

TimeBee also tracks website and application activity. These reports can help teams understand how working hours are distributed.

However, not all activities reflect actual development effort. Sometimes a developer just spends time reviewing documentation or discussing technical problems. Such work may not always appear in TimeBee as active computer use.

Apart from that, attendance, leave, and overtime records from TimeBee can help managers calculate sprint capacity. They can review developer availability before deciding how much work to include in the next sprint.

One thing to remember is that developer time tracking should help teams understand workload patterns. It shouldn't be used to monitor every minute of a developer's day. Management should be careful that the aim is to improve estimates and make more realistic sprint commitments.

Sprint retrospectives should include a review of how the planning is going. If you have made a plan, it doesn’t mean you cannot make changes to it. During sprints, keep comparing original estimates with actual task hours. Track your unfinished work for recurring delays.

Ask developers what caused significant differences. Some tasks may have required additional testing. Others may have been delayed by dependencies. Select one specific improvement for the next sprint.

Not every estimation difference indicates a planning failure. Unexpected technical challenges are part of software development.

The objective is to improve forecasts over time rather than eliminate every variance.

Historical time data provides a more stable foundation for sprint planning. Developer time tracking helps teams understand what is actually happening within the sprint rather than creating unnecessary pressure for them.

Other than that, the data also reveals how interruptions affect available development hours.

However, time data should guide planning rather than dictate it.

1. What is the difference between sprint velocity and time-based capacity planning?

Sprint velocity measures how much work a team has completed during a sprint. It is usually measured in story points. Contrary to this, time-based capacity planning calculates the hours available for planned work. It accounts for meetings and other responsibilities.

Velocity helps predict future delivery based on past performance. Capacity planning shows whether the team has enough time to meet its commitments.

2. Which time tracking metrics are most useful for improving Agile sprint forecasts? The most useful metrics include estimated versus actual hours, task completion time, and unplanned work.

Bug-fix time, rework, and blocked tasks also provide valuable insights. Teams should also review available capacity across previous sprints.

These metrics help sort out recurring delays and estimation errors. They allow teams to forecast workloads more accurately and make realistic sprint commitments.

**3. How can development teams improve estimates when historical time tracking data is incomplete? **

Teams can start with available task records and completed sprint backlogs. Developer feedback can help fill information gaps. Similar tasks from previous projects may also provide useful estimates.

When data is limited, teams should use estimate ranges instead of fixed hours. Consistent time tracking in future sprints will gradually provide more reliable planning data.

4. How can time tracking data help balance workloads across developers during sprint planning?

Time tracking data shows how much time developers spend on assigned tasks and other responsibilities. Managers can review these records to identify uneven workloads. They can then distribute upcoming tasks based on available capacity.

Technical expertise and task complexity should also influence assignments. This helps prevent over commitment and supports a more balanced workload across the development team.

Safety systems depending on a single service could lead to catastrophic results if that service fails.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fifteen guests at a hotel in Germany suffered from chlorine gas poisoning because of the recent Microsoft cloud services outage. The establishment had a “maintenance safety system” for its sauna area that relied on sending emails to warn the operators if the chlorine level in the area was too high. Unfortunately, the service disruption meant that the system's messages could not be sent, leading to increased levels that precipitated human injuries, writes Notebookcheck. German emergency services had to deploy 40 first responders to the site, with local media reporting that four victims were taken to the hospital for treatment, with one remaining for further observation.

The tech giant experienced a global outage affecting Outlook and other services from November 12 to 14, which led some Japanese workers to dust off their fax machines to keep their business running. Although this Microsoft outage wasn’t as large as the CrowdStrike fiasco in 2024, which led to a massive service disruption to a good number of corporate computer systems and sent shockwaves across the world, this incident has caused injuries and could’ve even led to something more catastrophic if the issue wasn’t caught earlier.

This is one of the issues that institutions must consider when using online services or the Internet of Things to automate systems, especially those that are crucial for safety. Architects of such systems should always have a physical or analog backup that will continue operating even if everything goes offline. More importantly, their people should know that they exist and be familiar with how they work. Alternatively, businesses can host their own servers, build their own automations, and run everything locally, although this would require a bit more involvement in building and programming the entire system. And there could be local infrastructure impacting issues like power cuts, still.

Aside from that, the Microsoft outage also highlights the corporate world’s increasing reliance on a few big tech companies. While tech giants like Microsoft, Google, and AWS have the advantage of economies of scale, allowing them to offer their services reliably and more affordably compared to smaller rivals or an in-house deployment, it also means that if they go down, they affect millions of businesses that rely on them and cause economic activity to grind to a halt.

#10324. Google Wallet rolling out digital Google Home keys with supported locks on Android

Google Wallet for Android is rolling out support for digital home keys if you have a compatible smart lock in Google Home.

After adding a home key to Google Wallet, you can Tap to Unlock with your phone. This leverages NFC and “works even when your phone screen is locked” by default. However, you can adjust verification settings in the Google Wallet app to require screen lock or biometric authentication. This requires Android 9+.

There’s also support for Unlock on Approach with an Aliro Ultra Wideband (UWB)-compatible Android phone (see below) and an Aliro UWB-compatible lock. Wear OS watches are not supported at launch.

Behind the scenes, the digital key is linked to the Google Home app rather than a single lock. As such, “each of your compatible Aliro locks will work with a single key in your Google Wallet.” Keys are added to Google Wallet using the Home app, which will prompt you to save after setup. You can also go to Home settings > Google Wallet key.

Crazy to me that Google's own smart lock with Yale doesn't have this functionality. Seems like a huge miss for them to not be forward looking with their own hardware here.

Afterward, your key “automatically syncs across compatible Android phones signed into your Google Wallet account.”

The card in Google Wallet features a simple Google Home logo with your home’s name in the top-right corner.

The following locks are supported at launch: Aqara u400 (UWB and NFC), Schlage Sense Pro (NFC at launch and UWB to follow), and Nuki Keypad 2 NFC. Support for more models is coming.

Additionally, support is rolling out first to the Google Home Public Preview before coming to all users “over the coming weeks.”

Die shots were collated from masters such as Pauli Rautakorpi, ZeptoBars, John McMaster, and Fritzchens Fritz.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A CPU enthusiast has put together an eye-popping visual database containing crystal-clear, detailed die shots of 357 legendary and some lesser-known processors. At sheets.works/data-viz/cpu-dies, you will find a sortable, searchable, and filterable gallery featuring the outstanding, freely shared die shots from the likes of Pauli Rautakorpi, ZeptoBars, John McMaster, and Fritzchens Fritz. Find one or two of your favorites, and peer into the details to enjoy a nostalgic technological trip down memory lane. That’s what I did.

The unnamed collator of this gallery might not have contributed any die shots, but has still done an admirable job putting these macrographs and micrographs together in this way. Beneath a brief introduction that credits the skilled photographers who share these images for free, you can glide through the 357-photo collection.

By default, the die shot gallery gives you the gallery view, ordered by the oldest silicon first. Those browsing the gallery can instantly switch to a True Scale gallery view, too, which provides some physical sizing context. The next view option for the gallery is a table, where you can see processor maker, year, die dimensions, and photo license at a glance, but it sacrifices visual impact by showing just tiny thumbnails.

Navigating the gallery is also quick and intuitive thanks to a built-in search function. Using this, it was easy to display only 486 CPUs, for example. For your information, there are 17 486 CPU variants in this gallery with samples produced by AMD, Cyrix, IBM, TI, UMC, VLSI, and Intel of course. You can click any of the thumbnails to jump to a larger view with notes of the design, as well as photographer details/credits. Though that click zooms in the image considerably, I found that a right-click – open image in new tab - was needed to enjoy the die shot’s full visual splendor.

It would be great to see the database/gallery maintained with the latest shareable die shots from the various contributors. Also, it could be improved by fully populating details such as the die area, which is not always present. Some more searchable and sortable fields, such as transistor count, might also make this resource more satisfying.

For my personal nostalgia, I enjoyed seeing CPUs like the Motorola 68000 and the AMD Athlon XP up close. Surprisingly, some eras, including the Intel Ivy Bridge and Haswell generations, seemed underrepresented, though.

#10320. The Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 would be my perfect Steam tablet if it didn’t cost $900

For every Android-powered slate I’ve used, only Nvidia’s Shield Tablet really stands out in my memory. Part of the company’s occasional (and all-but-dead) dip into hardware products, the Shield Tablet — and its revitalized K1 follow-up, which I also owned through a recall program on the original — carried me through the back half of college, frequently keeping my Chromebook in my backpack in lieu of a mini Bluetooth keyboard or the Shield Tablet’s built-in stylus. Its front-firing speakers made it great for movie-watching, and while I’m not much of a mobile gamer, I did find it to be a great device for emulation, especially when paired with an external controller.

Even if Nvidia hadn’t abandoned the hardware game at the end of the last decade, it’s found new and much more destructive ways to make piles of cash at the expense of your easy access to RAM. And considering the market for Android tablets in general, it’s not all too surprising to see very few companies trying to make headway into offering a miniature, gaming-focused tablet that can easily be thrown in a backpack. Lenovo, however, has managed to fill its spot quite well. 9to5Google’s own Ben Schoon found himself smitten with the Gen 3 model nearly two years ago, and now, its Gen 5 successor has found its way into my nostalgic hands.

But expectations around mobile experiences have come a long way since 2016. Whether the Legion Tab Gen 5 can win over your heart really depends on your patience with some old-school Android jank — and whether your wallet can withstand an exceptionally-high asking price. Still, with recent advancements in PC emulation, it’s hard to say Lenovo isn’t onto something.

Considering the decade between their respective releases, I’m actually quite surprised just how much this tablet reminds me of the original Shield Tablet. Its 8.8-inch 16:10 LCD panel combined with a boxy matte-black design and a near-identical weight meant that I immediately felt at home holding this thing in my hands. You lose out on a couple of clutch features — most notably the built-in stylus — but largely speaking, this feels like the correct size and shape for a miniature gaming tablet.

Still, it’s not all perfect. Take, for example, the completely unnecessary camera bump that prevents this slate from properly laying flat on a desk. No one is buying this thing to use the camera, and judging by my very limited experience trying it out, I’m fairly confident whatever potato sensor is shoved in here would fit fine flush with the chassis. I’m pretty fed up with OEMs leaning on camera bumps to make any device look or feel more premium than it actually is, and that goes double quadruple for tablets like this.

Just like its predecessor, this thing still picks up smudges and fingerprints at an unreasonable level, its matte-black finish unable to hide anything. 360 grams is also a little heavier than I’d expect for a slate of this size, though to be fair, it’s much more noticeable in portrait than landscape. Holding the tablet with two hands to watch a movie or make my way through another round of Balatro made its top-heaviness much less noticeable.

This display is sharp and fast — with one minor caveat — and reasonably bright in all circumstances except direct sunlight thanks to its 600 nits of brightness (and 800 in HBM). Really, it’s the LCD of it all that gets me here; this thing is nearly $1,000, and the lack of OLED alone makes it difficult to recommend at this price. It’s not an outright bad panel, but I found its contrast levels to be pretty lacking, with most blacks only ever showing up as dark grays on-screen.

Oh, and that caveat: On two different occasions, I caught the tablet stuck in 60Hz mode, regardless of what refresh rate option I selected in settings. Switching back and forth between modes a few times eventually unstuck it, but it’s definitely a bug worth being aware of.

I think I’d feel a lot better about recommending this to someone looking for a content consumption device if this screen looked a little more premium. Your mileage may vary though — if you can get your hands on a demo unit before buying one, if only to see the display, I’d recommend it. For everyone else, this price tag might have you waiting for the OLED panel rumored to be arriving on next year’s successor.

At $900 — or potentially more, considering this tablet actually launched at $850 — the Legion Tablet’s hardware leaves something to be desired. Biometrics are the most obvious weak spot; camera-based face unlock is the only biometric option provided here, without a fingerprint scanner in sight. I wouldn’t blame some if they saw this as a dealbreaker, because even if you’re willing to put up with the security concerns that a basic front-facing camera brings to the table, I can promise you you’ll be typing the code in all the time. Whether you’re trying to unlock in a darker environment or it’s just been four hours since you last unlocked the slate, make sure you have your pin memorized.

If you’re primarily buying this as a content consumption machine, I think you’ll mostly have a great time. Lenovo built stereo sound into this slate, but did so in one of the smartest ways I’ve ever seen, ensuring all speakers are located to the right side along the bottom and top of the device. This might sound a little unbalanced in portrait mode, but in landscape, it guarantees you’re never actually covering up the speakers while holding the slate in your hands, something practically every other equivalent tablet is guilty of. No headphone jack here, unfortunately, something I would’ve liked to have seen on a gaming-focused device.

I find battery life genuinely difficult to judge on tablets, especially if you don’t pick it up every single hour of every single day, but I’ve been impressed overall with the Legion Tab’s longevity. Some weekend YouTube binge watching sessions at relatively high brightness settings left me with plenty of juice in the tank, and its standby time between sessions has been excellent. Obviously, if you’re really pushing your graphical limits on this thing — or if you’re emulating non-native software through something like DroidDeck — you’re going to see a bit of a dip, but combined with fast charging and two USB-C ports for both portrait and landscape access, battery life gets a big thumbs-up from me.

Lenovo’s packed a couple of accessories in the box with this thing, but I wouldn’t get too excited. While it’s nice to see a 68W charger included for those aforementioned fast top-offs, the included folio case is just awful. Not only does the triangle-shaped flap barely stick together to form a proper stand, but one of the corners of my case was loose enough to frequently flex back and forth. Holding the tablet while wrapped in its case just felt bad, in the way that so many bundled cases often feel, and a quick look at Amazon shows that basically no recognizable brand — or unrecognizable, for that matter — has stepped up to offer something better.

The Legion Tablet also includes a screen protector in the box, if that’s how you roll.

Unsurprisingly, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 in here can handle effectively anything you dare to throw at it. While my mobile games might be limited to more casual, indie fare like Balatro — and, by the by, if you’re still enjoying Balatro a couple of years later, the size and shape of this device makes it perfect — graphically-intense games played fine. Asphalt Legends or the HoYoverse games might not be my cup of tea, but they perform excellently on this device, and compared to the 12-inch tablets companies like Samsung and Amazon have become obsessed with, the display size here actually feels perfect.

We definitely have to talk about emulation, though, because it’s increasingly becoming the main focus of mobile gamers everywhere, and this feels like a tablet perfectly designed for something like DroidDeck. Getting Steam emulation — complete with the Deck’s usual Big Picture mode UI — available as an application on the Legion Tab Gen 5 takes all of two minutes and a handful of taps on your display, and I have to say, I’m pretty shocked at just how impressive the overall experience is right now.

DroidDeck gave me the option to bring my mini gaming tablet experience full-circle. While my Steam library has no shortage of games I think could run without stressing this slate, I wanted to push the envelope a little bit. Persona 3 Reload felt like as good a candidate as any: a modern title that doesn’t necessarily require quick response times and fits virtual controls quite nicely. Plus, most of my gaming time on Nvidia’s tablet a decade ago was spent working through Persona 3 Portable; like poetry, it rhymes. I installed the game, ran it on the Legion Tab, and to my surprise and delight, it was absolutely in a playable state.

Now, there are some caveats here. I did drop the game’s graphics preset to low, and even still, there were some occasional hiccups while running around an early dungeon. The game’s initial intros and disclaimers actually gave the impression the title wouldn’t run at all, but I was able to sneak up on a shadow, use a slash attack to begin the battle — basically the only thing in P3R that remotely requires accurate timing — and issue commands to my player character and party mates.

Obviously, your experience emulating Steam titles on the Legion Tab will vary on what you want to play, and with such wide variables between experiences, I probably wouldn’t push most gamers to run out and pick one up right away. It might be early days for DroidDeck, but considering how we’ve already seen it progress, I wouldn’t be surprised to see some buyers picking this up as a Valve-esque take on a gaming tablet.

With all of that power under the hood, though, it’s Lenovo’s take on Android that leaves a lot to be desired. It’s not just that this feels like a rough-and-ready take on AOSP, an unrefined package that would feel more in line with devices from a decade ago, though, yes, that’s half the struggle here. But at its worst, the Legion Tab Gen 5 simply feels unoptimized in daily use.

Scrolling through web pages or various apps often felt sluggish and heavy, like the UI elements on screen never actually match the movement of my finger, and it’s unclear how much of that was due to the refresh rate bug I described above. Auto-rotate was both super finnicky and super sluggish, alternating back and forth between one state or the other, and the auto-rotate button that pops up when it’s disabled would frequently fail to appear. Occasionally, I’d run into app issues, such as choppy playback on a 1440p YouTube video that got so bad — regardless of what resolution I selected — that I had to fully force close the app in settings to fix it. Even getting the slate to reliably wake up (or not wake up) when picking it up was annoying, as it’s simultaneously sensitive enough to frequently turn on when I don’t want it to, or to stay asleep when I’m trying to unlock it. Inevitably, I turned that setting off.

You might think that shelling out $900 for an Android tablet would buy you an out from pre-installed bloatware; you’d be wrong. During setup, the Legion Tab attempts to install a whole host of apps and games, including Perplexity, TikTok, Temu, several match-three games that I’ve truly never heard of, and no less than two mahjong and solitaire titles each. In fact, there might actually be three solitaire titles depending on what “Jigsawcard Solitaire Puzzle” is, but I unchecked all of these apps during setup and didn’t deem the title worthy of bothering to check.

While Lenovo has been trying to improve its software update policies on some recent devices, this slate isn’t among that group. To my knowledge, there is no official update schedule for this device, but based on past performance, I’d expect somewhere around 2 OS upgrades and 4 years of security patches, give or take.

I would’ve loved nothing more than to recommend this year’s Legion Tab to small tablet fans and gamers everywhere, but when this thing is $200 more than Apple’s latest iPad Mini — which in and of itself is absolutely overpriced — and $100 more than the base OLED Steam Deck post-price hike, I just have a hard time telling anyone to buy it. Really, its Steam performance was one of the few areas that made me feel truly excited by this thing, but it’s simply too unpredictable an experience at this point (and price) for me to recommend.

Even setting aside the price, there’s simply too much here that feels unfinished or rough around the edges for my liking. A handful of bug fixes and a couple of additional optimization passes could fix a lot of my more minor quibbles, but despite what I just said, you can only ignore the $900 price tag for so long before it bites you in the ass.

We have seen a post-iPad Mini discount bringing this slate to an Apple-matching $700 ahead of the holidays, but even that price is $150 more than its predecessor was at launch without a whole lot to show for it. If you’re looking for a gamer-friendly tiny tablet, I do think Legion is a brand worth keeping your eye on, especially as DroidDeck and other Steam emulation apps continue to evolve. But at this point — and for this price — your best bet is waiting for whatever model follows this one. It might still be stupid expensive, but at least you’ll be getting OLED.

A decade ago, Nvidia’s Shield Tablet felt like a no-brainer addition to my everyday carry. But in this economy, gamers and tablet fans alike are simply better off dropping $900 elsewhere.

#10318. How to Improve Email Deliverability Rates

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.
